#29792. Tech Report: 12 terms that show how the inflation rate is built and what it leaves out

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4134 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 12 terms that show how the inflation rate is built and what it leaves out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Baskets, price indexes, core measures and more: 12 terms from the Cleveland Fed explain how the inflation rate is built.
  • In a recent development, most people look up the inflation rate and accept it as a plain fact about the economy.
  • In a recent development, nobody observes the inflation rate directly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Baskets, price indexes, core measures and more: 12 terms from the Cleveland Fed explain how the inflation rate is built.

In a recent development, most people look up the inflation rate and accept it as a plain fact about the economy. That habit matters more now that price growth has picked up. Consumer prices rose 2.9% from December 2023 to December 2024, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and BLS reports that the 12-month increase reached 3.8% by April 2026. Faster price growth takes more out of household budgets. When a number has that much effect on people's money, how it is made becomes the reader's business. Each term in the vocabulary of inflation marks a point where someone chose what to count, what to compare or what to ignore.

In a recent development, nobody observes the inflation rate directly. It is the change between price readings taken at two points in time, such as a month, a quarter or a year apart, and without both readings there is no rate. A lapse in federal appropriations left October 2025 without survey data, and BLS reports that 12-month changes for most series went unpublished in October 2026. The need for a second reading applies to every other choice behind the number. A different mix of goods, a different span of time or a different set of excluded items can change the headline even when no price has changed. A reader who knows where those choices sit can tell a real shift in the cost of living from a result of the method.

The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland set out to explain how inflation is gauged and to define the terms related to it, from the basket of goods behind every price index to median CPI, deflation and stagflation. Those terms fall into three groups. Some describe how the inflation number is built, and some describe how economists separate a lasting trend from a passing jolt. Others name extreme conditions, such as prices that rise out of control or fall for a long stretch. The value for a reader lies in knowing which question each term answers. With that knowledge, the next inflation headline can be read for what it actually says and for what it leaves out.

Sources indicate that inflation is measured from a chosen shopping list rather than from every price in the economy, so every reading carries the judgments built into that list. Measurement begins with a representative set of household purchases whose prices statisticians collect, and statisticians rebuild that set as spending habits change. The basket tries to capture what a typical household buys and also how much of each item it buys, and that quantity is an estimate. "The basket does not contain every good or service but is meant to be a good representation of both the types of items and the quantities of items that households typically consume," the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland stated. When statisticians revision that estimate of typical spending, the inflation reading can change even if no price tag does.

It has been revealed that the weights shape the answer as well as the prices do, though in January 2026 the effect on the headline was small. Each item counts in the basket at its quantity times its price, and statisticians add those values across all items. BLS reports that the monthly increase in consumer prices for January 2026 was 0.37% under the latest weights and 0.40% under the weights from 2023, using the same prices. Anyone who follows the headline can take some comfort from that, because refreshing the basket left the overall picture of the month intact. That total is an average across categories with very different results, and some of those categories shifted far more.

Thousands of separate price tags say nothing about inflation until statisticians combine them into one figure that people can compare over time. A price index sets what the whole basket costs today against what it cost in a base period, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and every inflation figure starts from that comparison. The result depends on a choice about whose purchases count. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports that its headline consumer price index follows how much prices move for shoppers in urban areas, averaged across all of them. The figure is precise about that average urban shopper and uncertain about any one family's costs.

Recent findings suggest that averaging is the purpose of an index, and it is also the reason large price shocks can sit unnoticed inside a calm headline. Across all items, the index rose 3.7% over the 12 months through September 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a moderate pace for a full year. Over the same year, gasoline cost 34.2% more. The headline blends gasoline with everything else households buy, so one steep increase moved the total far less than it moved the cost of filling a tank. A gap between the headline and particular purchases is therefore built into how an index works. A household that drives a lot faced a much steeper increase than the one reported in the news.

Anyone measuring inflation first has to decide how far back to compare, and the same prices give a different rate depending on that decision. Year to year is one common span, and inflation can also be measured over others such as quarter to quarter or month to month, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. No single span is the correct one, so a headline that reports "the" inflation rate gives readers one window among several. The yearly rate compares each month with the same month a year earlier. It shows how far prices moved over a full year but not the path they took in between, and a headline can mislead in that gap.

In a recent development, A violent swing in a single category can account for much of a sharp move in the yearly rate, because the overall rate blends every category in the basket. In July 2008, energy cost 29.3% more than a year earlier, according to BLS. Anyone checking the headline that month saw all items 5.6% pricier than a year before, which looked like a serious squeeze on household budgets. By December 2008, the same yearly comparison demonstrated energy 21.3% cheaper than a year earlier. In about one season, a steep annual rise in energy had turned into a steep annual fall. When the yearly rate jumps or plunges, a reader should ask whether one volatile category accounts for the move before concluding that prices across the board have changed course.

Industry observers note that the overall inflation rate cannot tell a short-lived increase in prices from one that will last, and underlying inflation is the measure built to separate the two. Policymakers use it to set aside temporary noise and see the price growth that persists. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland defines it as the price growth that would be left if brief jolts in the data could be stripped away. That condition makes underlying inflation an estimate rather than a direct reading. It also makes it another choice in how the number is built, because someone has to decide which price effects are short-lived and which will last.

In a recent development, underlying inflation tracks a trend over the medium run, a span of several years, and not the bill a shopper pays this month. A household can pay far more for a single item this month while underlying inflation barely changes, and both readings are accurate because each answers a different question. When something a household buys becomes sharply more expensive, the useful question is whether the increase is temporary or part of a lasting trend. Only the lasting kind is meant to appear in the underlying rate.

It has been revealed that once the inflation number has been built and cleaned up, people want to know where it is headed, and the most familiar answer comes from the job market rather than from prices. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that the Phillips curve links inflation and unemployment inversely, though other drivers can loosen the connection. In plain terms, price growth tends to be weaker when more people are out of work, and the idea carries that caveat from the start. It is named for the economist A. W. Phillips, which makes it an established economic concept that a reader can look up, not a market slogan. The relationship Phillips first described concerned wages, and later work extended it to price inflation. That means the jobs-to-prices link people cite today goes one step beyond what was first observed.

Industry observers note that falling prices look like good news to a shopper, but a lasting drop in prices is a warning about the economy. A price level that falls for a long stretch can lead people to cut back on what they buy, and that pullback can set off a cycle in which conditions keep getting worse, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. Consumer spending supports businesses and the jobs they provide. A broad, sustained slide in prices therefore points to an economy in trouble rather than a season of bargains.

According to recent reports, the danger of deflation is that it builds on itself instead of arriving as a single shock. Economists call this process a "deflationary spiral." Once prices start to fall, the decline can continue instead of settling at a latest, lower level. The risk for a household lies in where that pattern leads over months and years, not in any single price tag that has dropped.

In a recent development, stagflation is the extreme in which households face fast-rising prices, a weak economy and scarce work at the same time. It is high inflation alongside a weak economy and rising unemployment, the combination that the Phillips curve leads people to expect will not occur. Americans have lived through a severe version of it. Consumer price inflation was above 10% during the recessions of 1973–1975 and 1980, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. At that pace, the everyday purchases in a household's basket became sharply more expensive within a single year. Those double-digit increases took place during recessions, not booms, and that timing is what separates stagflation from ordinary overheating.

Industry observers note that the usual trade-off suggests that households hit by a weak job market would at least find some relief at the checkout as price growth slowed. Under stagflation, households lose that relief, and people lose income just as everything costs more. In both U.S. episodes, the unemployment rate was rising rapidly while prices were rising at double-digit rates. Stagflation is defined by two readings at once, and no inflation figure, however carefully built, can identify it alone. A reader can recognize it only by setting the price figures beside the jobs figures.

Recent findings suggest that under the newer weights, the increase for the groceries families buy every week was much sharper. The increase for fruits and vegetables in January 2026 was 1.01% under the new weights and 0.73% under the 2023 weights, according to BLS. The basket is a sample of typical consumption and not a full list of what anyone buys, so a household that spends heavily on produce faces a different inflation rate from the basket's average.

Reweighting changes only how much each price counts toward the total, never what a single price did. Gasoline was 2.52% cheaper that month under either set of weights, according to BLS. When a headline shifts after a basket enhancement, the mix has changed, not the price at the pump.

A reader whose costs seem to outrun the official rate should look first at what they buy, because the official rate can describe the basket accurately and still not match that reader's spending.

The price index gives a fair reading of the average household and a poor one for any single budget.

"Prices are high" and "inflation is high" sound like the same complaint, but they answer different questions. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that inflation measures how fast an index climbs in percentage terms, and that the index on its own reflects what living costs. In October 2026, the index that tracks prices paid by city shoppers stood at 337.511, according to BLS. That figure tells readers how costly everyday life has become, not the speed at which costs are rising. A household that feels squeezed at the store is reacting to the level. A calmer pace of inflation does not bring that level down; only an actual drop in prices would.

The significant index number is a record of the past, measured from a starting line that someone chose. Every index level compares today's overall prices with a base year, and for the consumer price index that base is the period from 1982 to 1984, according to BLS. The October 2026 reading is therefore a running total of price increases since the early 1980s, not a gauge of how fast prices are moving today. Its size means something only next to that chosen base, and the current direction of prices is visible only in how much the level grows from one period to the next.

Industry observers note that index points are a poor guide to how fast prices are rising. In a worked example, two items each had an index 18.0 points higher than before, according to BLS. For one item, that was an 8.0% increase, and for the other it was a 16.4% increase, because the two started from different levels. The same visible jump can hide very different speeds of price growth.

For any index, the question that reveals inflation is how much it changed in percentage terms, not how many points it moved.

Recent findings suggest that A large price move stays in the yearly rate for a full 12 months, and after that it becomes the starting point for the next comparison. In July 2009, all items cost 2.1% less than a year earlier, according to BLS, and that comparison reached back to the month of the 2008 energy surge. Part of the drop came from measuring current prices against an unusually high starting point. A negative yearly rate therefore does not prove that prices are sliding now, since it can mean that last year's spike has become the point of comparison.

Before trusting what a yearly rate says about today, a reader should check what prices were doing a year earlier.

Sources indicate that there is no single inflation rate, and a report about "inflation" rests on one index chosen from several. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland explains that different indexes weight different products, so they show price changes for households, for producers or for the whole economy. These indexes are not rival estimates of one true number. Each one gives its own answer to the question of whose prices count. Two indexes that the public treats as interchangeable can therefore report different results from the same price changes, and that gap comes from their design, not from an error.

In March 2026, software and computer accessories held a weight of 0.035% in core CPI, while the category's share of core PCE was 1.2%, according to the Federal Reserve Board. That category barely counts in one index and is a real input in the other. The two federal agencies build their weights from different kinds of data. The Bureau of Labor Statistics relies on what households report buying in its Consumer Expenditure Survey, while the Bureau of Economic Analysis relies on what companies tell the Census they shipped. One source tracks what people say they bought and the other tracks what businesses sent out, and the two do not agree. A jump in software prices therefore barely registers in the CPI but counts noticeably in PCE.

The two indexes also do not serve as independent checks on each other, because PCE takes its software prices from the CPI. The PCE price index for that category is derived from the CPI series for computer software and accessories, the Federal Reserve Board reports, so a problem in the CPI series passes into PCE without being caught. The CPI item behind that series, Computer Software and Blank Media, includes blank media, while the PCE category gives blank media no weight at all. A rise in memory product prices may therefore show up in a PCE category that contains no memory products. Correcting for that mismatch would lower the category's measured contribution to core goods inflation, but that correction is an estimate by Federal Reserve Board researchers Barbarino, Diercks and Miran, not an official revision by the Bureau of Economic Analysis or the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so the official numbers stand.

According to recent reports, whether goods inflation signals broad price pressure can depend on this single small category. Core goods PCE rose at a 5.5% annualized pace over the four months to March 2026 and at 2.7% without software, according to the Federal Reserve Board. Including software makes goods inflation look like a serious surge, while leaving it out shows a modest pace. Much of the alarm comes from a category whose measurement researchers question.

The number is not fake, but before reading a surge as economy-wide, a reader should ask which index produced it and what the category driving it contains.

Policymakers can respond differently depending on how they classify a rise. A rise they judge persistent may lead them to recommend raising interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive for households and businesses. One they judge temporary may leave rates where they were.

For households, that classification matters because a rise that policymakers read as lasting can lead to higher borrowing costs.

According to recent reports, the full consumer price index counts every sharp price swing, so a single month's reading can mislead anyone trying to judge where prices are heading. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland describes median CPI and core measures as practical ways to estimate underlying inflation, either by keeping only the middle price change or by dropping food and energy. Both approaches set aside real price changes on purpose. Readers should treat these measures as deliberate edits of the data, made by people who decided which prices to leave out.

It has been revealed that the two measures define noise in opposite ways. Median CPI judges a price change by its size rather than by what was bought, and it excludes every change except the middle one. Whatever moved most sharply in a given month is set aside, whether it was gasoline or haircuts. Core measures make the reverse choice and decide in advance which items to ignore. Food and energy stay out even in a month when their prices hold steady, while a wild swing in some other item stays in. Each method aims at the same trend and misses different price changes, and each reflects a judgment about which prices deserve trust.

It has been revealed that leaving prices out is a choice, not a requirement. Some gauges of the underlying trend keep every item in the basket. Deciding what counts as noise is therefore a method someone picked, and the measurement itself does not demand it. When a report claims underlying inflation is cooling or heating, the useful question is which method produced that reading and what it left out. A gap between a core reading and a median reading is not a contradiction to explain away. It demonstrates that two reasonable definitions of noise caught different price changes.

Industry observers note that the trade is easiest to see in a hypothetical slowdown. Suppose unemployment stands at 4% at the start and 7% at the end, a shift that would put many more people out of work and dominate the news. In the curve's logic, inflation over the same stretch is 5% at the start and 2% at the end. Price growth would go from a pace that strains household budgets to a much gentler one. Those figures illustrate what the idea predicts and are not drawn from any real episode. They show the curve's ideal shape, not evidence that the economy behaves this way. Even in that tidy form the bargain is grim, because calmer prices come at the cost of lost jobs.

Sources indicate that the job market is only one influence on prices, and that is why the tidy trade often fails to appear. "However, economic conditions are only one of the factors that determine inflation," the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland stated. One of those other factors is what people expect inflation to be, and no jobs report measures that. Changes in exchange rates are another, and they have nothing to do with how many people are working.

Readers should treat a weak jobs report as a reason prices may rise more slowly, not as a forecast that prices will fall.

Every measure of inflation in this guide assumes that prices change slowly enough for a comparison with last year to tell people something useful. Hyperinflation is the case where that assumption fails. It is extreme, accelerating inflation, commonly defined as above 50% per month, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. That definition counts inflation in months instead of years, so a shopper would face a sharply higher grocery bill before the next paycheck arrived. The word "accelerating" matters as much as the number, because in hyperinflation the pace of price increases typically keeps rising instead of holding steady at one high level. The term describes a breakdown in how prices behave, not just an unusually bad year for the cost of living.

In some of the most extreme cases, prices can double within days. At that speed, even a monthly inflation figure describes the past. By the time statisticians publish it, shoppers are already paying far more than it shows. For people living through hyperinflation, the inflation rate no longer helps them initiative. It records how much buying power they have already lost.

According to recent reports, hyperinflation can sound like a problem from old economics textbooks, but its cases are recent. People in Yugoslavia lived through it in the 1990s, within living memory in Europe, and Venezuelans began living with it in 2017. Modern economies are not protected from it.

Baskets, weights and core measures help people understand prices only while prices change at a pace statisticians can measure, and hyperinflation is the point where that stops.

Recent findings suggest that no single reading can show deflation, because it requires a fall in the overall price level that lasts. A one-month dip in an index does not qualify. A slowdown in inflation does not qualify either, because economists treat it as a separate condition with its own name, disinflation. The price level as a whole has to fall and keep falling.

Before calling a headline deflation, a reader should ask whether the overall price level has fallen and stayed lower over a long stretch.

Industry observers note that when a news report notes inflation is coming down, many people hear that prices are coming down, and disinflation is the term for the gap between those two ideas. Disinflation means the inflation rate slows, say from 6% to 4%, while prices still rise, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland. An inflation rate of 4% is still a positive rate. A household paying for groceries, rent and fuel still spends more than it did a year earlier, only by a smaller margin than it would at 6%. The improvement is in the pace of increases, not in what anything costs. A reader who hears only that the rate is falling can easily come away believing that the household budget is getting easier when it is only getting harder more slowly.

Disinflation offers narrow relief because it slows the rise in the overall price level without reversing it. The price level keeps going up for as long as disinflation lasts. The increases a household has already absorbed stay in place, and latest ones keep arriving on top of them, only smaller. A family whose budget was stretched by last year's prices gets no money back when the rate cools. It simply faces smaller additions to costs that remain high. When a headline says inflation is easing, the useful question is which number is easing: the rate of increase or the prices themselves.

Disinflation describes a cost of living that is still going up, only more slowly.

A high inflation reading alongside rising layoffs is the one pairing the usual rules say should not happen, and Americans have paid for it twice.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homeward has expanded its cash-offer product from 13 states to all 48 contiguous states, giving real estate agents nationwide a way to offer sellers a cash sale, the tech giant revealed on Wednesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homeward has expanded its cash-offer product from 13 states to all 48 contiguous states, giving real estate agents nationwide a way to offer sellers a cash sale, the tech giant revealed on Wednesday.

The Austin-based company, which works only through real estate agents, said agents in every contiguous state can now bring a Homeward cash offer to their listings. The product is designed to reduce the risk of failed transactions tied to buyer financing or last-minute cancellations.

It has been revealed that the move comes as contract fallout remains a concern. In a low-inventory, high-mortgage rate market, a canceled contract often means agents must re-market the property while managing client frustration and timing pressures around the seller’s next move.

“Agents are doing everything right and still watching deals fall apart at the finish line,” Tim Heyl, founder and CEO of the HousingWire Tech100 firm, mentioned in the announcement. “A cash offer fixes that, but most cash buyers make their money by underpaying the seller. We don’t. Now agents everywhere can give their clients a sale they can count on, without asking them to leave money on the table.”.

According to recent reports, through the cash-offer program, homeowners can sell to Homeward for cash in as little as 14 days and skip traditional showings, according to the company. Unlike many investor or iBuyer models, Homeward said any upside when the home is later resold is passed back to the seller rather than retained by the buyer.

Recent findings suggest that for listing agents, the pitch centers on certainty of close and timeline control. A cash buyer eliminates the need to navigate financing contingencies, re-negotiations after appraisal issues and the risk of a buyer walking away late in the process. That stability can be critical for sellers who must coordinate a purchase on their next home or who need proceeds on a specific schedule.

For housing professionals, products that convert financed buyers into effective cash buyers or that provide institutional cash to sellers have become more prominent as higher mortgage rates, tighter credit conditions and affordability constraints increase fallout risk. Homeward’s nationwide expansion gives brokerages and teams in smaller and midsize markets access to a tool that had been limited to 13 states.

Alongside the nationwide cash-offer launch, Homeward said its Buy Before You Sell program is on track to be available in most states by the first quarter of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the program is designed for move-up or move-down buyers who need to tap their existing equity but want to avoid a home sale contingency. Homeward pairs short-term bridge financing with a guaranteed backup offer on the customer’s existing home, allowing agents’ clients to write offers on a upcoming property without first selling their current one.

Buy Before You Sell is at the moment available in 16 states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Iowa, Maryland, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Washington.

Industry observers note that bridge-style and buy-before-sell products have gained traction over the past several years as a way to unlock trapped equity for existing homeowners. For agents, they can shorten transaction timelines, reduce dependence on contingent offers and help keep purchase deals intact if the client’s sale is delayed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Amsterdam-based speech recognition startup Resonate Labs B.V. today released its Rumble-2-Flash transcription model as a free download with open weights.

Designed for fast transcription of prerecorded audio, the 500 million-parameter model supports more than 40 languages. Reson8 is pitching the release at developers and researchers who need speech recognition built for languages other than English.

It has been revealed that according to the tech giant, the leading speech models are trained primarily on English, even though only about one in 20 people speak it as a first language. Specialist terms such as medication names are where accuracy is said to fall furthest once speech moves outside English. Reson8’s models are said to be in production use for meeting notetakers, artificial intelligence receptionists, customer support voice agents, medical transcription and captioning.

“Generic speech models are built for English and make noticeably more mistakes in other languages,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Raoul Ritter, who started the firm with Thomas Kluiters and Jarno Verhagen. “Languages like Dutch, Swedish and German are spoken by millions, yet they’re an afterthought.”.

Recent findings suggest that reson8 describes Rumble-2-Flash as one of the smallest models on Hugging Face Inc.’s Open ASR Leaderboard. In the tech giant’s own runs of the leaderboard’s multilingual tests, the model averaged a word error rate of 7.09% across seven languages, including German, French and Dutch. Its average error rate in English is claimed to be about 5%.

In a recent development, on a separate test covering 10 lower-resource languages such as Maltese and Basque, Rumble-2-Flash is remarked to have posted a mean word error rate of 17.6%. OpenAI Group PBC’s Whisper Large V3 had a mean word error rate of 39.82% on the same test, according to Reson8.

Beyond benchmark sets, Reson8’s models are said to be trained for noisy settings, including phone-line audio. The real world “doesn’t happen in a recording studio,” said Kluiters, the company’s head of AI.

In a recent development, today’s open-weights release follows the model’s Nov. 3 debut in Reson8’s application programming interface, a week before the company launched its flagship Rumble-2 model. Custom vocabulary support, which lets customers add up to 50,000 terms as text without fine-tuning, remains exclusive to Rumble-2.

Recent findings suggest that hosted on the manufacturer’s own graphics processing units in the Netherlands, Reson8’s service is remarked to retain no audio or transcripts. The company also claims ISO 27001 certification and compliance with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation and the bloc’s AI Act.

Available free under an Apache 2.0 license, Rumble-2-Flash can also be accessed through Reson8’s API at prices starting from €0.01 ($0.001) per hour of audio.

In a recent development, reson8 raised €5 million ($5.5 million) in pre-seed funding in March. Balderton Capital led the round, with NP-Hard Ventures also participating. Speech is “quickly becoming a default interface across software,” according to James Wise, a partner at Balderton.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am.
  • Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.
  • “Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am.

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The organization notes the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

Sources indicate that the company stated late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, noted on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He mentioned the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health remarked patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In Latest York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

Industry observers note that about the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”.

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”.

Industry observers note that the Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.).

Microsoft stated Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its consumers that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”.

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The largest ad fraud operation ever disclosed by bid volume also rented out its victims' home internet connections without consent.

Recent findings suggest that UPCOMING YORK, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- HUMAN Security, Inc., the trust layer for digital customer experiences in the agentic era, today announced that its Satori Threat Intelligence and Research Team disrupted BADBOX 3.0, the largest ad fraud operation by bid volume ever publicly disclosed. "At its peak, BADBOX 3.0 generated roughly 40 billion bid requests a day, more than three times the previous record holder, VASTFLUX.".

It has been revealed that BADBOX 3.0 also ties into IpMoYu, the residential proxy network operated by the threat actors behind the BADBOX family and exposed in the BADBOX 2.0 investigation. Researchers assess PXYEDGE to be IpMoYu's successor, reusing its infrastructure, proxy module lineage, and task servers. Researchers at Nokia independently reached similar conclusions in their published analysis.

According to recent reports, "BADBOX 3.0 is the largest ad fraud operation by bid volume ever publicly disclosed, and it ran on cheap TV boxes sitting in people's living rooms," remarked Gavin Reid, Chief Information Security Officer, HUMAN. "If you bought one, it was compromised before you plugged it in: playing video ads you could never see, and quietly renting out your home internet connection to strangers. Neither the advertisers paying for those ads nor the people who bought the boxes had any idea.".

According to recent reports, BADBOX 3.0 runs on low-cost, uncertified consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that HUMAN researchers recognised from the original BADBOX investigation and BADBOX 2.0. They run Android Open Source Project (AOSP), are built in mainland China, and ship internationally. They are not Android TV OS devices and are not Play Protect certified. Once compromised, they contact command-and-control servers and receive fraud modules from an actively maintained catalog distributed across public repositories and multiple backup locations. Hidden ad modules play video ads in windows device owners cannot see, while bid requests impersonate legitimate connected TV apps to make the traffic appear authentic. The same devices are also enrolled, without their owners' knowledge or consent, in 11 residential proxy networks. HUMAN also observed server-side ad insertion spoofing in some of the same supply paths. In July 2025, Google unveiled legal action against BADBOX 2.0 botnet operators.

Industry observers note that "We appreciate working with HUMAN to disrupt the BADBOX 3.0 operation," stated Shailesh Saini, Director of Android Security & Privacy Engineering & Assurance, Google. "Play Protect certified Android devices undergo rigorous security testing to keep consumers safe and we encourage users to ensure that their device is certified and built with Android TV OS.".

Satori researchers linked the BADBOX 3.0 catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, through several independent connections, including command-and-control infrastructure, domains, preinstalled software, device checks, repositories, and a related threat actor. A TXCZ domain provides download routes for payloads and configurations for hidden ads, and one repository distributing ad fraud launchers is hosted under an account name that incorporates TXCZ. Researchers found that the same devices and the same module catalogs, support both the hidden ad fraud and proxyjacking activity. Satori researchers continue to monitor threat actors for further adaptation.

The Human Defense Platform identifies malicious automated behavior on the basis of the behavior itself,  regardless of the network path it arrives on. Residential proxy routing does not conceal malicious behavior from HUMAN's detection. Customers partnering with HUMAN for Ad Fraud Defense and Ad Click Defense are protected from the impact of ad fraud attacks associated with BADBOX 3.0. Customers partnering with HUMAN for Sightline Cyberfraud Defense and AgenticTrust are protected from account takeover, fake account creation, and carding attacks routed through residential proxy infrastructure.

#29782. 4 AI flashpoints from TwitchCon 2026 that left streamers uneasy

4 AI flashpoints from TwitchCon 2026 that left streamers uneasy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Streamers at TwitchCon 2026 mocked OpenAI's hackathon, fought Twitch's opt-out AI training and split over which AI tools help creators.
  • Creators who argue about artificial intelligence now spend less time on what the technology can do and more on who controls the material it learns from.
  • Recent findings suggest that streamers' frustration lasted for months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streamers at TwitchCon 2026 mocked OpenAI's hackathon, fought Twitch's opt-out AI training and split over which AI tools help creators.

Creators who argue about artificial intelligence now spend less time on what the technology can do and more on who controls the material it learns from. That question follows them from one service to the next, because Twitch is not the only company that hosts creators and uses AI. YouTube Live, Netflix $NFLX and Roblox $RBLX use it too, according to CBC. For people who stream on Twitch, the company training AI on their channels is their own platform's parent, Amazon $AMZN. A live streamer's material is their face, their voice and the audience they gather in real time. For them, the dispute centers less on the technology itself than on whether they ever agreed to hand those things over.

Recent findings suggest that streamers' frustration lasted for months. Twitch announced its AI training policy in August and explained it on a livestream that same week, according to CBC. Streamers were still angry in mid-November, when they gathered in San Diego for TwitchCon, the platform's biggest event of the year. Anger that lasts that long reflects more than one unwelcome setting. Many streamers feel that companies are putting AI into their work without consulting them. That doesn't make them opponents of AI. Many of them separate AI that helps a streamer from AI that takes a streamer's work. That distinction explains their anger as much as the technology does.

Recent findings suggest that yahoo set out to sum up how AI controversies shaped the way streamers reacted at TwitchCon 2026. Its account runs from the fight over Amazon training AI on streamers' channels unless they opt out to the attendees who mocked OpenAI's presence on the convention floor. It also covers the answers Twitch's leaders gave and the AI tools some streamers were glad to use. Each controversy came down to whether streamers get a real say over how AI uses their work. Each also raised the question of whether the companies' answers give them that say.

The most visible AI flashpoint at TwitchCon came from OpenAI, a company from outside the streaming world, rather than from Twitch's own policies. Attendees mocked OpenAI's Codex hackathon, which offered $25,000 in prizes, according to Yahoo. OpenAI meant the contest as an invitation for streamers to build with its technology. The people it hoped to court answered with ridicule instead of signing up. A cash prize is a sales offer, and this crowd treated it as a joke.

In a recent development, openAI could not win streamers over with prize money, a sign that cash alone would not ease their concerns about AI. These streamers' own platform had already enrolled their channels in AI training without asking. To them, a firm arriving at their own gathering with money to spend could look like more of the same. The hackathon also gave them something they could see and laugh at in person. A default setting tucked inside their own accounts offered no such target, even though it touched their work far more directly. That makes OpenAI the most visible object of the anger rather than the whole story. Streamers' harder fight was with their own platform, where opting out took more than walking past a contest on the convention floor.

Streamers resent that Amazon $AMZN trains AI on their channels by default, with every channel enrolled automatically, according to Yahoo. The anger centers on consent that streamers never gave. That reverses the usual bargain, because refusing becomes the streamer's job rather than permission Amazon has to earn. Streamers who want out also have to hunt for the switch. To reach it, a streamer opens three menus in a row, starting at the profile picture and ending in the account's security and privacy options, according to CBC. Once a streamer finds it, the label is plain: "Training for Generative AI." The trouble is where Twitch put the switch, not what Twitch called it.

Twitch picked that default knowing that few streamers would turn the setting on by themselves. "If it was opt-in, nobody would opt-in ... that’s honestly the answer. So it’s going to be on by default," Mike Minton, Twitch's chief product officer, told CBC. His answer highlights the opt-out is not a courtesy to creators. Twitch designed it on the expectation that most people would leave it alone. Streamers therefore don't see the default as a neutral design choice.

A streamer's own switch also doesn't cover everything that streamer indicates on Twitch. Messages a streamer posts in another channel's chat follow that channel's settings, and every channel starts out enrolled. A streamer who opted out can still have those words used for training wherever the host hasn't turned the setting off. Each visitor's protection then depends on every host finding and flipping a switch that starts in the on position. On a platform where streamers and viewers move constantly between each other's chats, no one can fully opt out alone, and the grievance is about lost control rather than a forgotten setting.

Twitch has answered streamers' anger by reassuring them about what has already happened, not by pulling back from the policy. Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has argued that a channel sitting in the program by default has not necessarily had its data collected yet, and that a streamer who switches the setting off stops that collection, according to Yahoo. The person who runs the platform is defending the default itself. His case rests on the harm still being avoidable. Under his explanation, every channel stays enrolled unless its owner does something about it, and the opt-out design that set off the backlash remains in place.

Recent findings suggest that clancy's reassurance addresses a different question from the one streamers were mainly asking. Their complaint is that they were signed up without a say. His answer is about timing, and it tells them that nothing has been taken yet. That answer puts the work of staying out of AI training on each streamer, one account at a time. A streamer who wants out has to find the setting called "Training for Generative AI" and switch it off, and a streamer who never gets around to it stays in. Clancy's explanation may ease the fear that a channel's data is already gone, but it does little for the resentment. Telling streamers they can still stop the training is not the same as asking them first, and that difference keeps the concern alive.

Recent findings suggest that streamers at TwitchCon did not object to every kind of AI. Some attendees value AI helpers that caption streams, clip highlights and assist with moderation, Yahoo reports, while they oppose generative AI that would replace what creators make. After the scorn for OpenAI's hackathon and the anger over training data, it would be easy to assume the convention was full of people who want AI gone, but their objection is selective. They separate tools that relieve a streamer of chores from tools that would make the streamer unnecessary.

The tools that attendees support handle the work around a live performance, not the performance itself. With automatic captions, viewers who watch with the sound off, or who can't hear it, can still follow a stream, so the streamer reaches more people without anyone else speaking for them. Twitch's AI clip tools help a streamer package highlights as vertical video for phone screens, which takes the editing off the streamer's hands while the moments stay the streamer's own. Moderation tools help a streamer keep order in a live chat, a job that is hard to manage while also performing, and they protect the community the streamer built instead of drawing on it. In each case the streamer stays on camera and stays in charge of the work.

Seen this way, the backlash at TwitchCon looks less like fear of the technology and more like a demand to keep control of it. Streamers welcome AI that serves their work. They resent AI that takes their work to build something that could compete with them.

Any platform's AI prepares will have to pass the same test as the tools attendees praised: the streamer stays in control.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm.
  • Nvidia’s board indicates it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang.
  • The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm.

Nvidia’s board indicates it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia unveiled Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Sources indicate that colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Others would rather have Huang back.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk noted on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

According to recent reports, the case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

It has been revealed that arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

It has been revealed that he also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the manufacturer’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Industry observers note that haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas noted in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”.

In a recent development, one complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort rolled out to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

Sources indicate that A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

According to recent reports, the AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a newly introduced organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

Industry observers note that in 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

Sources indicate that he knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:.

Recent findings suggest that the insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s newly introduced, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

Recent findings suggest that one more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy remarked it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

According to recent reports, in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the organization. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

This represents an almost complete loss of investment value for those who bought at the all-time high.

Overall, Cardano is also down around 35% in the last month and almost 60% since the start of 2026.

As a result, Cardano’s market cap has fallen all the way down to around $5.7 billion, with ADA dropping to 18th place in CoinGecko’s crypto rankings.

This is a very precarious position for the once-dominant altcoin Cardano, which is now extremely close to falling out of the top 20.

It seems as though there are a few different factors at play behind Cardano’s poor performance.

In a recent development, first of all, there has been a huge sell-off in the broader crypto market. Bitcoin has seen major drops, leading to more selling pressure on major altcoins.

This decline has coincided with a falling technology stock market, ongoing macroeconomic uncertainty, outflows from crypto investment products, and mass liquidations of leveraged positions.

That noted, there are clearly some issues with Cardano beyond the wider market struggles.

Sources indicate that for one, Cardano has faced a lot of criticism over the years for the blockchain’s relatively low adoption, even after years of development. This is especially evident when compared to other chains like Ethereum and Solana.

In fact, Cardano’s decentralized finance ecosystem has recently seen around $46 million in total value locked, as reported by DefiLlama.

Elsewhere, Hoskinson recently found himself embroiled in another controversy surrounding Cardano’s future.

In another recent X post, Hoskinson lashed out at certain commentators who keep bashing the blockchain for its apparent lack of adoption.

He noted that critics initially claimed Cardano suffered from poor on-chain metrics, few real-world use cases and technology that no one wanted to use.

Then, when Hoskinson decided to work on developing apps that would be able to attract millions of people and billions in assets, it seemed as though those same critics began claiming he was scamming everyone.

“You people are both stupid and scum. I can’t fix stupid,” said Hoskinson. “Grow up.”.

XRP is trading at $0.96 after dipping to $0.89. The $1 threshold, which essentially enables a rapid decrease if broken, gave in on November 14. It's the first time XRP traded below $1 since mid-August.

Industry observers note that the market is bearish, and the RSI dropped into the 20-ish zone, which is considered "extremely oversold". Moving averages are still rapidly diverging, which might further reinforce the bearish dynamic.

In a recent development, even if XRP reclaims the round number, bulls might still stay sidelined. If bulls somehow wake up, a recovery toward $1.2 is the main priority, as it's the level where a lot of investors accumulated XRP in the past.

In a recent development, on the other hand, the Ledger indicates elevated activity, with the potential to go further and reclaim levels we haven't seen in the bear market. Still, elevated activity during a prolonged market descent is not something we should just shake off.

A lot of the Ledger activity might be automated, driven by either trading bots or sophisticated LLM models. The market is mostly driven by speculative interest rather than fundamental network usage.

The activity of investors who are trying to cash out or pull their holdings away from exchanges could be the key here. Growing payments volume most likely reflects growing fear among investors, as some of them move funds to exchanges in order to liquidate their coins.

Payments volume rises, but so does the bear market pressure, with a possibility of a further downturn that could make things worse than they already are.

#29773. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1616 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange.
  • MEXC says user assets remain secure.
  • According to recent reports, on November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, finCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

According to recent reports, on November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

It has been revealed that on the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

It has been revealed that the ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

Recent findings suggest that MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN indicates the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

It has been revealed that the charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

It has been revealed that on Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Industry observers note that iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN indicates the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary consumers anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Recent findings suggest that section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

In a recent development, one provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

Recent findings suggest that for most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN states plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Industry observers note that before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how people or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

It has been revealed that finCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Recent findings suggest that three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

#29772. Breaking: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1167 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.
  • The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy.
  • A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am.

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Industry observers note that sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the newly introduced moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

Sources indicate that the window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Recent findings suggest that competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”.

Industry observers note that the data flywheel. Early consumers generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each latest model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

Sources indicate that the data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Industry observers note that momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

According to recent reports, learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

In a recent development, jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its substantial commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

Recent findings suggest that at AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”.

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook claims Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”.

It has been revealed that prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”.

In a recent development, swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Sources indicate that farecast, the airfare prediction manufacturer I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

In a recent development, A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, stated it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”.

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

Recent findings suggest that to repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one claims, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

According to recent reports, in AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.
