UPDATED 09:28 EST / NOVEMBER 18 2026.

Sources indicate that quantum computing is shedding its reputation as speculative as gains in quantum error correction turn fragile machines into reliable ones. For the supercomputing community, which now measures data centers in gigawatts of power, the more pressing question is how quantum fits beside the processors already on the floor.

Industry observers note that for years, the field faced a trade-off between speed and reliability, because correcting errors inside a quantum computer slowed it down. That trade-off is fading fast, according to Rajeeb Hazra (pictured), chief executive officer of Quantinuum Inc., which listed on the Nasdaq in June.

Recent findings suggest that “We are now at a stage in 2026 where we have the ability to have tremendous amounts of computation at a very high reliability rate,” Hazra said. “Just two weeks ago, we unveiled we were doing up to a million operations with five errors. To put it in contrast, just two years ago, we were trying to do 1,000 operations with one error. That’s how fast it is.”.

According to recent reports, hazra spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed advances in quantum error correction and how AI and quantum computing work in tandem. (* Disclosure below.).

Quantinuum’s 100-qubit Helios system recently set an error-correction record, reaching logical fidelity equivalent to five errors per million operations. The company builds the full stack, from hardware to developer tools, so customers can model problems such as how a drug ages and loses potency, Hazra explained. That positions quantum less as a rival to AI than as a tool AI will lean on for accurate simulation.

Recent findings suggest that “We see AI and quantum working in tandem, or rather AI using quantum computers,” Hazra stated. “I don’t think it’s people using quantum computers; it’s AI programming quantum computers to get the data they need to do what AI does best, which is reasoning and prediction.”.

Sources indicate that two cloud service providers have already struck deals with Quantinuum, and most of its use-case customers are commercial companies in pharma, energy, chemicals and financial services, Hazra explained. With quantum error correction maturing, the payoff lies in designing materials that release medicine only where the body needs it.

According to recent reports, “My view is in five to seven years max, you’re not going to get a prescription for amoxicillin,” Hazra remarked. “You’re going to get a sheet of paper that basically says this is your pathology. It’ll get matched up at CVS Pharmacy with the available proteins, if you will, and you will get your personalized medicine.”.

#29769. We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it

We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions.
  • Sources indicate that alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina.
  • For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I run Tutorela, a U.S. tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions. I’m saying that up front because this piece argues for that model, and because we learned the lesson behind it the hard way.

Sources indicate that alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina. As districts decide how much of the school day to hand to software, they should hear what happened when we gave students the best learning tool we could build.

For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons. To fill the gap between those lessons, we built a math learning and practice app with more than 10,000 exercises. Every problem came with a full solution in text and video, and we made the whole thing a game, with progress and rewards, so practice would feel less like homework. A year ago we added an AI assistant that could walk a student through any step, any time, for free.

Industry observers note that by any product standard it was the best a student could get. Only about 10% of students used it, and most of those who started didn’t stick around. The exercises were excellent and the AI was patient and clear, but none of that mattered, because the students weren’t showing up.

A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools, published this year by the National Bureau of Economic Research, found the same thing with Khanmigo, Khan Academy’s AI tutor. Nearly every student tried it, but the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced, and in only 17% of the practice sessions where they made a mistake. Most messages were one- or two-word answers or clicks on suggested prompts. The math gains matched what Khan Academy practice delivers without any AI. Khan Academy itself says only about 15% of students with access to Khanmigo engage with it. “It may be that human attention is the key ingredient,” the researchers wrote.

Industry observers note that at Limud Naim we didn’t change the app. We changed who was in charge of it. Each student’s tutor began managing their learning: picking the practice that fit where the student was, assigning it, and following up at the next lesson.

According to recent reports, everything changed. More than half of the students who got assignments from their tutor completed them, up from about 10% who used the app on their own. It was the same app with the same exercises. The only fresh ingredient was a human who knew the student and expected the work to get done.

That result is why we built Tutorela as a hybrid from day one.

In a recent development, this is the part AI-first education gets wrong. The bet behind an AI-run school day is that if content is personalized enough and feedback is instant enough, students will learn. Our experience and the Khanmigo data both say content was never the bottleneck. Students already have more free, high-quality explanations than any generation in history. What they’re missing is someone who notices whether they did the work and cares how it went.

A child practices fractions on a Tuesday night because their tutor, whom they’ll see on Thursday, asked them to. AI can generate the perfect worksheet, but it can’t make a 12-year-old feel that someone is counting on them.

None of this makes me an AI skeptic. I believe AI makes tutoring better, as long as the tutor sets the direction. Then AI makes the time between lessons count: it answers the question at 9 p.m., explains a step a third time without frustration, and offers more practice than any human could grade. The tutor gets a better-prepared student, and the student gets help exactly when they’re stuck.

Industry observers note that put AI in charge and remove the human, and the system loses its engine. You keep the explanations and lose the reason to show up.

For school leaders weighing AI-heavy models, the question isn’t whether the software is good. It usually is, and ours was too. The question is who will hold each student accountable for using it. If the answer is “the software,” expect what we and the Tennessee researchers saw: wide access, thin engagement, and students who quietly stop.

In a recent development, for parents, the advice is simple. Use AI tools, but pair them with a person, whether a tutor, a teacher, or a parent who checks in, who sets the goals and follows up.

The future of learning isn’t AI instead of teachers. It’s a teacher in charge, with AI for everything in between.

Sources indicate that the real test is not whether a company can succeed in a market once. It is whether it can keep adapting as consumers and technology evolve. It is no longer enough for leaders to see where the future is headed. The best leaders build organizations capable of riding on the opportunities and challenges.

  • A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 2:31 pm.

Recent findings suggest that update, Tuesday Nov. 17: ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests Vulcan’s first stage underperformed just after liftoff. Read our follow-up story for details. This story has been updated with ULA’s preliminary findings.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed to reach orbit Sunday, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

Sources indicate that it was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan debuts that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said Sunday that it didn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it would work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as rapidly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term intends for Vulcan.”.

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

ULA said Tuesday that early data suggests the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to reach orbit. The Centaur, powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris, appears to have started normally and couldn’t make up for the shortfall. ULA appears to have lost telemetry and the mission about 10 minutes into the flight.

Sources indicate that spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation highlighted the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t mentioned what caused the shortfall.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

It has been revealed that melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had mentioned the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 rolls out reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

According to recent reports, in June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it looks an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

It has been revealed that vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security rolls out after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the Upcoming Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

In a recent development, ULA is also under fresh leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

THOMASTON, Conn., Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Why is precision metal forming becoming increasingly key in modern industrial production?

HelloNation has published the answer in an article featuring insights from Manufacturing Expert Michele Caulfield of Stevens Company, Inc., in Thomaston, CT.

In a recent development, the HelloNation article explains that precision metal forming plays a critical role in producing reliable components for demanding industrial applications. As industries require stronger materials, tighter tolerances, and greater consistency, manufacturers continue turning to advanced forming methods capable of supporting high performance manufacturing environments. Precision metal forming helps create durable components that perform reliably while supporting production efficiency at scale.

The article describes precision metal forming as a manufacturing process that reshapes metal into highly accurate parts while maintaining structural integrity. Unlike methods that rely heavily on cutting or machining, precision metal forming preserves material consistency while improving efficiency and reducing waste. This allows manufacturers to create durable components capable of meeting strict engineering and performance requirements.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant advantages discussed in the article is the ability to maintain tight tolerances across large production runs. Industries such as aerospace, industrial equipment, and medical manufacturing often require exact specifications because even minor dimensional inconsistencies can affect performance or safety. Precision metal forming supports high-volume manufacturing by producing repeatable parts that consistently meet strict dimensional standards.

According to recent reports, the article also highlights the importance of repeatability in high performance manufacturing. Automated production systems and complex assemblies depend on components functioning exactly as intended. Precision metal forming helps manufacturers maintain consistent quality throughout high-volume manufacturing operations while reducing variation between production runs.

According to recent reports, durability is another major benefit covered in the article. Components used in industrial applications are often exposed to pressure, vibration, heat, and continuous operation. Precision metal forming strengthens material through controlled shaping processes that maintain continuity and reduce weak points commonly associated with alternative manufacturing methods. The result is stronger and more durable components designed for demanding operating environments.

Recent findings suggest that material efficiency also remains an key factor in modern manufacturing. The article explains that precision metal forming generally produces less waste than subtractive manufacturing methods that remove large amounts of material during production. Improved efficiency helps manufacturers better manage material costs while maintaining the structural requirements needed for high performance manufacturing applications.

The aerospace industry is one example discussed in the article where precision metal forming plays an essential role. Aerospace systems often require lightweight yet durable components capable of operating under extreme conditions. Precision metal forming supports these industrial applications by producing parts that meet demanding performance and reliability standards.

According to recent reports, medical manufacturing is another field that depends heavily on precision metal forming. Medical devices and equipment require exceptional accuracy and consistency because small dimensional variations can affect device functionality and patient safety. The article explains that precision metal forming supports medical manufacturing by producing reliable components with tight tolerances and dependable repeatability.

Recent findings suggest that industrial equipment manufacturers also benefit from the consistency provided by precision metal forming. Machinery used in transportation, energy production, and heavy industry often depends on durable components capable of maintaining performance under continuous stress. Precision metal forming helps manufacturers create parts designed for long-term reliability and efficient assembly within complex industrial applications.

Recent findings suggest that the article also notes that automation has increased the importance of precision metal forming in high-volume manufacturing environments. Automated systems depend on repeatable dimensions and predictable performance to maintain quality control and efficient production workflows. Precision metal forming supports these goals by producing durable components with consistent specifications across large-scale operations.

Sources indicate that the article concludes that precision metal forming remains essential to high performance manufacturing because it combines efficiency, consistency, and structural reliability. Through tight tolerances, repeatable production, and durable components, precision metal forming continues to support advanced industrial applications across aerospace, medical manufacturing, and modern industrial production.

In a recent development, according to CoinGlass, the cumulative volume delta (CVD) on the Coinbase spot market reached -$1.08 billion between Oct. 31 and Nov. 15. CVD shows the difference between the volume of market buy orders and market sell orders, and a negative CVD means that sellers were more active on the exchange.

Over the same period, the CVD on the spot markets of OKX, Bybit and Binance stood at $240.3 million, $65.17 million and $51.88 million, respectively, so buyers were more active on these three exchanges.

Sources indicate that the price of Bitcoin went down from $81,188 on Nov. 4 to $61,956 on Nov. 14, according to CoinGlass data, and the decline amounted to around 24%. On Sunday, Bitcoin recovered to around $65,400.

It has been revealed that the data comes amid claims that Binance has been pushing the price of Bitcoin down. The exchange lost $6.4 billion in a hack on Oct. 29, and some users on X then claimed that Binance was selling crypto to cover its losses. Two weeks after the attack, Binance published a Proof of Reserves report that indicated client balances on the exchange were fully backed.

This week, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared a comparison of Bitcoin charts ahead of the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs and called it "an interesting analysis." Several users in the replies to his post blamed the drop in Bitcoin on selling by Binance.

Industry observers note that binance is the largest crypto exchange by trading volume, and a large share of futures liquidations takes place on the platform. On Nov. 13, crypto exchanges liquidated 187,389 traders for a total of $1.65 billion in 24 hours, and 88% of that amount came from long positions, according to CoinGlass. Still, the CVD on the Binance spot market has stayed positive since Oct. 31.

In a recent development, coinbase is the custodian for most U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, including BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, and many U.S. institutional investors trade on the platform through Coinbase Prime.

Anthropic is set to start trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19, and the selling on Coinbase comes ahead of the listing. Fundstrat managing partner Tom Lee has called the recent drawdown in Bitcoin a temporary rotation of money into mega-IPOs, and in the 50 days before the Anthropic IPO, Bitcoin has lost around 18%.

The CVD on Coinbase fell most sharply between Nov. 10 and Nov. 14, and Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 during this period, according to CoinGlass data.

Latest Update: ‘The Romans are laughing at us’: physical AI founder raises $97 million in quest to stop wasting time with archaic infrastructure maintenance

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.”.
  • Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune: “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure.
  • In a recent development, hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alex Hawkinson keeps a collection of Roman artifacts at BrightAI’s robot demo center, and he has a saying to go with them: “The Romans are laughing at us.”.

Think of the way the Romans inspected their roads, Hawkinson told Fortune: “They sent teams of technicians out periodically on schedule” to check on their infrastructure. Two thousand years later, power companies, water utilities, and pipeline operators still do. In his telling, two out of three of those trips turn up nothing to fix, and the failures that matter happen in between visits anyway.

In a recent development, hawkinson is convinced this can change, and investors are paying for the idea. BrightAI remarked Wednesday it has raised $97 million in a round led by Smith Point Capital, the growth-stage firm started by former Salesforce co-CEO Keith Block. GE Vernova, already a BrightAI customer, also invested, along with Cobalt Capital, Marlinspike Partners, Zero Infinity Partners as well as existing backers Khosla Ventures, Inspired Capital, and Upfront Ventures. The round brings total funding to $184 million and values BrightAI at $750 million, according to a person familiar with the matter. Hawkinson insisted he “doesn’t care” about so-called unicorn status: The point is bring infrastructure out of the ancient Roman era.

His pitch has three parts. Replace scheduled human inspections with sensors and AI that watch infrastructure all the time. Go after what BrightAI estimates is more than $7 trillion a year in waste worldwide. And along the way, create a kind of data that has never existed: a continuous record of how pipes, poles, and pumps actually wear out. If it works, the companies running the world’s power and water get to stop paying for trips that find nothing.

Industry observers note that the Romans knew the problem well. Frontinus, who was named Rome’s water commissioner by the emperor Nerva in the late first century A.D., wrote a treatise on running the city’s aqueducts. He worried about leaks in underground channels that were hard to find and fix, about people tapping the lines without permission, and about trees whose roots could damage the masonry.

BrightAI’s release says the systems that power modern life “still operate on a centuries-old model: inspect, detect, and react.” Hawkinson is a believer from personal experience. In 2011, the power went out at his family’s cabin in Leadville, Colo., a remote mountain town, and nobody knew until the pipes had frozen and burst and water had run through the walls. He built a connected sensor hub in his garage, rolled out it on Kickstarter as SmartThings, and sold the organization to Samsung in 2014. He has cofounded eight companies and run four as CEO, all of which exited. He bootstrapped BrightAI, founded in 2019, for its first four years.

He spent the first half of his career in software as a service, and his SmartThings put sensors in people’s homes, not substations or sewers.

Sources indicate that “I wasn’t from infrastructure,” he said. When he started going out in the field, at one point in a hard hat in a sewer, he was “shocked” by how the systems everyone depends on are actually monitored and break down. In industry after industry, he asked frontline technicians how often they get sent out and find nothing to fix. The answer kept coming back at 50% to 70% of the time. BrightAI’s release puts it more conservatively, at more than half of scheduled inspections.

Industry observers note that he assumed at first the operators were doing it wrong. He came to see it as an equilibrium. Send crews less often, and something breaks catastrophically, so you send them more often. Send them more often, and the labor, which is expensive and often dangerous, becomes unaffordable. Operators settle where “two out of every three times they send somebody out, even the most talented operators, it’s unnecessary,” he said, and failures still slip through between visits.

It has been revealed that the wooden power pole is his favorite example. By his count, the U.S. has about 150 million of them, “little matchsticks sticking up,” and each one sees a human inspector roughly every eight to 10 years. The 2018 Camp Fire—California’s deadliest wildfire—killed 85 people after a worn hook on an aging PG&E transmission tower gave way. Cal Fire determined the utility’s lines caused it. Hawkinson’s point is that the hook was “completely invisible in the world” until it failed.

In a recent development, the $7 trillion figure is BrightAI’s own. The company claims it surveyed 12,158 operators across 16 industries and put the addressable annual impact at more than $7.5 trillion. It also found 98% of those operators lack adequate visibility into their assets. It tallies the wasted trips, the labor, and the cost of letting things break, which he said is far more expensive to fix than to maintain. The outside research the release cites—from the Energy Department, the EPA, Swiss Re and the National Safety Council—puts the cost of infrastructure failure alone at $2.5 trillion a year.

It has been revealed that the examples Hawkinson gives are mundane, which is part of his point. He cited one customer, a UK water utility that has about a thousand pumps and can’t tell which ones will be the next to fail. Its limited staff runs around “like chickens with their heads cut off” trying to catch them. When heavy rain hits, failed pumps send raw sewage into rivers.

Hawkinson mentioned he’s a Lord of the Rings fan, and this breaks his heart, to see raw sewage being pumped into a landscape that looks “just like the Shire.” (This Fortune interviewer agreed, saying Hawkinson’s physical AI descriptions sound a bit like something Gandalf would get up to; Hawkinson laughed, but didn’t quite agree.).

Closer to home, a break in the Potomac Interceptor sewer line in January released an estimated 243 million gallons of untreated wastewater into the Potomac River, according to the Maryland Department of the Environment.

There’s also copious waste in replacing parts that are fine. Hawkinson described a customer COO who suspected his tech giant was swapping out spark plugs in its machines too early, at a cost of tens of millions of dollars a year. Once BrightAI’s models had the sensor data, Hawkinson said, they found about half of the replacements were premature. The call depended on some 30 variables no technician would track.

Sources indicate that brightAI’s platform, Stateful, pairs edge sensors on poles, pipelines, compressors, and tanks with autonomous robots, drones and wearable AI copilots for field crews. The company says it runs at more than 50,000 locations and processes tens of trillions of sensor readings. Customers include GE Vernova, Reworld, Osmose Utilities Services, Azuria Water Solutions, Kodiak Gas Services, and Diamondback Energy. On average, Hawkinson mentioned, customers see trouble coming 51 days before what would have been a catastrophic failure.

Sources indicate that GE Vernova, whose equipment helps generate about one-quarter of the world’s electricity, wanted in. Hawkinson said BrightAI hadn’t planned to take money from strategic investors this round, but GE Vernova insisted. The release indicates it will use BrightAI across its Power, Wind, and Electrification businesses.

Industry observers note that most of the newly introduced money goes to taking the platform global. BrightAI states nearly 60% of its addressable market is outside North America, and it’s opening offices abroad after doubling its headcount in 2025. Hawkinson mentioned bringing on a new customer used to take two to three years, and now takes less than six months.

The coming year, he said, is about going from “proven concept” to deployments at scale with the biggest utilities. Until then, most of America’s 150 million wooden poles will keep getting checked the Roman way, about once a decade.

Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.
  • It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows.
  • These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am.

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows customers are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”.

Instead, the Copilot as “a latest OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Recent findings suggest that many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

Recent findings suggest that the high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

It has been revealed that operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

Sources indicate that the Upcoming OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Presently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the upcoming Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as Upcoming OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

Sources indicate that if you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

Industry observers note that “We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” remarked Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

Recent findings suggest that the Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple blamed an internal enhancement for its Nov.
  • Most people expect a bank transfer, a flight check-in or a work email to go through without a second thought, and few notice how small a group of systems all of that depends on.
  • A run of failures this close together makes it easy to assume someone is attacking these systems, but officials and companies keep finding no attacker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple blamed an internal enhancement for its Nov. 17 outage. Here are 5 aspects, from cause and status to stores.

Most people expect a bank transfer, a flight check-in or a work email to go through without a second thought, and few notice how small a group of systems all of that depends on. That expectation kept breaking this month, when a major system somewhere ran into serious trouble every business day for four days running, according to CNBC, including the Thursday outage that cut Microsoft $MSFT Outlook customers off from their mail. The trouble reached industries with little in common. The Associated Press reports that a technical problem at JPMorgan $JPM Chase spread to Zelle and to customers at several other banks, and that United Airlines' outage ran more than 90 minutes. When so much ordinary activity depends on so few systems, one breakdown can stop work that people never thought was connected to it.

A run of failures this close together makes it easy to assume someone is attacking these systems, but officials and companies keep finding no attacker. "This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack or AI agents as the cause of its own outage, according to The Associated Press. Clayton ties the wider run of outages to upgrades, with some upgraded systems and some handoffs between systems not working as expected afterward, ABC News reports, though the root cause of the FAA's router failure has not yet been determined. In Clayton's account, the trouble comes from upgrade work, which is supposed to improve systems. Naming a general trigger has not settled why one change can do so much damage, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has asked for a congressional briefing, according to CNBC. For now, the explanation covers the run of outages in broad terms, while individual failures still lack one.

TIME set out to summarize the cause, the timeline and the affected services of Apple $AAPL's outage, which joined this run of failures. Apple's case is worth following because the trouble reached both Apple Pay and in-store purchases at Apple's own stores. The questions to carry through are what Apple's own change broke, how much of it is truly back and what remains unexplained.

According to recent reports, apple $AAPL blames its outage on a change it made to its own systems. Losing payments and cloud storage at the same moment can look like the work of an intruder, but the company indicates the trouble began with an internal update, according to TIME. ABC News reports that Apple gave the same explanation, which puts the start of the failure inside the company in Apple's own account. That account comes only from Apple, and the company has offered no detail on what the update changed or which part of its systems failed. A reader therefore knows where Apple says the trouble began, but not what went wrong. "Internal update" names a type of mistake. It does not diagnose this one.

An update by itself does not explain why so many Apple services failed at once. Liz Fong-Jones, a tech labour organiser, offers one place to look. "Part of the resilience of a system comes from people who are experienced with a system," Fong-Jones told ABC News. Her remark concerns systems in general, but it raises a fair question for Apple: how much experience did the people who made this change have with the systems they changed? Nothing on record connects Apple's failure to its staffing, so that question is a lead to pursue and not a finding about the company.

Until Apple states what its revision changed, the cause of the outage remains a label rather than an explanation.

Apple $AAPL's outage counts as fixed only for the day as a whole, so a reader should treat the recovery as partial. TIME reports that the outage occurred on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, and was resolved by that evening. That resolution applies to the outage in general. The trouble began in the morning and ended by evening, but no exact times are on record, and nothing shows when any single service, such as a payment or a sign-in, came back. After an outage, most people need to know whether the thing they rely on works again. A reader whose payment still fails gains little from an all-clear for the day.

Apple itself claimed less than a full recovery. "Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal patch caused some outages this morning," Apple said in an emailed statement, as reported by the Associated Press. "Many" is not "all," and the company's own wording leaves the evening all-clear an open question. The rest of Apple's systems were still being brought online, with no timeline given. Apple offered no date for those services, and the evening resolution names none of them, so a reader cannot plan around the return of any specific one. The accurate label is "partly restored." A reader who still sees errors after Tuesday should not assume Apple's fix has reached every service.

Apple has mentioned what set off the outage, but it has not said when each of its services came back.

Industry observers note that on an iPhone, paying, emailing and saving a file feel like separate tasks, but this outage reached all of them. Apple $AAPL Pay was among the services affected, according to TIME. Email and stored files were hit too. iCloud went down along with iCloud Mail, which affected mail kept on an Apple account as well as the photos and files people store there. Moving to a laptop browser offered no way around the problem, because iCloud's web apps were down as well. The App Store was also among the affected services, so getting a newly introduced app or an update was not a reliable option either. Payments, mail, files and apps that people treat as separate tools all appeared on the same list of services the outage touched.

At least one security researcher sees disruptions such as this one as a sign that the technology industry has not yet grown up. "We're in the weird teenage phase of technology not quite maturing enough to know how to do this without disrupting services and so forth," Tom Hegel, research head at SentinelOne, told CNBC. Until companies can change their systems without disrupting services, people who run payments, mail and files through one account are accepting that all of them can fail on the same day. The practical step is modest. A physical card and a way to reach crucial email outside an Apple account let people pay and stay in touch when the phone's services are down.

The more of the day people run through a single account, the more of the day they lose when one update fails.

Recent findings suggest that apple $AAPL's own support service was caught up in the outage along with the products it exists to help fix. When an iPhone payment or an iCloud sign-in stops working, most customers turn to Apple for help. This time AppleCare, the manufacturer's support service, was among the services affected, according to TIME. The support channel that customers would normally rely on during a breakdown was itself part of the breakdown. A customer with a stalled device could not count on the usual first step to work normally on Tuesday. Apple has not remarked how badly AppleCare was affected or which parts of it failed, so the size of the gap in support remains unclear.

The failure also reached organizations, not only individual customers. Apple Business, a service named for companies, was among the affected services. The outage therefore became a problem for employers and the staff who use Apple's tools at work, not only for people trying to pay for coffee or open their email. Schools were caught in it too. Apple School Manager and SchoolWork, two tools named for schools, both appear among the affected services. Schools that use them depended on systems that failed alongside the consumer apps. Because the fault came from an update inside Apple, nothing a school's staff did on their own side could restore those tools.

Businesses and schools depend on Apple's systems but control no part of them, and a single change inside Apple reached them all the same.

During the outage, staff at some Apple $AAPL stores could not sell anything at the counter. In-store purchases were among the affected retail functions, according to TIME. NBC10 Philadelphia reports that store employees could not complete purchases after the internal software they use stopped working. The problem was not on a shopper's phone or in a customer app. It was in the tools Apple's own workers use to ring up a sale. Appointment scheduling failed too, and employees could not book customers for help, so the store could not serve as a place to get an iPhone or Mac looked at in person. Both of those failures happened behind the counter, on the staff side. Apple's internal systems, the ones its own employees work on, appear to have failed along with its public services, though no account confirms exactly which internal systems broke.

How widely the store trouble spread is unclear. Only some locations were affected, and nobody has given a count of the stores involved. The staff accounts came from employees who spoke to NBC News, according to NBC10 Philadelphia, and nothing on record shows that the same problems reached every store. The store problems show that the failure went deep into Apple's systems. They do not show that Apple's whole retail operation shut down.

During an outage like this one, a trip to an Apple store is not a reliable workaround, because the store counter runs on Apple's internal systems too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Virtual CFO Platform, built by AI software developers and tested by CPA firms, puts every client's financial picture at a firm's fingertips.

NEW YORK, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- AI can now do the analysis that once took a team of accountants, and CPA firms are wondering how to adapt. Today, Netsurit and Southwestern Talent announced the Virtual CFO Platform, an AI-powered advisory engine that turns raw client financial data into CFO-grade insight, so firms can build advisory practices without hiring a team of advisory specialists.

The question facing CPA firms has changed. It is no longer whether AI can do accounting analysis, but what firms do now that it can. In October 2026, Mercor published a study that put a frontier AI model head-to-head with 12 licensed U.S. CPAs on well defined accounting tasks. The CPAs working alone met an average of 37% of the grading criteria. The AI, working alone, met nearly all of them, in a fraction of the time and at a fraction of the cost.

Recent findings suggest that the work firms have long billed by the hour is the work AI now does best, while the pipeline of latest CPAs has thinned. Unique CPA exam candidates fell by about a third between 2016 and 2022, according to the AICPA's 2025 Trends Report, and are only now beginning to recover.

Industry observers note that many firm leaders see business advisory as the way forward. A full-time CFO costs $350,000 or more a year, and even a fractional CFO runs thousands of dollars a month, which leaves most small businesses without CFO-level guidance. AI makes it possible to offer that guidance at a price those clients will pay, with the CPA supplying the judgment and the trust.

According to recent reports, the obstacle is delivery. Advisory is often priced like compliance, built from scratch for each client, and dependent on one or two partners. Building a bench of specialists to change that is difficult for any firm, and harder when talent is this scarce.

Industry observers note that the Virtual CFO Platform was built to close that gap. A dedicated team of AI software developers built it for CPA firms, and practicing CPA firms and managing partners tested and validated each module before release.

Industry News: I’ve coached the world’s most marketable athlete for 8 years. New CEOs should copy how her team handles expert advice

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are a lot of latest CEOs coming into the market right now.
  • When someone takes over a new leadership role, they’re getting a ton of advice.
  • It’s from the experience and knowledge of all these other people, which is fantastic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a lot of latest CEOs coming into the market right now. Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 1,337 CEO exits in the first nine months of this year, including 111 in September. On September 1, John Ternus took over at Apple, with Tim Cook staying on as executive chairman.

When someone takes over a new leadership role, they’re getting a ton of advice. Even the good advice is often too much. “This is what worked really well for us.” “This has been a problem this whole time.” It comes from staff members and even the former CEO.

It’s from the experience and knowledge of all these other people, which is fantastic. But the problem I see is it’s an overdose. You start to lose touch with your own instincts, your own gut. And when you must make the tough decisions your gut already knows, you hesitate.

For the past eight years, I have coached Aryna Sabalenka, a multiple Grand Slam champion who has spent more than 100 weeks at world No. 1. She was just named the most marketable athlete in the world, out of all sports. You can imagine how many people are approaching us these days.

Anton Dubrov is her tennis coach. I am her performance coach. A big part of our job is filtering. Whether we’re speaking with specialists, agents or Aryna directly, we’re constantly filtering what’s getting through and who has the access.

Recent findings suggest that in 2022, her serve was falling apart. She finished that year with 428 double faults, more than anyone else on the tour. In San Jose, she lost the same way, frustrated and crying, talking about how we’d done everything. I remember telling her, “We have done everything except the one thing you’re most afraid of”: addressing her serve. What started as a technical matter had become a massive mental barrier.

Sources indicate that so we brought in a specialist, a biomechanist. This guy was amazing. The challenge is that when you bring in someone who’s highly specialized, they can find 20 different things to fix. That’s when advice becomes noise and interference.

He wanted to address the rhythm and timing of her acceleration and where she produced it. Her foot placement, her rotation, where and when she loaded her legs, her toss, her general movement quality. Then he wanted to get into her forehand too. All valid points, and way too much at once.

It has been revealed that there’s another thing you have to manage. When someone is given an opportunity like that, it’s natural for them to want to find problems they can fix, or to show how much they know. That’s a common human response, and it adds to the noise.

Nothing in a serve works in isolation. So Anton and I sat down with him and worked out which one or two things would influence everything else. We picked two. The first was her left arm, and the direction it was driving down after her toss. The second was the motion of her right arm and the way her right wrist turned over through contact. Improve those two, and much of the rest would self-correct. Everything else on his list, we held back.

Then we decided who would deliver it, and when. He coached her only at specific practices, and only at specific moments within those practices, with Anton always right there with him. Some weeks he traveled with us, same setup. The rest of the time, Anton delivered the message, with me alongside as an outside eye. Anton and I drove the when, the where and the what.

Recent findings suggest that my job was making sure she had the right amount of coaching and enough time to make it her own, and doing the movement training so she could physically do the work. She is the one performing, so it has to match her personality and her style. She can’t just copy and paste someone else’s ideas.

Aryna heard one clear, consistent message, no matter who was delivering it. That built trust that we were on the right track. If we had allowed him to come in and just give tons of advice, she would have started overanalyzing, lost touch with herself and stopped acting. It would have gotten worse.

Instead, a few months later, she won her first Grand Slam at the Australian Open, and she has been consistently dominating the tour ever since.

According to recent reports, I see a lot of CEOs run into the same thing. They’re getting a ton of amazing advice, and they lose themselves in all this information. The noise starts to become interference.

The person bringing you advice brings their nerves and their history along with it. Earlier in Aryna’s career, people on the team brought a lot of anxiety into this space. My job was to stand with Anton and step in between her and that noise. Sometimes it meant asking people to leave the team, or at least leave that room. For a newly introduced CEO, that urgency can come from your board, or from old team members still emotionally attached to the old plans.

All this advice can also become a hiding place. More meetings, another deck. Leaders feel like they’re being responsible, but their gut knows there are decisions they’re hiding from.

According to recent reports, when I was 13, I was homeless. One of the places that helped me get off the streets and become the person I am today was a dojo, a martial arts school stuck between an adult bookstore and a pawnshop.

In a recent development, the sensei, Jan Sunderlin, used to tell me something I didn’t fully grasp until recent years: “Through loyalty you gain trust. With trust comes freedom. To maintain that freedom, remain loyal.”.

In a recent development, I see loyalty as having many layers, and the first layer is loyalty to yourself, to your own code and your gut. That’s what got you this job in the first place. When you have that in place, people around you feel that stability way before you must go out and prove it. This is where real trust comes from. And that trust buys you the freedom to lead the way you need to lead.

Industry observers note that of course the person who got you there needs to grow into the person who keeps you there. But if you let every piece of advice in, it’s going to dilute your code. And when pressure hits, you will hesitate and make decisions that aren’t truly yours.

It has been revealed that before your first massive meeting, take a piece of paper and write down who you are. What are the values you hold, even if it’s going to cost you? Write down the one or two things you want to achieve your quarter, then your first year.

Then write down whose voice you’re going to trust to filter the advice coming from all angles, the way Anton and I do for Aryna. That might be a chief of staff, a COO or one board member. If the former CEO is still in the building, agree early on how their advice will reach you.

Every time you get a piece of advice, hold it up against that page and ask yourself: Does this make me more aligned with who I am at my best, or is this advice going to direct me to become someone I’m not?

In a recent development, early days with Aryna’s team, Anton and I used to share hotel rooms and look for the cheapest flights. There was nobody lining up to give her advice on anything. Now everybody is coming knocking on the door, and the job has not changed. It’s still to protect the person who must perform.

Now that’s your job, but the person you’re protecting is you.

It has been revealed that we don’t rise to the occasion. We fall back to the level of our code.

In your first 90 days, make sure that code is still yours.

Long-term, pay-per-gallon agreement provides [NPDES-compliant] treatment and renewable natural gas production with no upfront capital from the client. About 102 million gallons are treated annually.

It has been revealed that HOUSTON, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cambrian Innovation has commissioned and is operating a wastewater treatment and resource recovery system at a dairy processing plant in Wisconsin. The system treats approximately 280,000 gallons per day, or about 102 million gallons annually, and converts the plant's organic waste into renewable natural gas (RNG). Cambrian designed, built, owns, and operates the system under a 20-year, pay-per-gallon agreement, with no upfront capital cost to the plant.

The system replaces lagoon-based treatment and the spray application of roughly 100 million gallons of partially treated water per year. The plant's objectives were long-term regulatory compliance and lower operating costs. Treated water is discharged to a local tributary under the site's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit, and RNG is prepared for injection into the local pipeline.

"The engineering of this particular system was instrumental in protecting the environment and generating a valuable resource of natural gas," remarked Joshua Hanlon, VP of Operations at Cambrian. "The advanced treatment of ethylene effluent meets stringent NPDES requirements for discharge to a local small creek. High quality renewable natural gas is produced from the waste and sold back to the local community.".

In a recent development, the project reflects Cambrian's resource-recovery approach: treated water returns to the watershed, biosolids return to land as beneficial reuse, and organic waste is converted to pipeline-grade renewable energy. Cambrian's own operators run the system day to day, including solids processing, which removes the operation of the wastewater system from the plant's scope. Cambrian offers the same pay-per-gallon model across manufacturing and commercial industries.

According to recent reports, founded in 2011, Cambrian offers wastewater treatment and reuse to a wide range of industries: food and beverage, data center, pulp and paper, pharmaceutical, oil and gas, steel, and more. Cambrian's vision is industry as an ecosystem. Biological systems are inherently sustainable, and Cambrian applies them to industrial wastewater treatment and resource recovery. Cambrian designs, builds, owns, and operates these systems on-site as a service, with no upfront capital cost to the client. Cambrian-owned systems operate at more than 35 sites and have treated nearly 5 billion gallons of water.

#29756. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (820 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.
  • Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.
  • That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am.

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”.

Industry observers note that microsoft claims active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the firm posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Sources indicate that microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

Industry observers note that when traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:.

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The firm certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that the safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

In a recent development, the gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t rapidly undo one that was months old.

The tech giant’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Sources indicate that charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put upcoming limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate problem,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t mentioned what it was.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on the day the U.S. officially lost its measles-elimination status, Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner had a warning for the country that went beyond one virus.

“It’s a reminder,” Boerner mentioned Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, after Fortune’s Diane Brady opened their conversation with the news. The U.S. leads the world in upcoming medicines, he said: 90% of them launch here, often two to three years before other rich countries get them. “That’s a real benefit that we have, but it’s not a birthright.”.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization stated the U.S. no longer meets the standard it first cleared in 2000: no single chain of measles transmission lasting 12 months or longer. The CDC has counted more than 5,400 cases so far in 2026, after 2,289 last year, many of them in outbreaks that began in close-knit Mennonite communities and spread, CBS News reported. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status too. Canada lost its status last year.

The numbers behind the decision have been building. In the 2025–26 school year, 92.4% of U.S. kindergartners had their MMR shots, CDC data show. That was down from 95.2% before the pandemic and under the 95% that epidemiologists say measles herd immunity requires. Exemptions hit a record 4.2%.

Boerner didn’t name Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or any specific policy. He did spell out what he thinks keeps the U.S. ahead: a public-private partnership built around the NIH, a deep biotech scene, access to capital, drugmakers that work from discovery to sale, and “an FDA that’s the sort of global standard.” Under all of it, he noted, sits “a respect for science.”.

Sources indicate that “Whenever you undermine any piece of that ecosystem, it impacts the whole,” he remarked. “If we want to continue to benefit from advanced therapies, including some of the world’s best vaccines, I think we need to be mindful of improving that ecosystem and being very careful about policies that don’t.”.

Pressed on how he felt personally, he called it “clearly troubling.”.

Recent findings suggest that his restraint stands out against his peers. Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla told investors last December that “science is replaced with political beliefs” at HHS, BioSpace reported. At Davos in January, asked what stands in the way of a better vaccine conversation, Bourla answered: “The Secretary of Health.”.

In December 2025, Bristol Myers was one of nine drugmakers to sign most-favored-nation pricing deals with the White House. On Tuesday, Boerner credited the president with getting one big thing “absolutely” right, which is that other countries “are not paying their fair share.” He pointed to the U.K.’s pledge, in its pharmaceutical trade deal with the U.S., to double its spending on innovative medicines over about a decade.

The CDC, for its part, played down the designation. “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz noted in a statement Tuesday, pointing to $100 million the agency has sent to state and local health departments.

According to recent reports, on cost, Boerner went straight at the system around his industry. Medicines are about 10% to 15% of U.S. health spending and have been for a decade, he remarked, so “we got to bring the other 85% to the table.” Roughly 50 cents of every dollar spent on a branded drug goes to someone who had nothing to do with discovering or developing it. “That screams inefficiency,” he said, borrowing the president’s word, “middlemen.” He said BMS runs assistance programs for uninsured and underinsured patients that it is “prohibited by statute” from offering to people on Medicare. “That’s unacceptable. We should fix that.” He also said he’d happily be paid more when a drug works and less when it doesn’t. U.S. rules make those deals hard, so BMS does far more of them abroad.

In a recent development, inside the manufacturer, he’s rebuilding how drugs get made. Last week BMS said it will fold research and development into a single organization under chief medical officer Cristian Massacesi starting Jan. 1. Chief research officer Robert Plenge will leave after an advisory stint through March. The traditional boundaries between research and development “are collapsing,” Boerner said in the announcement. AI is part of the reason. He told Brady the technology lets BMS run in parallel work that used to happen in sequence. The company has committed to cutting the time from a drug entering the clinic to approval by 30%. Boerner thinks AI “will beat that by a mile.”.

PAHO expects the U.S. to submit a proposal in the coming weeks to stop measles transmission. Getting the status back means going at least a year without an unbroken chain of spread. Boerner’s prescription went wider than one virus. “We’ve got to be mindful of the entire ecosystem,” he mentioned, “and treat it like an ecosystem.”.

14 key facts about the DEFIANCE Act and Paris Hilton's push for it
