💡 Key Takeaways
  • 14 facts on the DEFIANCE Act, from the right to sue and damages to Paris Hilton's push and the House vote that has not happened.
  • In a recent development, sexual deepfakes have stopped being an occasional celebrity scandal and become something people produce in bulk.
  • That broad agreement has not given victims a federal way to go after the person behind an image themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

14 facts on the DEFIANCE Act, from the right to sue and damages to Paris Hilton's push and the House vote that has not happened.

In a recent development, sexual deepfakes have stopped being an occasional celebrity scandal and become something people produce in bulk. The number of nonconsensual deepfake porn videos online has grown ninefold since 2019, according to one researcher's count reported by the Senate Judiciary Committee. The volume has since moved well past the figures in the policy debate. At least 1.8 million explicit images were shared through the Grok chatbot in just nine days, according to a New York Times analysis reported by ABC News. For a victim, the problem is no longer a single image to report and remove but an unknown number of copies spread across the internet. Few people defend the practice. In a poll published in 2024, 84% of respondents told the Artificial Intelligence Policy Institute that deepfake porn should be illegal, according to TIME. The harm itself is not in dispute.

That broad agreement has not given victims a federal way to go after the person behind an image themselves. The argument in Washington is over which tool fits the harm. Prosecutors could bring criminal charges, platforms could be forced to take images down, or victims could file lawsuits that they control. The DEFIANCE Act would supply the third option, and even it would have a hard edge. The bill would apply in the United States only, according to ABC News. A creator working from another country would fall outside its remedy. Because of that limit, the real test of each provision is what it can do for a victim and what it cannot.

Congress.gov set out to outline what the DEFIANCE Act does and why Paris Hilton backs it, weighing the bill's mechanics alongside its most visible champion, from suing under a pseudonym to the time victims would have to bring a case and the end of the "it's only a fake" defense. Every one of those protections is conditional. The bill has passed the Senate, but the House has not voted, so none of these rights exists yet for anyone harmed by a sexual deepfake. Two questions remain for each provision: whether it fills a gap that existing law leaves open, and whether a lawsuit would work against creators who are anonymous or hard to find.

Recent findings suggest that the DEFIANCE Act would let the person shown in a sexual deepfake decide whether a case goes forward. Under the bill, someone depicted in such an image could file a civil suit in federal court against whoever made or spread it, according to Congress.gov. Rep. Joe Morelle's separate federal proposal, the Preventing Deepfakes of Intimate Images Act, was a criminal bill, according to TIME. Under a criminal law, prosecutors decide which cases to bring. Under DEFIANCE, a victim would not have to wait for her case to become a prosecutor's priority before someone answers for the harm. The bill would also cover more people than the one who made the image. A person who shares or publishes a deepfake made by someone else could be sued, and passing an image along would carry its own legal risk. Anyone who solicits a deepfake could be sued as well, which reaches the person who commissions an image before it exists. A threat to distribute one would be grounds for a suit on its own. A victim facing blackmail could go to court before the image ever spreads.

A federal claim would give victims the same standing in every state. In January 2024, only ten states had criminal laws against nonconsensual deepfakes, and Morelle's criminal bill had seen no action since its introduction, according to TIME. A civil suit in federal court would not depend on where a victim lives or on what her state legislature has passed. The bill's backers present it as a right that belongs to the victim, not as a crackdown run by the government. "Innocent people have a right to defend their reputations and hold perpetrators accountable in court," Sen. Josh Hawley, one of four lawmakers who introduced the bill, stated.

Sources indicate that A lawsuit can make a person pay, but it cannot by itself remove an image from the internet. A victim could win her case and still find the picture online. Keeping deepfakes off social media will take a commitment of resources from the companies that run those sites, and legislation alone will not do it, according to comments by Nina Brown, a Syracuse University professor of media law and technology, reported by TIME. The bill would give a victim leverage over the person behind an image, but not over the sites that host it.

That leaves an open question: whether a victim can identify and reach the person she needs to sue.

A victim who wins a DEFIANCE Act case could leave court with more than a check, because a judge could also order the images taken offline and make the defendant cover her legal costs, according to CNBC. Those two remedies address a victim's most practical needs: getting the image down and not paying for the fight herself. The bill would also let a victim seek punitive damages, an award that goes beyond repaying what she lost. Those damages penalize the person who made or spread the image. For the bill's best-known advocate, that penalty is the point. "People need to know that there's going to be consequences for their actions," said Paris Hilton, chief advocacy officer at Loti AI. Backers want the money to deter the next creator as well as to compensate the person depicted.

Sources indicate that the bill also puts a dollar figure on a win. Damages under the DEFIANCE Act would start at $150,000, according to Bloomberg Law figures reported by Congress.gov. A victim and her lawyer would have that figure in hand when deciding whether a case is worth the time and the exposure of going to court. Taken together, the remedies would make a deepfake expensive for whoever made or spread it, from the removal order through the punitive award.

The bill pairs a way to get the image offline with a real cost for the person behind it.

Under the DEFIANCE Act, a victim of a sexual deepfake would have 10 years to sue, according to Congress.gov and the University of Cincinnati Law Review. That period would not begin on the day someone first posted the image. Under the bill, it would start on whichever comes later: the day the victim discovers the image or the day she turns 18. A deepfake that appears long before its subject learns of it would still be grounds for a lawsuit when she finally finds it.

The two starting points protect two groups of victims. A person depicted as a child would not lose any of her time to sue while she was still a minor. Her period would begin at adulthood, so she could decide for herself, as an adult, whether to go to court. A person who finds an image years after it surfaced would keep the full period from the moment she learns of it. That matters for a harm that spreads through copies a victim may never see until a friend, an employer or a search result turns one up. Under a deadline tied to the first posting, those victims could lose their right to sue before they knew they had a case.

The 10 years would also give a victim room to find a lawyer, gather evidence and weigh whether to go forward. She would not have to make that choice in the first weeks after a painful discovery.

A victim who learns of a deepfake late would not, under this bill, find that she had also learned of it too late.

The DEFIANCE Act cleared the Senate without a single dissent, and the House has yet to vote on it. The Senate passed the bill unanimously on Jan. 13, 2026, according to Congress.gov, with no senator willing to stand against it. The bill has stalled in the House since then. "For 10 months, this critical legislation has sat untouched in the House, just waiting to be put on the floor," Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from Upcoming York, stated, as reported by Parade. Until the House acts, none of the new protections in the bill is available to victims.

Sources indicate that congress has stalled on this bill before, and earlier versions of it never got through the House. The Senate passed one of those versions unanimously in 2024, according to Parade, and senators passed the bill again in 2026. Each latest round of Senate support indicates the same agreement again without bringing the bill any closer to law.

Recent findings suggest that the holdup does not run along party lines. The bill has bipartisan support, and its House cosponsors include Rep. Laurel Lee, a Republican from Florida, alongside Ocasio-Cortez, according to Parade. Advocates have therefore turned from winning votes to winning a place on the House schedule. The bill does not need more supporters. It needs House leaders to bring it to the floor.

Until they do, the Senate's unanimous support remains a promise to deepfake victims rather than a right they can use.

According to recent reports, paris Hilton argues for the DEFIANCE Act as a victim first and a spokesperson second. An intimate video of Hilton leaked in 2003, when she was 19, according to Congress.gov. Hilton says that the law offered her no protection then and that the harm had no name. A lawsuit she could file on her own behalf is exactly what she lacked at 19, and it is what this bill would create.

The 2003 leak explains how Hilton came to the cause, but the harm behind her advocacy is happening now and keeps growing. Over 100,000 explicit AI deepfake images of her exist, according to Hilton's own count reported by ABC News, and no one has checked that figure independently. Each new image brings the harm back. Hilton noted that "each time a new one appears, that horrible feeling returns, that fear that someone somewhere is looking at it right now and thinking it's real." Her injury comes from what a stranger might believe about each image as well as from the image itself, so it returns with every new copy. That makes her a victim whose case is still open, not a survivor recalling an old scandal.

Hilton has pressed the issue in Washington before. ABC News reports that in 2022 she took her case to officials at the White House under President Joe Biden. She also holds the title of chief advocacy officer at Loti AI. Her return to Washington years after that meeting makes her case harder for lawmakers to dismiss as a publicity stop.

For Hilton, the bill is about the next new image as much as the video that leaked in 2003.

In a recent development, for Paris Hilton, the bill's best-known champion, sexual deepfakes are a flood of images rather than a single fake to report and remove. Loti AI has removed more than 60,000 deepfakes of her, according to Hilton's figures reported by Congress.gov. Removals on that scale are far beyond what any one person could manage alone. No one has mentioned how many remain online, so even a cleanup effort that large has no clear finish line. The removal count deserves some caution, because Hilton is chief advocacy officer at Loti AI and has a stake in how the company's work is seen. Takedowns deal with the images, not with the people who make them. A right to sue is meant to reach those people.

Sexual deepfakes also target women who hold public power, including women in Congress. Research by Hilton's team, as she described it, counted 83 women with sexual deepfakes of themselves online among the 156 women serving in the 119th Congress. No independent count has confirmed that finding. If it holds, a majority of the women in Congress have been targeted by the same kind of image the bill addresses. The harm would then reach inside the institution weighing the bill, not only celebrities and private citizens.

The bill's backers are not asking Congress to imagine a harm that, by Hilton's count, has already reached many of its own members.

A victim of a sexual deepfake can already see an abuser charged with a crime and can make a platform remove the image. She has no federal right to take the creator to court herself. Victims have lived with that gap since the TAKE IT DOWN Act became law in May 2025, according to the NYU Annual Survey of American Law. That law makes publishing intimate depictions, including sexual deepfakes, a crime, but it gives victims no civil cause of action. Prosecutors and platforms hold the controls under the existing law. The DEFIANCE Act would give victims a civil suit of their own, according to Congress.gov. That makes the bill a companion to TAKE IT DOWN rather than a rival, and the case for it rests on what the first law leaves undone.

It has been revealed that A takedown moves quickly once a platform learns of an image, but the clock does not start before then. Under TAKE IT DOWN, platforms face a 48-hour takedown requirement that begins when they are notified, the NYU Annual Survey of American Law reports, and someone has to find a copy and report it first. Each removal erases one copy and costs the person who made it nothing. Under the DEFIANCE Act, the defendants would be the creators and distributors of an image. Sites that host the images keep broad protection for what their consumers post under Section 230, at 47 U.S.C. § 230, so the bill aims at the people behind an image rather than the sites that carry it.

A right to sue gives victims an option, not a fix for every case. Many victims want the image gone and nothing more, and many would rather stay away from police and courtrooms altogether, according to comments by Carrie Goldberg, an attorney and image-based abuse expert at the firm C.A. Goldberg, reported by the NYU Annual Survey of American Law. Victims are best served by having both laws. A takedown serves the victim who wants the image gone, and a suit would serve the victim who wants its maker held to account.

Federal law already offers removal, and the DEFIANCE Act would let a victim go after the person who made the image.

If the DEFIANCE Act becomes law, the Senate's version is the likeliest text to carry it, because it has already passed one chamber. The Senate passed S. 1837 on Jan. 13, 2026, and the House has yet to act on it, according to Congress.gov. Its sponsor is Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., who serves as Senate Democratic Whip and Judiciary Committee Ranking Member, according to the Senate Judiciary Committee. A whip's job is to count votes, and Durbin used that position to move the bill through the Senate. He also had a partner in Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham as co-lead, so senators took up the bill as a measure from both parties rather than one.

Sources indicate that the Senate's unanimous vote means that no senator tried to stop the bill, which is a narrower kind of support than the word "unanimous" suggests. The Senate Judiciary Committee reports that no senator objected to its passage. That result demonstrates that no senator was willing to oppose the bill openly. It does not show how hard any senator would work to see it through. For a victim waiting on the right to sue, the clean Senate result signals goodwill but guarantees nothing.

Recent findings suggest that durbin treated the Senate win as half the job. "Now, let's pass this in the House and make it the law of the land," Durbin remarked, as reported by the Senate Judiciary Committee. The senator who carried the bill through his own chamber knows that the vote there does nothing for victims until the House votes too.

That leaves the bill's fate with the House, the chamber that has not yet voted.

Recent findings suggest that victims cannot use the rights in the DEFIANCE Act unless the House passes a bill of its own, and House members have already introduced one. The House version of the DEFIANCE Act carries the number H.R. 3562, according to Congress.gov, which gives readers a specific bill to follow. As a companion bill, it asks House members to take up the same protections the Senate bill contains rather than write a new approach to sexual deepfakes. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is one of its two leaders. Rep. Laurel Lee, R-Fla., leads it with her, so a lawmaker from each party has put her name at the top of the House bill.

Industry observers note that that pairing means neither party in the House can treat a deepfake victim's right to sue as the other side's cause. A lead sponsor from each party still sets no date for a floor vote, though. Lawmakers can introduce a bill and stand behind it for months without the House ever taking it up. Backing for H.R. 3562 is already in place, and the decision to bring it to a vote has not been made. Until the House makes that decision, the federal right to sue over a sexual deepfake that the DEFIANCE Act would create remains out of reach for victims.

In a recent development, for anyone waiting on that right, H.R. 3562 is now the bill to watch.

The DEFIANCE Act would not add a newly introduced law to the federal books. Congress would instead rewrite one that already exists. Under the bill, the changes would go into 15 U.S.C. 6851, an existing section of the U.S. Code, and would extend it to cover what the bill calls "intimate digital forgeries," according to Congress.gov. With that language, the statute would name sexual deepfakes outright. A victim would then bring her claim under a section of federal law that already deals with intimate images rather than under a statute written from nothing.

Sources indicate that the statute Congress would amend is recent. Congress enacted it as Section 1309 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022, a large spending package, and the DEFIANCE Act amends that section rather than replacing it with a separate law. Congress is being asked to broaden a remedy it has already enacted, not to design one from the start. That shapes the decision in front of the House. Members would not be debating whether federal law should address intimate-image abuse at all, because the 2022 law already exists. They would be deciding whether that remedy should name forged images explicitly. For victims, the change would place a deepfake claim inside a section of law that has been on the books since 2022, not in an untested upcoming statute.

Until the House passes the change, the 2022 statute stays as written, without the words "intimate digital forgeries.".

According to recent reports, A sexual deepfake usually damages a victim's reputation, safety and peace of mind, and that kind of harm rarely highlights up on a pay stub or a medical bill. Under the DEFIANCE Act, a victim would not have to prove any financial loss to seek damages of $150,000, according to Congress.gov. The harm would count even when it cost her nothing she could measure. A woman who kept her job and lost no income but still has to live with the image would have a claim worth bringing. If damages depended on proven losses, she would have had little to claim.

According to recent reports, that sum works as a limit on the standard award, and the difference matters to anyone weighing a lawsuit. The University of Cincinnati Law Review describes $150,000 as the cap for standard liquidated damages, so a court could award that much but not more in an ordinary case. A victim should treat the figure as the most the basic award offers, not as a set check she can expect to collect.

Recent findings suggest that A court could award more when the image is part of a wider campaign against a victim. When a deepfake is connected to stalking, harassment or a sexual assault, the cap rises to $250,000, according to the University of Cincinnati Law Review. The higher limit depends on danger to the victim, not on how far the image spread. The victims facing the most physical risk could recover the most.

Any award is a judgment against a person, and many creators of sexual deepfakes post from anonymous accounts that are hard to trace. Kennedy Aikey, an associate member of the University of Cincinnati Law Review, argues that the bill needs added tools, such as provenance metadata and identity checks on high-risk AI tools, to put the remedy within reach. "Without such measures, the civil remedies promised by the DEFIANCE Act may remain largely symbolic, offering recognition of harm without a realistic path to justice," Aikey wrote. A victim would no longer have to prove loss, but she would still have to find the defendant.

Whether she can name the person to sue matters more than the size of the award, and these dollar limits do nothing to answer that question.

A single fixed award cannot fit every case of deepfake abuse, and the DEFIANCE Act would let victims seek other kinds of compensation as well. A winning victim could recover actual losses and the defendant's profits and could ask a court to order the images removed, according to Congress.gov. Under that remedy, a person who makes these images to sell could be ordered to hand over what the sales earned and would be left with nothing to show for the work. The removal order addresses the rest of the harm. A payment alone would leave the image online, where people could keep finding it and the injury to the victim would continue.

Sources indicate that courts could also punish a defendant on top of repaying the victim. Punitive damages are among the remedies, which means the law would treat a sexual deepfake as wrongdoing to deter rather than as a debt to settle. The cost of the case would not stay with the victim, either. A right to sue means little to someone who would spend more on the lawsuit than a win would return. A victim who prevailed could make the defendant cover her lawyer's bill and the expenses of bringing the case, so her own savings would not pay for holding someone to account.

Instead of one sum for everyone, a court could match the award to what a particular victim lost and what a particular defendant gained.

Industry observers note that under the DEFIANCE Act, calling a sexual deepfake fake would not protect the person who made it. The easiest defense open to a maker is to admit the image isn't real and argue that nobody is harmed when nobody is fooled. The bill rejects that argument: a disclaimer saying the image is fake would not make it lawful, according to Congress.gov. A maker who stamped a label on the picture would face the same lawsuit as one who passed it off as genuine. The injury, in practice, becomes the sexual depiction of a real person without consent, and whether a viewer believes the image is real would not decide the case.

For a victim, the rule removes a fight before it starts. She would not have to prove that anyone mistook the image for a real photograph, and that proof would be hard to supply when the image is openly labeled as fake. The rule also takes away an easy workaround for anyone who would otherwise caption an image "parody" or "AI-generated" and keep sharing it. Under the bill, that caption would offer no legal cover. A victim's case would turn on what the image highlights and on whether she agreed to it, not on how a stranger might read it.

A maker's honesty about the forgery would earn no protection under the bill, and only the victim's consent would.

For a victim of a sexual deepfake, filing a lawsuit is a public act that can attach her real name to the image she wants to disappear. The DEFIANCE Act would let a victim file her case under an assumed name, so that the public record of the lawsuit would not reveal who she is, according to Congress.gov. That provision decides who can realistically bring a case. The right to sue would no longer belong only to people willing to see their names in court filings beside a description of a sexual image. A victim who wants the creator held to account would not have to give up her privacy a second time to do it. Without a pseudonym, the damages, the removal orders and the long window to file would all carry a cost that many victims would refuse to pay. With one, those remedies become something a private person could actually use, and not just a celebrity whose name is already public.

The protection covers only the person who brings the suit. It keeps the plaintiff's identity private, and it notes nothing about the identity of the person who made or shared the image. A victim who files under a pseudonym would still have to name a defendant, and many creators of sexual deepfakes post through anonymous accounts. The pseudonym provision gives a victim no help in learning who that person is.

Under the bill, a victim could keep her own name out of the case, but the person who harmed her could stay unnamed as well.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. serves Trump Jollibee in a moment of culinary diplomacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (457 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Jollibee is a very, very popular chain, and one of their main products is fried chicken,” Marcos said at the opening of his bilateral meeting with Trump on Wednesday.
  • In a recent development, while in Manila, Trump revealed that he’d agreed “a very massive trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far” with the Philippines, yet offered no details.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he sent President Donald Trump a “taste of Manila”—sending fried chicken from Jollibee, the Philippines’ largest fast-food chain, to the U.S. president and his delegation as a late-night snack on Tuesday, ahead of their bilateral meeting in Manila on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that “Jollibee is a very, very popular chain, and one of their main products is fried chicken,” Marcos said at the opening of his bilateral meeting with Trump on Wednesday. “We are very proud to say that we have surpassed KFC in the United States in terms of popularity.”.

In a recent development, while in Manila, Trump revealed that he’d agreed “a very massive trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far” with the Philippines, yet offered no details. Marcos’s office has not confirmed the agreement of a trade deal.

The delivery was culinary diplomacy for a chain that’s become a national symbol at home and has ambitions to break into the U.S. market.

Industry observers note that started in 1975 as an ice cream parlor by Filipino businessman Tony Tan Caktiong, Jollibee is best known for its “Chickenjoy” fried chicken and a sweet-style spaghetti topped with sliced hot dogs. The chain has more than 1,600 stores across 17 countries, according to its website.

According to recent reports, its parent, Jollibee Foods Corporation, runs a portfolio of about 20 brands—including Chinese-food chain Chowking, dim sum chain Tim Ho Wan, and U.S. burger chain Smashburger—with more than 10,000 stores and cafés across 33 countries. With $5.3 billion in annual revenue, Jollibee ranks No. 71 on the Fortune Southeast Asia 500.

In January, Jollibee said it would separate its domestic and international businesses; in September, the company named the international unit Jollibee Foods Corporation International (JFCI) and chose Hong Kong for its proposed listing.

Marcos may be overstating his claim about Jollibee’s popularity in the U.S. Jollibee has just over 100 stores in North America, including Canada. KFC, by comparison, has over 3,500 U.S. locations, according to its official website. Yum Brands, KFC’s parent company, reported $8.2 billion in revenue last year.

Jollibee has become an obligatory stop for visiting leaders.

Fresh Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon ate at a Jollibee in Manila’s business district on the first day of an official visit in April 2024; Marcos posted his own Jollibee order—hamburgers, fried chicken, and palabok, a Filipino noodle dish—to Facebook afterward.

In a recent development, on Nov. 15, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese visited a Jollibee restaurant as the chain declared plans to expand into Australia, where more than 400,000 people were born in the Philippines, making the Filipino-born population the country’s fifth-largest diaspora community, according to a statement from Albanese’s office.

#29750. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1347 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nulltx ↗ Open Full Page

SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text.
  • Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft.
  • Sources indicate that the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, the SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list states a lot.

Sources indicate that the White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets claims it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Recent findings suggest that review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule highlights up in a White House queue.

Industry observers note that "Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record notes what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Industry observers note that rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

Industry observers note that the SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Industry observers note that existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ claims a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency prepares for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

In a recent development, commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move swiftly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Sources indicate that crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

Industry observers note that the sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am.
  • Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.
  • The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am.

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Industry observers note that amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he noted in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

In a recent development, pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s aims for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk.

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, remarked in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”.

It has been revealed that some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”.

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”.

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others remarked the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She swiftly responded via text.

Recent findings suggest that “No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A look at 10 of the biggest IPOs in history, from NTT DoCoMo in 1998 to Saudi Aramco in 2019, spanning banks, tech, telecom, insurance, autos and energy.
  • The size of an initial public offering sounds like a simple number, but it rarely is.
  • Sources indicate that the first variable is the greenshoe, also called the overallotment option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A look at 10 of the biggest IPOs in history, from NTT DoCoMo in 1998 to Saudi Aramco in 2019, spanning banks, tech, telecom, insurance, autos and energy.

The size of an initial public offering sounds like a simple number, but it rarely is. Two lists of the biggest IPOs in history can put the same deals in a different order, and neither list has to be wrong. The gap usually comes down to what gets counted.

Sources indicate that the first variable is the greenshoe, also called the overallotment option. It lets underwriters sell more shares than a organization first planned to offer when demand is strong. Some tallies count only the base deal. Others count the full amount raised once the greenshoe is exercised. On a large offering, that choice can move a deal up or down a list.

Industry observers note that the second variable is the dual listing. Some companies sell shares on two exchanges at about the same time, often one in mainland China and one in Hong Kong. Combining both portions produces a larger figure than counting either market alone. Currency conversion adds another layer. Many of these deals were priced in riyals, yen, yuan or Hong Kong dollars rather than U.S. dollars. Dollar totals depend on the exchange rate used.

Sources indicate that for those reasons, this piece does not offer a definitive ranking. It covers 10 of the largest stock market debuts on record, presented in chronological order rather than by size. The selection runs from a Japanese mobile carrier in 1998 to a Saudi oil producer in 2019.

Recent findings suggest that the deals span six trading venues: the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Shanghai, Hong Kong, the New York Stock Exchange, Nasdaq $NDAQ and Saudi Arabia's Tadawul. They also cross industries. Chinese lenders sit alongside a payment network, a social network, an e-commerce group, an Asia-focused insurer, a carmaker and two Japanese telecom operators.

In a recent development, the reasons behind the offerings varied as much as the companies did. Some were partial sales by state owners or parent companies. Others followed a corporate rescue or a breakup. A few gave public investors their first chance to own shares in a large internet business.

Each slide covers when and where the firm went public, how the deal was priced or sized, and what set the listing apart at the time it happened.

Recent findings suggest that NTT DoCoMo, the mobile phone unit of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, went public in Japan in 1998. The offering was one of the largest IPOs of its era.

According to recent reports, the deal turned a wireless division into a listed firm of its own. Before the offering, outside investors could gain exposure to the mobile business only through its parent. After the listing, they could buy shares in the mobile operator directly.

DoCoMo remained a unit of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone after the listing. The parent kept its ties to the mobile business even as public shareholders came on board.

According to recent reports, this kind of transaction is known as a carve-out listing. A large parent sells shares in one of its businesses while keeping a connection to that business. The parent can raise money this way. The market, in turn, puts a separate price on the unit.

The 1998 date makes DoCoMo's offering an early example of a very large telecom listing. It came years before the Chinese bank, U.S. technology and Saudi energy offerings of the 2000s and 2010s.

According to recent reports, industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) raised roughly $21.9 billion in October 2006 through a dual listing in Shanghai and Hong Kong. It was among the first very large Chinese bank listings.

It has been revealed that ICBC is a state-owned commercial bank headquartered in Beijing. It is one of the large state-owned lenders at the center of China's banking system.

The bank divided its offering between two exchanges. One portion of the shares listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in mainland China. The other portion listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

It has been revealed that shares of mainland Chinese companies that trade in Shanghai are known as A shares. They are priced in yuan. Shares of mainland companies that trade in Hong Kong are known as H shares. They are priced in Hong Kong dollars. ICBC's offering used both share classes.

In a recent development, agricultural Bank of China, a state-owned lender, went public in July 2010 in an offering that raised roughly $22 billion. It sold shares on two markets, Shanghai and Hong Kong.

The listing gave public investors on both exchanges a way to own shares in a Chinese state-owned bank.

Recent findings suggest that published totals for the deal differ from one report to another. The roughly $22 billion figure is an approximation, not an exact sum.

Industry observers note that the offering arrived in a busy year for very large listings. AIA Group went public in Hong Kong in October 2010. General Motors $GM returned to public markets in November 2010.

General Motors $GM returned to public markets in November 2010, pricing its common shares at $33 each. The offering ranked among the largest U.S. stock sales of its time.

The listing followed the automaker's 2009 bankruptcy restructuring and a rescue by the U.S. government. That sequence set it apart from most deals on lists of record IPOs.

Sources indicate that many of the largest offerings involve a tech giant selling shares to outside investors for the first time. A state-owned bank, a subsidiary separated from its parent or a privately held tech business would fit that pattern. General Motors had been a public company before its bankruptcy. Its 2010 sale was a return to the market rather than a first appearance.

Sources indicate that alibaba Group's initial public offering on the Upcoming York Stock Exchange in September 2014 raised about $25 billion once the overallotment option was exercised. It was the largest U.S. IPO, and the manufacturer behind it was not American.

Industry observers note that alibaba is a Chinese e-commerce group. It priced its shares at $68 each for its NYSE debut.

The roughly $25 billion total includes the extra shares sold through the greenshoe. A count limited to the base deal would put a smaller figure on the same offering.

The deal also stood out for where it took place. Alibaba chose a U.S. exchange for its listing rather than a market in China.

That choice meant a foreign manufacturer carried out the largest IPO on a U.S. exchange. The record went to a Chinese e-commerce business listing in New York, not to an American company.

Saudi Aramco raised about $25.6 billion when it went public on Saudi Arabia's Tadawul exchange in December 2019. The oil manufacturer was valued at about $1.7 trillion at listing.

The shares were priced at 32 riyals each. Aramco sold them on its home exchange. It did not add a listing in New York or Hong Kong.

That choice set the deal apart from several other very large offerings. Some companies went public on a foreign market. Others sold shares on two markets at about the same time. Aramco's offering took place on a single domestic exchange and was priced in the country's own currency.

In a recent development, the $25.6 billion figure counts the greenshoe. Aramco's total reached that level only after the overallotment option was exercised. Any comparison with another offering depends on whether that deal's total was measured the same way.

The two-market structure gave the bank access to two separate pools of investors. Domestic buyers could take part through Shanghai. Foreign investors faced limits on buying mainland-listed shares at the time. They could take part through Hong Kong instead.

Recent findings suggest that the listing made ICBC a publicly traded organization. The Chinese state remained its controlling shareholder after the offering.

Visa $V went public on the Fresh York Stock Exchange in March 2008, selling shares at $44 each. The offering raised about $17.9 billion, making it the largest U.S. IPO at the time of its listing.

It has been revealed that visa runs a payment network. Its system carries transactions between the banks that matter Visa-branded cards, the merchants that accept those cards and the cardholders who use them.

Industry observers note that visa does not lend money to cardholders. The banks that issue the cards handle the lending. Investors in the offering were buying into the network that moves card payments, not a lender holding consumer debt on its own books.

Sources indicate that before the IPO, Visa was owned by the financial institutions that belonged to its network. Those banks were both its owners and its customers. The offering changed that arrangement. Outside investors could now hold a stake in the organization alongside the banks that had built it.

The $44 figure was the offer price. Investors who received shares in the offering paid that amount. The price was set before the stock began trading. After the opening, the share price moved with buying and selling on the exchange.

Sources indicate that the amount an IPO raises reflects the cash the offering brings in. It is not a measure of what the whole company is worth. Visa's total described the money raised from the shares it sold, not a valuation of the business.

The record Visa set applied to U.S. exchanges. No earlier IPO on a U.S. exchange had raised as much when Visa listed. The mark belonged to that moment rather than standing as a permanent high for U.S. offerings.

Sources indicate that the timing also set the deal apart. Visa listed in the same month that Bear Stearns agreed to a sale to JPMorgan $JPM Chase in a rescue backed by the Federal Reserve. A record-size offering went ahead while U.S. financial markets were under heavy strain.

Recent findings suggest that AIA Group, an insurer focused on Asia, went public on the Hong Kong stock exchange in October 2010 and raised about $20.5 billion. The listing followed AIA's separation from its former parent, American International Group (AIG).

That separation set the deal apart from a typical IPO. In a standard first-time offering, a organization that built itself up independently sells shares to outside investors. AIA had a different history. It was an established insurance business that operated inside a larger U.S. group before it became a standalone company.

According to recent reports, A listing of this kind is often called a carve-out. A parent takes a business it already owns and sets it up as a separate organization. Investors are then offered shares in that business directly. In a carve-out, the seller of the shares can be the parent group rather than the business being listed.

For AIA, the result was an independent insurer with its own shares trading in Hong Kong. Before the split, an investor who wanted a stake in its operations had to buy into AIG as a whole. After the listing, AIA could be owned on its own.

Sources indicate that that change gave investors what markets often call a pure play. AIA's share price would track the results of one Asian insurance business, not the wider mix of operations held inside AIG.

The choice of exchange matched the organization's footprint. AIA's business is concentrated in Asia. A Hong Kong listing put its shares on an exchange inside the region where it operates.

Recent findings suggest that the amount raised is the reason the deal appears among the largest IPOs on record. At about $20.5 billion, the AIA offering reached a size more often associated with state-owned banks, large technology companies and national energy producers. Among the 10 offerings in this selection, it is the only one from the insurance industry.

It has been revealed that the offering came after the bankruptcy process and the government rescue. It put the carmaker's common shares back in front of public investors.

Recent findings suggest that accounts of the total amount raised differ. The gap depends on whether preferred shares sold in the deal are counted alongside the common stock. The $33 price for common shares is the figure that stays consistent across those accounts.

In a recent development, the deal highlights that a place on lists of the largest stock market debuts does not always mean a company was fresh to investors. A carmaker coming out of bankruptcy appears in the same company as banks and tech businesses that were going public for the first time.

According to recent reports, facebook $META went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ in May 2012, pricing its shares at $38 each. The offering raised about $16 billion and valued the social network at roughly $104 billion at pricing.

Those two figures measure different things. The $16 billion is the cash raised by selling shares in the offering. The $104 billion is the value that the $38 price placed on the whole firm.

Sources indicate that seen together, they show that the IPO was a partial sale. Public investors bought a portion of the business, not the entire company. Existing shareholders kept the rest.

The $104 billion figure was also a snapshot taken before trading began. It reflected the offer price, not a price set by buyers and sellers on the open market. Once the shares started trading, the tech giant's market value moved with the stock price.

Recent findings suggest that facebook also stood apart from many large IPO candidates. It was a consumer service known well beyond the investment world. The listing gave public investors a way to buy shares in the social network on an exchange.

In a recent development, the company chose Nasdaq over the Upcoming York Stock Exchange. Nasdaq has long been the listing venue for many large U.S. technology companies. That choice tied the debut to Nasdaq's own trading systems.

According to recent reports, the first trading session did not run smoothly. Technical problems at Nasdaq disrupted the debut and affected trading in the newly introduced shares. The trouble drew attention to the exchange's systems as well as to the stock.

It has been revealed that by the close, Facebook shares had finished close to the $38 offer price. The stock ended its first session with little change from the level set in the offering. Investors who bought at the offer price ended the day with little gain or loss on paper.

The tech giant that sold those shares now operates as Meta Platforms. The May 2012 offering marks the point at which the social network first became a publicly traded company.

SoftBank Corp, the mobile carrier unit of SoftBank Group, went public on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in December 2018. The offering raised roughly $23.5 billion, which made it one of the largest IPOs ever.

The shares sold belonged to the carrier, not to its parent. SoftBank Group is a Tokyo-based conglomerate founded by Masayoshi Son. Son started the group in 1981. It holds stakes in technology businesses around the world. The mobile network is one business inside that group, and it was the part offered to public investors.

It has been revealed that the carrier traces its roots to the group's 2006 purchase of Vodafone's Japanese mobile business. SoftBank rebranded that operation under its own name. By the time of the listing, it was one of Japan's three major mobile carriers, alongside NTT DoCoMo and KDDI. It also sells plans under the Y!mobile brand.

A parent firm can sell shares in a subsidiary while its own stock stays listed. The deal raises cash from a business the parent already owns without selling the whole group. SoftBank Group kept majority control of the carrier after the offering. Buyers of the fresh shares gained direct exposure to the carrier's operations. They did not gain a claim on the parent's wider portfolio of investments.

Recent findings suggest that the Tokyo Stock Exchange is Japan's largest equity market. Japan had seen a large mobile listing before. NTT DoCoMo, the mobile arm of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, went public in Japan in 1998. Both companies were mobile units of larger Japanese telecom groups.

It has been revealed that softBank Corp's debut followed Alibaba's 2014 listing in New York. It preceded Saudi Aramco's December 2019 share sale on Saudi Arabia's Tadawul exchange.

The valuation and the amount raised measure different things. The roughly $1.7 trillion figure put a price on the whole of Aramco. The $25.6 billion figure is the money raised from the shares on offer. Investors in the IPO bought only a small slice of the company.

Industry observers note that the two numbers sit on different scales. One is counted in trillions of dollars, the other in billions. That gap is what a small sale of a very large organization looks like on paper.

In a recent development, it also explains how one listing could sit among the largest stock market debuts on record while most of Aramco's shares stayed out of public trading. The offering set a market value for the entire oil producer, even though the cash came from selling only part of it.

Dogecoin co-creator Billy Markus, who goes by Shibetoshi Nakamoto on X, has weighed in on Bitcoin's potential role as an alternative to traditional retirement savings, describing Bitcoin as having the "best reason to exist.".

A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement savings plan in the United States that typically allows workers to invest through a selection of financial products, often including mutual funds and exchange-traded funds.

According to recent reports, the discussion began on X as market participants reacted to the ongoing market crash, which has seen millions of dollars in liquidations in the last 24 hours. Leveraged traders took the brunt, with $1.92 billion of liquidations over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data. Longs accounted for the majority of the damage at $1.59 billion, while short liquidations totaled $341.26 million.

Bitcoin fell to a three-month low below $63,000; Dogecoin fell to a low of $0.055, last seen in June 2023. At the time of writing, Dogecoin was down 4.63% over the last 24 hours to $0.059.

An X user commented, apparently in light of the market drop, "Cash out or crash out.".

@mikethree bitcoin has the best reason to exist as the og, ethereum is a massive failure of its own goals but has positive brand recognition, they’re all dumb tokens for degenerates.

Dogecoin cofounder Billy Markus responded, saying, "I just sell immediately and hold very little since the market is just a delusion indicator and that’s too random to track.".

Another X user joined the discussion, saying Bitcoin remains "a good 401k replacement imo but depends on risk profile obviously." Markus replied to this, saying, "Bitcoin has the best reason to exist as the OG.".

As cryptocurrency adoption increases, more traditionally-minded investors have begun exploring digital assets as part of their retirement intends.

Sources indicate that asset manager Fidelity allows Bitcoin in 401(k) looks, depending on employer approval. Fidelity is primarily known for its huge portfolio of retirement accounts and is among the largest 401(k) providers in the U.S. Fidelity also has a standard account option, announced in April 2022, that allows employees with 401(k) accounts to add Bitcoin, in addition to its more traditional accounts.

Fidelity Investments confirmed a latest retirement strategy in 2025 allowing U.S. adults to directly invest in cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum and Litecoin.

Does the Nvidia turmoil spell trouble for the Gulf’s AI ambitions?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The downfall of Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs—including one involving a suspected Chinese spy—and the turmoil that has engulfed Nvidia in its wake have gripped the world’s attention over the past week.
  • Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy.
  • President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled aims to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The downfall of Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs—including one involving a suspected Chinese spy—and the turmoil that has engulfed Nvidia in its wake have gripped the world’s attention over the past week.

Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy.

During U.S. President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled aims to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. Once complete, it will be the largest facility of its kind outside the U.S. At the heart of the project is Stargate UAE, a 1-GW computing cluster developed by Abu Dhabi-backed G42 in partnership with a host of U.S. companies, including Nvidia, which will supply its Grace Blackwell chips (GB300s).

Recent findings suggest that nvidia has also forged a strong commercial alliance with Saudi Arabia, with Huang among a select group of U.S. tech leaders invited to meet with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his much-feted visit to the White House last November.

During the visit, Elon Musk announced a 500-MW data center in partnership with Saudi government-backed AI manufacturer, Humain, which will be powered by Nvidia’s computing chips.

Trump also hosted Mohammed bin Salman, alongside Huang and Elon Musk, at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum on November 19 last year.

Recent findings suggest that just hours later, the U.S. Commerce Department authorized the export of up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell GB300 chips to both G42 and Humain. Earlier in the day, Humain said it planned to purchase 600,000 Nvidia AI chips.

This relationship was deepened last month when Humain confirmed plans with Nvidia to deploy around 27,000 GPUs and develop up to 84-MW of AI computing capacity in the kingdom across a multi-phase program starting in the fourth quarter of this year and followed by planned large-scale deployments beginning in mid-2027.

While the existing partnerships Nvidia holds with the UAE and Saudi are unlikely to be threatened by Huang’s departure, it could weaken the relationship’s momentum, according to Mohammed Soliman, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, where he focuses on technology and geopolitics.

Recent findings suggest that “The relationship with Nvidia is pretty solid and institutional at this point,” he said. “The deals with G42 and Humain sit on government-to-government agreements that were already in place. That said, Jensen matters a lot and his leaving will have an impact. The overall direction doesn’t change, but losing him as the main driver takes something off the table.”.

Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, expects that the change in leadership at Nvidia could make the company more circumspect in its business dealings with the Gulf.

“Huang was the public face of Nvidia’s sovereign AI pitch and had his own relationships with Gulf leaders, which will be hard to replace swiftly,” said Winter-Levy, whose research focuses on the geopolitics of AI.

“I would assume Nvidia will honor its existing contracts with the Gulf, probably with more attention to compliance and things like end-use checks, but to make fewer splashy announcements of new deals.”.

In July, Washington relaxed export restrictions on the UAE, granting approved organizations greater access to Nvidia chips and other advanced technologies.

For Gulf governments, a more immediate concern is whether the upheaval at Nvidia could make Washington more reluctant to approve further exports of advanced chips, thereby slowing the pace of the region’s AI buildout.

The upheaval has given U.S. lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control bills, such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Last week, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urged Congress to pass the bills, while House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar called for chip export controls to be included in the annual defense policy bill.

“Congress has limited direct power here, since export licenses lie with the executive branch, and the administration has removed many of the license requirements that slowed chip deliveries to the UAE in the past,” mentioned Winter-Levy.

“But oversight raises the political cost of newly introduced Gulf deals, and Congress can attach conditions such as chip location verification to new bills like the NDAA.”.

Chip location verification is a technical and regulatory method used to track the physical location of advanced processors—such as GPUs—to ensure they do not get smuggled or diverted to restricted countries.

According to recent reports, however, on Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, issued an interim rule that requires companies to obtain licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if the equipment could be used by a list of 22 embargoed countries, which includes China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from data centers in third countries.

“The latest remote access rule primarily affects Gulf companies if they are renting large amounts of compute to Chinese-parented firms, but otherwise does not fundamentally change the situation for the UAE,” stated Winter-Levy.

“It does, however, signal that the administration is increasingly prepared to crack down on chip diversion and remote access if it becomes politically salient enough.”.

In the future, it seems increasingly likely that the Gulf will become more vulnerable to U.S. export controls given that, even before Huang’s abrupt departure, Democratic lawmakers had already pushed back against what they viewed as its preferential treatment. They frequently cited fears that China could obtain backdoor access to sensitive U.S. technology through the Gulf.

“There will probably be more political noise out of Washington that could slow some deliveries or stretch timelines,” noted Soliman.

However, the region’s growing role in financing and supporting America’s AI infrastructure could also give the region some leverage in return, according to Winter-Levy.

Recent findings suggest that “The dependence isn’t entirely one-way,” he remarked. “Gulf capital is now part of the American AI buildout, which gives them some leverage. And if U.S. companies come to rely on large quantities of compute housed in the Gulf, that will give the Gulf a degree of leverage over those companies. But the asymmetry is large, since Washington can slow the Gulf’s AI plans with a regulatory notice.”.

Ultimately, Nvidia’s upheaval is unlikely to derail the Gulf’s AI ambitions, but it exposes just how dependent those ambitions remain on decisions made in Washington and Silicon Valley.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia have invested heavily in positioning themselves as global AI powerhouses, but their ability to deliver on those looks hinges on continued access to U.S. technology and political goodwill.

In a recent development, as scrutiny of chip exports intensifies, the challenge for both countries will be to maintain their strategic partnerships while reducing their exposure to shifting U.S. political priorities. For the Gulf, the question is no longer simply whether Nvidia can deliver the chips, but whether Washington will continue to let them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call, the first for CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, came less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned.
  • In a recent development, “Our momentum is real.
  • Board Chair Harvey Jones ended speculation about Huang’s return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good morning. Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call, the first for CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO, came less than a week after Jensen Huang resigned. The firm delivered stronger-than-expected results, but the leadership transition and a latest emphasis on board oversight put governance and regulatory compliance front and center.

In a recent development, “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing,” Kress stated Tuesday on the call.

Board Chair Harvey Jones ended speculation about Huang’s return. “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones mentioned. The board is conducting an independent investigation after Huang disclosed personal behavior inconsistent with company standards.

Heidrick & Struggles has been retained to conduct an internal and external search for Huang’s permanent replacement. Jones stated the board is “enhancing our oversight capacity going forward.” He noted the formation of the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee to oversee national security policies, export-control compliance and global trade risks. Nvidia’s national security and trade compliance teams will report directly to the committee and to Kress for day-to-day operations.

The move underscores the growing importance of compliance for Nvidia and its fresh leadership amid questions about the potential diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

Sources indicate that the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced Monday an interim final rule addressing remote access to advanced computing technology through overseas data centers. Developed at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council, the rule is intended to prevent companies in restricted countries from bypassing export controls through remote computing.

At the center of the glitch are questions about whether advanced Nvidia chips supplied through Megaspeed were diverted to China. U.S. export rules have allowed certain overseas data centers to provide remote computing services to Chinese customers, a distinction from unauthorized transfers of restricted physical chips, Fortune reported.

Industry observers note that kress noted third-quarter sales of licensed Hopper data center products to China totaled $2.4 billion. However, she added: “Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China.”.

For CFOs and corporate directors, Nvidia’s predicament illustrates a broader challenge: As companies expand into strategically sensitive markets, financial performance increasingly depends on the strength of their compliance systems, third-party oversight and internal controls.

For the third quarter ended Oct. 25, Nvidia reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year, and data center revenue of $107.6 billion, up 110%.

Industry observers note that nvidia also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75%, up from its previous projection of 70% and based on a higher fiscal 2027 revenue base, Kress mentioned. Shares rose about 4% in overnight trading.

In a recent development, dan Ives, partner and senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note Wednesday morning that the board had drawn a line on Huang’s reinstatement, Kress had raised the number that matters most, and the financing discipline investors wanted appeared unprompted. The firm maintains its outperform rating and $225 price target.

“The CEO search, the investigation, and the 15% special meeting threshold are the open questions we are still waiting on,” he added.

With a growth engine that remains powerful, the more difficult test for Nvidia’s newly introduced leadership will be showing that the company’s governance and compliance structures are equally capable of managing the risks.

Sheryl EstradaSheryl.Estrada@fortune.com.

From CFO to CEO:Richard McPhail, EVP and CFO of The Home Depot (No. 25), was promoted to CEO, effective Nov. 23. McPhail will succeed Ted Decker, who has returned from a temporary medical leave of absence, but will step down as president and CEO, and he will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors.

McPhail joined the company in 2005 and was named EVP and CFO in September 2019, In this role, he oversaw several transformative acquisitions including HD Supply, SRS Distribution, GMS, Construction Resources and Mingledorff's, which have "helped position The Home Depot as a premier distributor and full-service partner for Pros of all sizes," the company stated.

Jordan Broggi was promoted to EVP and CFO at The Home Depot. Broggi is a 13-year veteran of the firm, most recently serving as EVP of interconnected retail. In this role, he led the online business and customer experience for the company's digital properties, as well as loyalty, credit services and payments. Broggi has held several leadership positions during his tenure, including senior vice president of finance.

The weekly Fortune 500 Power Moves column tracks Fortune 500 firm C-suite shifts—see the most recent edition.

Consumers are increasingly trading down to lower-cost retailers and restaurants as they look for ways to offset rising prices, according to a November report from Bank of America Institute.

Sources indicate that drawing on the bank’s deposit account and credit and debit card spending data, the report found that its Spending Tier Composite, a proxy for trading-down activity, reached its lowest level since 2021, suggesting a greater shift toward value-oriented merchants. Millennials are leading the trend, with their spending tier falling faster than that of Gen X or baby boomers since 2022, particularly in apparel and groceries.

While consumers are choosing less-expensive options for clothing and dining, some households may be forgoing travel altogether rather than switching to cheaper alternatives, the report noted.

"Today, it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first released that flight, which is absurd.".

—Delta CEO Ed Bastian told Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday.

According to recent reports, chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has mentioned that the organization's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

It has been revealed that according to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very promptly in the three months," he noted.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang noted.

In a recent development, fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

Industry observers note that according to Fang, trust is the main problem for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang mentioned.

t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang stated that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

"The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang stated.

#29742. 11 flood safety steps, from the first alert to emotional recovery
