11 flood safety steps, from the first alert to emotional recovery

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learn the difference between a flood watch and a warning, and 9 more safety steps for before, during and after a flood.
  • Staying safe in a flood depends on moving early, because a whole community faces the same flood at the same time.
  • The danger also lasts long after the water drains away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Learn the difference between a flood watch and a warning, and 9 more safety steps for before, during and after a flood.

Staying safe in a flood depends on moving early, because a whole community faces the same flood at the same time. Many people picture a flood as a private emergency at their own front door, judged by the hour when the water stands highest. In practice, neighbors reach for the same roads, the same supplies and the same help all at once. In a single Ottawa flood, the number of basements reported underwater topped 6,000, according to CBC News. The roads out fill up as well, and the CDC advises evacuees to expect heavy traffic on evacuation routes. A household that waits to see what everyone else does has already waited too long, so the useful work has to happen before the water rises.

The danger also lasts long after the water drains away. A falling waterline feels like the end of the emergency, and that is the moment many people relax. The harm keeps coming in the weeks that follow. People face contaminated water and spoiled food, mold in walls nobody dried in time, fumes from generators run in the wrong place, injuries during cleanup and the strain of living through all of it. The signals people rely on are easy to mistake for an all-clear. A flood alert, a line on a flood map and a depth at which water turns dangerous each show where danger starts, not where safety begins. A person on the safe side of any of them can still be at risk. Staying safe means acting before the official signal turns urgent and staying careful well after the flood looks finished.

The American Red Cross laid out flood safety advice that runs from reading the first alert to recovering emotionally afterward. That advice covers the difference between a watch and a warning, the mold that grows in a home left wet, the carbon monoxide that no one can see or smell, and the emotional toll that stays with people after the repairs are done. Taken together, the guidance forms a timeline that starts before the first raindrop and continues well past the cleanup. The reader's job along that timeline is to act sooner at the start and to stay careful longer at the end.

Recent findings suggest that many people hear "watch" and "warning" as two levels of the same alert, but the real difference between them is time. A watch means flooding is merely possible, while a warning means flooding is occurring now or soon, according to the American Red Cross. A household that knows which one is in effect knows whether it still has time or has to act immediately. The CDC claims that people should evacuate when a flood warning is issued or when authorities direct them to leave. A warning is the moment to go. Anyone who starts getting ready at that point has already lost the hours the work required.

The watch stage sounds like permission to wait, but most of the preparation belongs there. During a watch, the CDC's National Center for Environmental Health advises households to fill their vehicle's gas tank, put essential documents in waterproof material and set aside enough water to last at least three days. A full tank lets a family drive out before anyone tells it to go. The papers and the water are already packed when it does. Flooding is only possible during a watch, but that is when nearly all of a household's preparation should happen.

Authorities can also order people to leave, and once they do, a household has no decision left to weigh. "Never ignore an evacuation order," the CDC said.

A household that finished its work during the watch can follow that order in minutes, while one that waited spends the warning packing as the water rises.

Flood risk can change from one block to the next, so the question that matters is whether a particular house is exposed, not whether the region floods. The American Red Cross directs residents to FEMA's Flood Map Service Center, where anyone can search for a home's flood zone by its address. The answer is only as current as the map behind it, and Harris County, Texas, last gave its floodplain maps a comprehensive overhaul in 2007, according to the Houston Chronicle. A house labeled as outside the floodplain is not necessarily free of risk, and the label is where a homeowner's research should begin.

In a recent development, when officials redraw a map, the label on file can change for a great many homes at once. The Houston Chronicle reports that draft maps could shift more than 420,000 properties in the Houston area to a higher-risk rating. If those drafts take effect, the rating those owners have known would no longer describe their risk. The change would not be spread evenly. In Hunterwood, about 85% of parcels, 650 of 764, may be moved to higher risk, the highest share among Houston's super neighborhoods. An owner or buyer should therefore check how the drafts treat the surrounding neighborhood, along with the zone listed for the address.

A flood-zone line also determines what some homeowners must pay. Inside the 100-year floodplain, owners whose mortgages are federally backed are required to buy flood insurance. For those households, a change on a map becomes a new bill. The maps are drafts, and any single home's label could change before they take effect.

The sensible move is to look up the address today and strategy as if the higher-risk label already applied, rather than waiting for a final line or treating the old one as protection.

Most flood safety advice assumes there will be some time between the first alert and the arrival of the water, enough time to understand the threat, weigh the options and move. A flash flood may come with little to no warning, according to the American Red Cross. People caught in one may have no time at all to decide where to go. That changes what preparation means. A household facing a flash flood can't count on an alert to start its planning. The decisions it made in advance are the only ones it can rely on once the water starts to rise.

The plan this threat calls for is simple: choose a spot of higher ground ahead of time, one the household can reach quickly. Speed is the test that matters most. When there is little or no warning, a hill or upper floor that takes too long to reach does nothing for the people who can't get there in time, however high it is. A family should judge each option by how fast everyone in the household could get to it on foot or by car, and pick the closest one that is truly above the water. That choice has to be made on a dry day, when people have time to look at the routes, compare the options and settle on a single place. Every person in the home should know where it is, so no one has to stop and discuss it when the time comes.

A household that already knows where it is going needs no warning time to start moving.

Industry observers note that when forecasters predict a river flood or a storm surge, many households decide to stay put and wait to see how high the water gets. The American Red Cross advises households to learn whether their area is prone to these floods and to review their evacuation strategy so they can leave quickly. The first of those steps belongs well before any alert. A family that learns only on the day of the flood that a river or the sea can reach its home has already lost the head start the rest of the plan depends on. The second step sets the standard for readiness: a plan reviewed in advance turns leaving into a matter of minutes instead of a debate at the kitchen table. A household in a flood-prone area should treat departure as a real possibility and have it worked out before officials make the call. The real decision is made days earlier, and the hours before the water comes should go to carrying it out.

According to recent reports, leaving early also keeps people out of the water itself, and contact with floodwater carries risks that have nothing to do with its depth or speed. Most people judge floodwater by whether it can knock them over or sweep them away. But what is in the water is a hazard of its own, and the safer course is to stay out of it entirely rather than guess how clean or shallow it looks. Some coastal waters naturally carry vibrio bacteria, and a cut exposed to that water during a flood can become infected, according to the CDC. The risk weighs most on anyone who already has a cut, scrape or wound. For them, leaving before the surge arrives keeps broken skin away from water that may hold those bacteria.

A household that gets out ahead of a river or the sea keeps its members clear of the current and of whatever the water carries.

A flooded road rarely looks dangerous, because the water seems shallow and a car feels heavy enough to push through it. Yet a person can be knocked off their feet in 6 inches of fast-moving water, and 12 inches is enough to float a vehicle, according to the American Red Cross. The weight of a car gives no protection in water that shallow, and a driver who stays behind the wheel is inside the vehicle once it floats. The Red Cross places this advice among the steps for the middle of a flood, when the time for preparing has run out. At the water's edge, a driver faces one decision and has seconds to make it: drive in or turn back.

Recent findings suggest that those figures are not a limit to measure the road against. A number invites a driver to treat anything under 6 inches as safe to cross, and that reading is the trap. The CDC's National Center for Environmental Health sets no safe depth for moving water at all. Taken together with the Red Cross thresholds, that position indicates what the figures really mark. They show how promptly floodwater turns deadly, not a level below which wading or driving is safe. The numbers are worth knowing only as proof that very little water is enough to kill.

According to recent reports, two separate safety agencies reduce this advice to a rule rather than a measurement. The Red Cross sums up the point in a short slogan, and the CDC uses the same four words. "Never drive in flooded areas—turn around, don't drown!" the CDC said. The word "never" leaves no exception for a driver who thinks a few inches can be crossed.

Industry observers note that the decision that counts is made before the tires touch the water. Once a car is in the current, the driver has few good choices left.

Sources indicate that the American Red Cross offers a free phone app, the Red Cross Emergency App, that a household can install on its own before a flood arrives. The app costs nothing, so no household has to go without it because of price. The Red Cross also offers a Spanish version, and families who read Spanish rather than English can use the app as well. A household needs to install it before the forecast turns, while there is still time to act ahead of everyone else.

Industry observers note that red Cross help also covers the weeks after the flood, when people feel they should be coping on their own. The Red Cross lists the Disaster Distress Helpline, 1-800-985-5990, under taking care of yourself after a flood. The line is free and takes calls or texts, so anyone can reach help for flood stress from home, without waiting for an office to open or a shelter bed to free up. A household that saves the number when it installs the app will have both ready before anyone needs them.

In a recent development, local recovery help through the Red Cross can come with a fixed end date and a spending limit. On July 15, 2026, Ottawa's city council voted to fund Red Cross recovery work after a local flood, but only for six months and with no more than $400,000 from the city, according to CBC News. Ottawa residents who expect that help to last as long as their own repairs may find it gone before the work is done.

A household that sets up the app and the helpline today, and prepares its repairs without counting on local help to last, will be ready on both counts.

Industry observers note that people need protection before they begin cleaning up after a flood, because the cleanup is where much of the harm happens. Once a house is dry enough to enter, many people go straight back in to clear it, as if the dangerous part were over. The property can stay hazardous long after the flood, with electrocution risk, falling trees and debris among the dangers, according to the American Red Cross. Clearing a home puts people directly among those hazards. "Many injuries happen during cleanup," the Red Cross remarked. Cleanup workers and volunteers should be up to date on tetanus shots, ideally before cleanup begins, according to the CDC. That protection has to be in place on the first day of work, and a tetanus check belongs on the to-do list before the cleanup weekend, not after someone gets cut.

After a flood, the wound to worry about is the one that gets dirty, even if it doesn't look serious at the time. The tetanus concern lies with wounds contaminated by floodwater, soil, waste or saliva, not with contact with the water itself, according to the CDC. Crushing damage also carries a higher chance of infection than a slice through the skin. A finger or foot caught under shifting debris therefore deserves more attention than an open gash that looks worse. Anyone hurt during cleanup should watch a dirty or crushed wound until it heals rather than dismiss it on the day it happens.

A household can finish clearing the house while a wound from that work is still at risk of infection.

In a recent development, the health risk from a flood stays behind after the water drains, in everything the water soaked. "Stay away from floodwaters. They may contain sewage, sharp items, and chemicals that can make you ill," the American Red Cross warned. For that reason, the CDC notes that anything edible the flood or storm reached belongs in the trash. Contact alone is enough to make the food unsafe. After losing so much, people want to save what they can, but food the water reached is a loss, and no amount of cleaning brings it back.

Industry observers note that A kitchen the water never reached can be lost as well. The CDC advises throwing out perishable food that sat unrefrigerated through a power outage, and for anything uncertain it gives the same rule as the Red Cross: if you aren't sure the food is safe, discard it. A refrigerator on a dry upper floor may therefore need emptying as surely as the flooded basement. With that standard, a household has to know food is safe before keeping it rather than prove it spoiled before tossing it. Anything nobody can vouch for after the outage belongs in the trash.

A home the flood never entered can still have unsafe water. Surface water can contaminate groundwater, the CDC reports, and that can affect private wells as well as city systems that draw on groundwater. A household with a private well in a flooded area needs to have the water tested before using it, and the well owner is the one who has to confirm it is safe. Until then, suspect water is off-limits for far more than drinking: mixing baby formula, making ice, cooking, washing hands or dishes and brushing teeth all have to wait. People who would never drink a glass of that water can still be exposed through those routine tasks.

Industry observers note that owners have only hours to dry out a flooded home, and many use up that time before they reach the front door. Most people expect cleanup to begin once the water is gone and they are back inside with time to work. The American Red Cross says a house still wet after 24 to 48 hours should be treated as moldy. Families kept away by an evacuation or a blocked road who can't get back within that time should walk in expecting mold rather than hoping they can still prevent it. For a household that evacuated, those hours may pass before anyone has seen the damage.

It has been revealed that the rule asks owners to act before they see any mold. The 24-to-48-hour mark is a reason to assume mold and act. It is not a confirmed finding that a particular home has mold, so a clean-looking wall after that point is no sign that the room is safe. Owners who wait for visible proof will act too late. The safer habit is to treat any part of the home that stayed wet past that mark as moldy. Before that point, owners should keep air moving through every damp room so it has a chance to dry in time. Some losses also have to be accepted early. Anything soaked that can be neither fixed nor dried out should go out with the debris. Keeping those things in the hope that they recover only delays the rest of the work.

When mold is measured in hours, airing out the house and clearing out what can't be saved belong at the top of the cleanup list.

In a recent development, after a flood, people head for the nearest dry, enclosed space, and that instinct is where the carbon monoxide risk begins. The American Red Cross rules out the home itself as a place to run anything that gives off carbon monoxide. Getting back inside a house is therefore not the same as being safe inside it. A garage can feel connected to the outdoors, but it is on the same prohibited list, and a wide door does not make the air in it safe to breathe. Families who move into a camper while their repairs go on face the same rule, because a camper is named too. The home, the garage and the camper are the places a displaced family is most likely to shelter, and the rule covers all three.

An open window does not solve the problem either, and setting equipment outdoors near an open window is also prohibited. People cannot judge this danger for themselves. "Carbon monoxide can’t be seen or smelled, but it can kill you fast," the American Red Cross said. A person's own body gives the main signal, and anyone who begins to feel ill, lightheaded or weak may be breathing the gas. Those complaints are ordinary enough to pass for the tiredness of a long day of cleanup. The gas can kill promptly, so those symptoms leave little time to act. The safer course is to keep this equipment out of every place on the list, including the ground just outside an open window, from the first time anyone switches it on.

In a recent development, A household can dry its walls and confirm that its tap water is safe and still not be finished with the flood. The people who lived through it may stay shaken long after the house is livable again, and that reaction is an expected result of the disaster, not a personal failing. "It's normal to have a lot of bad feelings, stress, or anxiety," the American Red Cross mentioned. Anyone who feels that way is not overreacting and has no reason to wait until the strain gets worse before dealing with it. Disaster stress has its own dedicated source of help, the Disaster Distress Helpline, so reaching out is a standard part of flood care rather than a last resort. The helpline is free, which means repair bills that already stretch a household's budget are no reason to put off a call.

Industry observers note that recovery from stress starts with ordinary care of the body. Eating healthy food and getting enough sleep both help a person cope, and those basics deserve the same priority as drying out rooms or replacing spoiled food. They should not get only the time left over once the house is handled. The helpline number, 1-800-985-5990, belongs in a phone now, before the strain arrives, so that reaching out later takes a single step.

A flood isn't over for a household until the people in it have recovered too.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 17, 2026 at 3:48 pm.

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Sources indicate that guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”.

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability and explored in an associated website, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

Sources indicate that the researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Recent findings suggest that nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

In a recent development, the study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

Recent findings suggest that all three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for fresh clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its owners that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange stated in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its owners that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance claims scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the tech giant.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

It has been revealed that binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto users to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Consumers should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

Recent findings suggest that no one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly.

Sources indicate that when you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

In a recent development, even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”.

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit.

It has been revealed that oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A major change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas.

When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out:.

Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Sources indicate that if you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:.

To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more.

For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

Recent findings suggest that the price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that alex Macedo knew how to get people talking about Burger King. At 34, when he became president of its U.S. business, he had to learn what it took for franchisees to deliver on the promises his marketing made. Today, Macedo is the co-founder and CEO of Authentic Restaurant Brands.

According to recent reports, macedo had worked in consumer goods, including beer, and had some success in marketing at other businesses backed by the private equity group that bought Burger King. He joined the chain as head of marketing. He was appointed president shortly afterward.

Industry observers note that “I was the perfect candidate,” Macedo jokes. He’d never worked in restaurants, in franchising or in the U.S. He remembers franchisees being nervous about his appointment.

In a recent development, as head of marketing, Macedo had benched the King mascot to help the chain appeal to more people, including older customers and women. “The King is a polarizing character,” he says. As president, he brought him back for a handful of appearances, including a walkout with Floyd Mayweather and a visit to the Kentucky Derby.

In a recent development, A push to rebrand the chain also involved launching several menu items at once. The team gave them funky names and expected massive things. “And they didn’t work,” Macedo says.

Industry observers note that three fresh items were manageable in a test kitchen. Across a franchise system, each operator had to train crews to make all three while keeping orders moving. A nine-minute drive-thru wait could spoil a meal before a customer took a bite.

“When I started working at restaurants, the product is everything,” Macedo notes.

He learned to judge upcoming ideas by whether franchisees could carry them out and make money doing it. That meant putting more emphasis on what brought customers to Burger King in the first place, including the Whopper, and on how swiftly and consistently crews could serve it.

In a recent development, “We had five fantastic years,” Macedo notes. He recalls franchisee profitability rising and Burger King going from closing restaurants to opening latest ones.

By the time he left Burger King, some of the same franchisees who’d wondered how a marketing executive would lead their restaurants were inviting him to stay in their homes. He’d learned the business from the people he’d been hired to lead.

Macedo looks for the kind of restaurant people swear by. It’s the place they keep going back to, the one where they feel so welcome it’s “like it’s your second home.” At Authentic Restaurant Brands, that feeling is part of what makes a regional chain worth buying.

Recent findings suggest that “They are loved, right?” Macedo indicates. “Their Google scores are the highest, their engagement scores are the highest, their reviews are the highest, their NPS is the highest.”.

Industry observers note that he also looks for strong sales and margins. A restaurant can mean a lot to its regulars and still be a difficult business to run. Macedo wants to see both kinds of evidence: that people care about the place and that enough of them come back to sustain it.

According to recent reports, tavern in the Square, a casual dining chain, was already doing about $7.5 million in sales per restaurant when Authentic Restaurant Brands bought it, Macedo indicates. It had reached that volume without a loyalty program. His team brought in a provider it uses across the portfolio, and Tavern got its own program. The operators liked the point-of-sale system they already had, so they kept it. By the time of the interview, Macedo says, sales had risen to about $8.6 million per restaurant, and the four newest locations were tracking above $10.5 million each.

The same thinking extends to the food. Authentic Restaurant Brands can buy insurance together, but chicken purchasing is left to the individual chains. Each has its own specifications, and Macedo doesn’t want a bulk discount tempting anyone to change them. He indicates he’d “prefer to serve better food the way that people have always done.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Macedo, part of buying a restaurant people love is knowing which decisions to leave with the team that earned that loyalty. A upcoming rewards program can give regulars another reason to come back. When they do, they’re still coming back for the place they knew.

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Industry observers note that menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a firm’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company stated.

Recent findings suggest that it works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the tech giant said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

According to recent reports, “Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”.

Recent findings suggest that noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Recent findings suggest that guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

In a recent development, choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

It has been revealed that noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

These 10 IPO first-day pops and flops, from VA Linux and Netscape to Facebook and Peloton, show how far a first trading day can move from the IPO price.

An initial public offering has two prices that matter on day one. The first is the IPO price, which the firm and its underwriting banks set shortly before trading begins. The second is the closing price at the end of the first session. That close comes after a full day in which public investors could trade the shares freely for the first time. The distance between those two numbers is what traders call a pop or a flop.

A large pop looks like a win, and for investors who received shares at the IPO price, it is. For the manufacturer, it can mean something else. Every share sold below what the market proved willing to pay is money the company did not collect. A flop sends the opposite signal. The price was set higher than public demand could support on the first day.

Industry observers note that this list of IPO first-day pops and flops gathers 10 stock market debuts that show both outcomes. It is a selection, not a complete ranking. Every percentage is rounded and measured the same way, from the IPO price to the first-day close. Opening trades and intraday highs are left aside. Each debut is judged on that single measure.

The first six slides cover gains, ordered from the largest percentage move to the smallest within this group. They run from VA Linux Systems, whose December 1999 debut opens the list, to Netscape, which went public in August 1995. Between them sit The Globe.com, Beyond Meat, Airbnb $ABNB and Snowflake $SNOW.

The last four slides cover debuts that disappointed. Facebook $META comes first, because its shares closed almost exactly at the $38 IPO price in May 2012. That was a flat result rather than a loss. It still fell short of the expectations that surrounded the offering. Uber $UBER, Robinhood and Peloton follow, and each closed its first session below its IPO price.

Sources indicate that the dates cluster in two periods. Three of the gains came between 1995 and 1999, during the run-up in internet stocks. Six of the remaining seven debuts took place between 2019 and 2021, with Facebook's 2012 offering the exception. Each slide stands on its own figures: the IPO price, the first-day close and the percent move between them.

VA Linux Systems priced its IPO at $30 a share on December 9, 1999, and closed its first day of trading at $239.25. That rise of about 698% is widely cited as the largest first-day gain for a U.S. IPO.

In dollar terms, each share added $209.25 in a single session. An investor who received stock at the offer price held shares worth nearly eight times their cost by the closing bell.

Industry observers note that the organization did not create Linux. It built and sold computer hardware, chiefly servers and workstations, configured to run the Linux operating system. Linux is open-source software, meaning its code is free to use, copy and modify.

Recent findings suggest that finnish programmer Linus Torvalds released the first Linux kernel in 1991. By the late 1990s, the system had become a common choice for running web servers. VA Linux sold machines built for that kind of work.

Industry observers note that VA Linux was not the first Linux-focused firm to go public that year. Red Hat, which distributed a commercial version of the Linux software, held its IPO in August 1999. VA Linux offered public investors a hardware route into the same open-source trend four months later.

The Globe.com priced its initial public offering at $9 a share on November 13, 1998. The stock closed its first trading day at $63.50, a gain of about 606% over that offering price.

According to recent reports, that close left each share $54.50 above the price set for the offering. Put another way, the stock ended its first session worth a little more than seven times its IPO price.

Sources indicate that the organization began on a college campus. Stephan Paternot and Todd Krizelman founded the site while they were students at Cornell University in Ithaca, Fresh York.

Recent findings suggest that the Globe.com was an online community. Members could build personal home pages, talk in chat rooms and post on message boards. Much of what appeared on the site came from its own consumers. That model was an early version of what later became known as social networking.

Sources indicate that airbnb $ABNB priced its IPO at $68 a share on December 10, 2020, and the stock closed its first trading day at $144.71. That was a gain of about 113%, more than double the offering price.

It has been revealed that the $68 price came after Airbnb raised its target range for the offering. The shares listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker ABNB.

According to recent reports, airbnb went public during the COVID-19 pandemic, at a time when travel demand had collapsed. Border closures, lockdowns and quarantine rules cut into the short-term stays at the center of its business.

Netscape Communications priced its shares at $28 on August 9, 1995, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. That close left the stock about 108% above its offering price.

Sources indicate that the $28 price was a revision. The company had first planned to sell shares at $14, then doubled the price before the stock began trading. Netscape listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker NSCP.

It has been revealed that netscape made Navigator, a web browser. Navigator gave ordinary computer customers a point-and-click way to view pages on the World Wide Web. In 1995, it was the product most people linked to the company's name.

Marc Andreessen was a co-founder. Before Netscape, he co-wrote Mosaic, an early graphical browser built at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois. His co-founder was Jim Clark, who had earlier founded Silicon Graphics.

According to recent reports, uber $UBER Technologies priced its IPO at $45 a share on May 10, 2019, and closed its first trading day at $41.57. That left the stock down about 7.6% from its offering price.

The gap worked out to $3.43 a share. An investor who bought at the IPO price and held through the close had a paper loss on each share.

The offering raised about $8.1 billion. The shares trade on the Newly introduced York Stock Exchange under the ticker UBER.

Sources indicate that garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick founded Uber in San Francisco in 2009. It began as a service for booking black cars through a smartphone app. It later added lower-cost ride-hailing, food delivery through.

Recent findings suggest that peloton priced its IPO at $29 a share on September 26, 2019, and closed its first day of trading at $25.76. That put the stock down about 11% from its offering price in its Nasdaq $NDAQ debut.

Industry observers note that the shares finished the session $3.24 below the price set for the offering. Investors who bought at $29 ended the day holding stock worth less than they paid.

According to recent reports, on Wall Street, a debut that closes under its offering price is known as a broken IPO. Peloton's listing fit that description at the end of its first session.

It has been revealed that the tech giant traded under the ticker PTON. Its business combined two things: connected exercise bikes and subscription classes streamed to those machines. That mix made Peloton part equipment maker and part media company.

The company traced its roots to VA Research, which Larry Augustin co-founded in 1993 while a graduate student at Stanford University. The business adopted the VA Linux Systems name before going public.

VA Linux listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker LNUX. Nasdaq was the main listing venue for technology and internet companies of the era.

The debut came near the height of dot-com enthusiasm. The offering priced about three months before the Nasdaq Composite index reached its peak in March 2000.

The company later moved away from the hardware business that defined its IPO. It became VA Software in 2001 and SourceForge in 2007, taking the second name from the software development website it operated.

The business sold no physical product and no packaged software. What it offered advertisers and investors was an audience, gathered in one place by the content its members made themselves. Like many websites of that period, it earned revenue by selling advertising on the pages those members visited.

Recent findings suggest that the 606% move is the second-largest percentage gain among the six pops in this selection. Only VA Linux Systems, which listed a little more than a year later, closed its first day further above its IPO price. Netscape, the oldest debut in the group, gained about 108% in August 1995. Netscape sold browser software, and its first-day move was a fraction of The Globe.com's.

Industry observers note that the listing came in late 1998. That was more than a year before the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite index reached its dot-com peak in March 2000. The Globe.com debut arrived while investor appetite for internet shares was still building toward that high point. In that market, a site whose main asset was user traffic closed its first day far above the price its own offering had set.

In a recent development, beyond Meat priced its initial public offering at $25 a share on May 2, 2019, above its marketed range, and the stock closed its first trading day at $65.75. That was a gain of about 163% over the IPO price.

Industry observers note that the plant-based meat maker listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker BYND. An investor who received shares at the offering price held a $40.75 per-share gain by the close.

In a recent development, the manufacturer and its underwriters had marketed the offering to investors at a lower range. Setting the final price above it showed that orders exceeded what the original range had assumed. The first-day climb meant buyers who missed an allocation paid well above even that higher price in the open market.

It has been revealed that beyond Meat makes meat substitutes from plant ingredients rather than animal protein. Its best-known product is the Beyond Burger, a patty made mainly from pea protein and designed to cook and look like ground beef. The company sold it in the meat case of grocery stores, alongside conventional beef, rather than in a separate vegetarian aisle. It also sold plant-based links under the Beyond Sausage name.

In a recent development, restaurant chains had added the product before the listing. Carl's Jr. began offering a burger made with a Beyond Meat patty in early 2019.

Ethan Brown founded the company in 2009, and it was based in El Segundo, California. Its private backers before the IPO included Bill Gates and Leonardo DiCaprio. Tyson Foods, one of the largest U.S. meat processors, had also invested and then sold its stake before the offering.

It has been revealed that at the time of the debut, Beyond Meat's best-known rival, Impossible Foods, was privately held. Public stock investors could not buy shares in Impossible Foods directly.

Both companies were pushing into fast food that spring. In April 2019, Burger King began testing the Impossible Whopper in St. Louis, built on an Impossible Foods patty. Plant-based burgers from both companies were on mainstream chain menus in the weeks before the BYND shares began trading.

Sources indicate that the company made cuts of its own that year. In May 2020, co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky announced that Airbnb would lay off about 1,900 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff. In the same message, Chesky said Airbnb expected its 2020 revenue to come in at less than half of its 2019 total.

The listing plan predated the crisis. Airbnb stated in September 2019 that it expected to become a public tech giant in 2020. It filed its registration statement publicly with the Securities and Exchange Commission in November 2020, weeks before the shares began trading.

Airbnb was founded in San Francisco in 2008 by Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia and Nathan Blecharczyk. The idea began in 2007, when Chesky and Gebbia rented air mattresses in their apartment to visitors in town for a design conference. The early name, AirBed & Breakfast, came from that setup. The startup went through the Y Combinator accelerator in early 2009.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer runs an online marketplace rather than a hotel chain. Hosts list homes, apartments and private rooms, and guests book them through the platform. Airbnb earns revenue from service fees on those bookings. It does not own the properties listed on its site.

Airbnb's debut came one day after another large consumer-tech listing. DoorDash, the food delivery firm, began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on December 9, 2020.

Recent findings suggest that snowflake $SNOW priced its IPO at $120 a share on September 16, 2020, and closed its first trading day at $253.93. That was a gain of about 112%, or $133.93 per share above the offering price.

Industry observers note that the offering raised about $3.4 billion. At the time, that made it the largest software IPO. The shares listed on the Fresh York Stock Exchange under the ticker SNOW.

Snowflake sells a cloud-based data platform. Companies use it to store large volumes of business data and to run queries and analysis on that data. The service runs on the major public clouds, including Amazon $AMZN Web Services, Microsoft $MSFT Azure and Google $GOOGL Cloud, rather than on hardware Snowflake owns.

That setup also puts Snowflake in competition with its hosts. Amazon, Microsoft and Google each sell their own data warehouse services, such as Amazon Redshift and Google BigQuery.

A core part of Snowflake's design separates data storage from computing power. Customers can scale each one up or down on its own. Snowflake charges largely by consumption. Customers pay for the computing they use instead of buying a fixed software license.

The tech giant was founded in 2012 by Benoit Dageville, Thierry Cruanes and Marcin Żukowski. Dageville and Cruanes had previously worked at Oracle $ORCL, the database company. Frank Slootman was chief executive at the time of the listing. He had earlier run Data Domain, a data storage company, and ServiceNow $NOW, a maker of IT workflow software. Both of those companies went public while he was in charge, Data Domain in 2007 and ServiceNow in 2012.

In a recent development, two outside investors were tied to the offering. Berkshire Hathaway $BRK.B, the conglomerate run by Warren Buffett, bought shares in a private placement at the IPO price. That meant Berkshire paid $120 a share, the same price set for the public offering, rather than the first-day closing price.

Berkshire seldom invests in newly public companies, and its purchase drew wide attention for that reason. Salesforce $CRM, the customer relationship management software tech giant, also invested in Snowflake.

Netscape was founded in 1994 under the name Mosaic Communications Corp. It took the Netscape name later that year after a dispute with the University of Illinois over the Mosaic name. The company was based in Mountain View, California.

Netscape had not turned a profit when it went public. Investors were buying into a young organization whose value rested on the growth of web use rather than on earnings.

The Netscape IPO is often cited as the start of the dot-com boom.

Microsoft $MSFT released the first version of Internet Explorer later in August 1995. The rivalry between Navigator and Internet Explorer became known as the browser wars. In 1998, the U.S. Justice Department filed an antitrust case against Microsoft. The case focused in part on how Microsoft bundled Internet Explorer with Windows.

Industry observers note that netscape released Navigator's source code in 1998, and that project became Mozilla. The Mozilla project later produced the Firefox browser. America Online agreed to buy Netscape in November 1998. The deal closed in 1999, ending Netscape's run as an independent public company.

Sources indicate that facebook $META priced its IPO at $38 a share on May 18, 2012, and closed its first trading day at $38.23. That was a gain of about 0.6%, or 23 cents a share above the offering price.

Industry observers note that the offering raised about $16 billion. At $38 a share, the social network carried a valuation of roughly $104 billion. Morgan Stanley $MS led the group of banks that underwrote the deal.

Mark Zuckerberg started Facebook in 2004 with several of his Harvard classmates. The company filed for its IPO in February 2012. It went public eight years after its founding. Its shares listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker FB.

Zuckerberg rang Nasdaq's opening bell from Facebook's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, rather than from the exchange in Upcoming York. The ceremony went ahead on schedule. The trading did not.

In a recent development, trading in Facebook shares had been scheduled to begin at 11 a.m. Eastern time. Technical problems at Nasdaq delayed the start by about half an hour. The same problems left some brokers and investors waiting to learn whether their orders had been filled, and at what price.

The episode drew a regulatory response. In May 2013, the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Nasdaq over its handling of the Facebook offering. The exchange agreed to pay a $10 million penalty to settle the charges.

According to recent reports, buyers who received shares at $38 did not lose money on the first day. The debut is still described as a flop because the shares delivered almost none of the first-day gain that investors had expected.

It has been revealed that for Facebook, the flat close meant it sold its shares at close to the price public buyers were willing to pay that day. For investors who bought at the offering price, it meant almost no immediate return.

The company has since changed its name. Facebook's parent became Meta Platforms in October 2021. Its stock ticker switched from FB to META in 2022.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer stayed private for about a decade before listing. In that time it raised money through a long run of private funding rounds. Its backers included the venture firm Benchmark, Japan's SoftBank and Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Many early investors had bought shares years before the listing. The IPO gave them a public market in which those shares could eventually be sold. Public buyers on May 10 came in at a price set after years of private fundraising.

Leadership had changed before the listing. Kalanick resigned as chief executive in 2017. Dara Khosrowshahi, who had run Expedia $EXPE, became CEO that year and led Uber through the IPO.

In a recent development, ride-hailing already had a public reference point. Lyft $LYFT, Uber's main U.S. rival, went public on Nasdaq $NDAQ in March 2019, weeks before Uber. Uber's own debut gave investors a second listed ride-hailing stock to weigh.

Industry observers note that drivers also drew attention to the offering. On May 8, 2019, two days before the IPO, drivers in several U.S. cities and other countries staged protests over pay and working conditions.

Sources indicate that robinhood Markets priced its IPO at $38 a share on July 29, 2021, and closed its first trading day at $34.82. That left the stock down about 8.4% from its offering price.

Sources indicate that each share finished $3.18 below where it started. Robinhood had marketed the deal to investors in a range of $38 to $42 a share. The final price landed at the bottom of that range.

Robinhood listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ under the ticker HOOD. The company runs a brokerage app built around commission-free trading of stocks, options and cryptocurrency. Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt co-founded the company, which is based in Menlo Park, California.

In a recent development, the offering departed from a common IPO practice. Most latest shares in a typical deal go to institutional investors such as mutual funds and hedge funds. Robinhood set aside part of its offering for its own retail customers. They could request shares through the app before trading began.

Recent findings suggest that that structure matched the organization's pitch to small investors. It also meant that some of the buyers at the offering price were individual owners of the app. Those who bought at $38 and held through the close ended the session with a paper loss.

Sources indicate that the listing came about six months after the January 2021 surge in GameStop $GME and other meme stocks. During that episode, Robinhood temporarily restricted purchases of several heavily traded stocks. The move drew complaints from owners. Tenev testified about it before the House Financial Services Committee on February 18, 2021.

Recent findings suggest that robinhood's revenue model also faced scrutiny before the IPO. Much of its income came from payment for order flow. Under that arrangement, market makers pay a broker to route its customers' trades to them. In December 2020, Robinhood agreed to pay $65 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges. The charges centered on how Robinhood had described those payments to customers.

Each bike carried a touchscreen that played instructor-led cycling sessions. Riders could join a class live or choose from a library of recorded workouts. An on-screen leaderboard let riders see how their output compared with others in the same class.

Owners paid a monthly fee for access to that class library, on top of the upfront cost of the equipment. The fee gave Peloton recurring revenue alongside its hardware sales.

According to recent reports, john Foley, a former Barnes & Noble executive, co-founded Peloton in 2012. The company was based in New York City and filmed many of its classes in its own studios there. Before it had a product on the market, Peloton raised early money for its first bike through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign in 2013.

By the time of the IPO, the product line reached beyond cycling to a treadmill called the Tread. It used the same streamed-class format as the bike.

Industry observers note that peloton also sold a digital membership through its app for people who did not own its equipment. App users could stream classes such as strength training, yoga and meditation on phones and other devices.

5 Things to Consider Before Leaving Your Career to Start a Business

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For many professionals, the idea of starting a business begins with a simple question: What if I worked for myself?

Perhaps you’ve spent years building someone else’s business, reached a point where career advancement feels limited or simply want more control over your professional future. Whatever the motivation, entrepreneurship can be an exciting next chapter. But enthusiasm alone isn’t enough to build a sustainable business.

Before handing in your resignation, consider these five factors that can help you make a more informed transition.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest misconceptions about entrepreneurship is that you need an entirely upcoming set of skills to start a business. Many of the abilities you’ve developed throughout your career may translate directly into business ownership.

Even if your previous career has little connection to the industry you’re considering, these transferable skills can provide a meaningful foundation.

The key is recognizing what you already bring to the table — and identifying where additional training or experience may be needed.

Not every business requires a storefront, employees, inventory or a large upfront investment. Today’s entrepreneurs can choose from a variety of business models, including consulting, professional services, online businesses and relationship-driven industries.

Before committing to an opportunity, ask yourself:.

It’s also vital to distinguish between owning a business and simply creating another demanding job for yourself.

A business model that looks attractive on paper may not be the right fit for your personality, financial situation or long-term goals.

Starting a business involves more than calculating the initial investment.

There may be expenses for training, technology, marketing, insurance, professional services and everyday operations. Some businesses also require ongoing spending before they begin generating consistent revenue. Equally vital is understanding your personal financial obligations.

Consider creating a realistic budget that accounts for:.

According to recent reports, don’t assume that revenue will arrive immediately or consistently. A thoughtful financial plan can help you make decisions based on realistic expectations rather than unnecessary pressure.

Entrepreneurs often focus on what they need to know. But who they know — and the relationships they develop — can be equally important.

Depending on the industry, relationships with suppliers, professional advisers, referral partners, customers and other business owners can create opportunities that would be difficult to develop independently.

Industry observers note that strong business relationships aren’t built simply by collecting contacts. They require trust, reliability, communication and a willingness to provide value.

According to recent reports, as you explore a new business, consider which professional relationships you’ll need and how you’ll begin developing them. You may also benefit from experienced mentors who understand the challenges of operating in your chosen industry.

While mentorship doesn’t eliminate the difficulties of entrepreneurship, it can provide perspective when you’re facing unfamiliar decisions.

One of the most overlooked aspects of starting a business is customer acquisition.

It’s easy to become absorbed in choosing a company name, designing a logo, creating a website or setting up an office. Those activities may be necessary, but none guarantees that customers will find you.

Before launching, think carefully about how you intend to generate business.

Marketing should be part of your business strategy from the beginning, not something you figure out after opening your doors.

A clear strategy for reaching potential customers can help you prioritize your time, spending and daily activities.

Leaving an established career to start a business is a significant decision, and there’s no single path that works for everyone.

It has been revealed that some entrepreneurs transition gradually while maintaining their current employment. Others decide to make a complete career change after carefully evaluating their financial position and business opportunity.

Neither approach guarantees success. What matters is understanding the responsibilities of business ownership, choosing an opportunity that fits your circumstances and developing a realistic blueprint for moving forward.

Entrepreneurship isn’t simply about leaving a job. It’s about taking responsibility for building something of your own. And the more thoughtfully you prepare for that transition, the better equipped you’ll be to navigate the challenges and opportunities ahead.

Before handing in your resignation, consider these five factors that can help you make a more informed transition.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm.

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the organization declared Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

It has been revealed that fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

In a recent development, guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the firm mentioned. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the firm states other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon noted in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”.

According to recent reports, breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The firm went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Recent findings suggest that fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The organization has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Recent findings suggest that fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the tech giant in February.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ACryptoS lost about $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains after a missing input check let attackers mint most of a vault's shares with a tiny deposit. Five exploiter addresses have been published.A vault is supposed to hand out shares in proportion to what you put in. ACryptoS's vaults handed out most of the pool for the price of one small token deposit, because a function never checked how many amounts it had been given.

Recent findings suggest that ACryptoS, a DeFi yield aggregator, disclosed on November 9 that its vaults had been exploited for roughly $665,000 across 77 vaults on five chains. In its announcement on X, the project blamed a lack of input validation that let an attacker mint the majority of a vault's shares by depositing only a minimal amount of tokens.

Industry observers note that it then disabled deposits, left withdrawals open, said it can no longer maintain the project and offered the attacker a 10% bounty in exchange for returning the funds.The most specific technical account comes from SlowMist's hack database. It traces the bug to the `depositMulti` function, where the length of the amounts array was never verified against the number of tokens. An attacker could deposit a tiny amount of a single token, receive the vast majority of vault shares and then withdraw a proportional share of both tokens. SlowMist lists the affected chains as Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.

Multi-token vaults, like those behind liquidity-pair strategies, take deposits in more than one asset. A function such as `depositMulti` receives a list of amounts, one for each token the vault holds. The contract then values that bundle against the pool and problems shares accordingly.The safeguard is basic: the number of amounts supplied must equal the number of tokens in the vault. When the two don't match, the contract is working from incomplete or mismatched input, and its valuation logic can behave in ways its authors never intended. According to SlowMist, that check was absent.How ordinary this flaw is deserves a mention. It isn't an oracle trick or a flash-loan puzzle. It's a missing `require` statement on a public function, exactly the kind of slip that audits and fuzzing exist to catch.

A simplified illustration indicates how the numbers work. ACryptoS's published analysis doesn't include the exact contract code, so what follows describes the mechanics of this class of bug, not a line-by-line reconstruction.In a healthy vault, shares are minted in proportion to the deposit's share of the pool. Suppose a vault holds $10,000 in assets and has issued 10,000 shares. A $1 deposit should mint about 1 share, or 0.01% of the supply, and redeeming those shares returns about $1.Now let mismatched inputs throw off the mint calculation. The ratio of deposit to pool collapses or inverts, and the contract might credit the attacker with 90,000 new shares for that $1. The attacker then holds 90,000 of 100,000 shares, or 90% of the supply. Because withdrawals pay out pro rata, redeeming those shares returns about 90% of each token in the pool, roughly $9,000, for a $1 deposit.The reported total fits that scale. Spread across 77 vaults, $665,000 averages about $8,600 per vault, which points to relatively small pools drained repeatedly rather than a few large ones. It also explains why the attack could be repeated mechanically: each vault offered the same function and carried the same flaw.

According to recent reports, yield aggregators usually deploy vaults from a shared template, and each vault's strategy contract inherits the same logic. As a result, one unchecked function in that template turns into one exploit multiplied by every deployment. Seventy-seven vaults on five chains is what that multiplication looks like.The setup also keeps the cost of attack low. Once the flaw is understood, a script can walk through every vault on every chain, call the same function and withdraw. On top of that, ACryptoS notes the stolen funds have been moved through several cross-chain protocols, a pattern that complicates recovery.

ACryptoS has asked exchanges and bridges to flag five exploiter addresses in a follow-up post on X:.

The request targets exit points. With the stolen funds hopping across chains, the places where they are most likely to be cashed out or bridged are the ones best placed to slow the attacker down. These are EVM addresses and the exploit spanned five networks, so anyone investigating should check each address on Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Base and Optimism.The rest of the response is blunt. Deposits are disabled and withdrawals remain open, with owners urged to pull their assets promptly. ACryptoS cited an inability to keep maintaining the protocol, so further patching is unlikely. Remaining users should assume vault pools may be thin, withdraw while the function still works and revoke token approvals granted to ACryptoS contracts afterward. A 10% bounty is a common offer in situations like this, but whether the attacker responds is unknown, and users shouldn't plan around a recovery.

For developers, the lessons are narrow and testable. Every public function that takes an array should check its length against the data it is supposed to match. Share-minting should be tested against an invariant: the value of shares issued can never exceed the value deposited. The ERC-4626 standard defines how vault share accounting should behave, and fuzz tests built on its rules would likely have flagged this.Sunsetting a protocol needs a strategy as well. A deprecated vault that still holds funds and still exposes live deposit functions is an open target. Pausing deposits and migrating balances before the maintainers leave costs little compared with leaving an unmaintained contract holding user money.For owners, the story repeats a familiar warning. Small, older yield protocols with shrinking teams are the ones most likely to carry unpatched code. This incident has less to do with a clever attack than with maintenance running out before the code was safe, so the best protection is to treat vault deposits in aging projects as temporary.
