💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced international students at U.S.
  • The total looks calmer: 1,146,163 international students, down 3%.
  • At a cabinet meeting in August 2025, defending a blueprint to admit 600,000 Chinese students, Trump stated that without them, “our college system would go to hell very quickly and it wouldn’t be the top colleges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced international students at U.S. colleges fell 18% in the 2025–26 school year, to 228,123, the Institute of International Education mentioned Monday in its annual Open Doors report. The first look at this fall points to a second straight drop. In IIE’s fall 2026 snapshot of more than 800 schools, new international enrollment fell another 15%.

The total looks calmer: 1,146,163 international students, down 3%. But that count includes 335,785 graduates on Optional Practical Training, the program that lets them work in the U.S. after their degree. That group rose 14%, and it pays no tuition. Take it out and the number of international students enrolled in classes fell about 8%, by Fortune’s math. That’s about 73,000 fewer students paying tuition.

The president saw this coming. At a cabinet meeting in August 2025, defending a blueprint to admit 600,000 Chinese students, Trump stated that without them, “our college system would go to hell very quickly and it wouldn’t be the top colleges. It would be colleges that struggle on the bottom.” His base pushed back. Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene said that if keeping Chinese students out made some schools fail, “these schools should fail anyways because they are being propped up by the CCP.”.

According to recent reports, since then, his administration has moved the other way. In May 2025 the State Department paused student visa interviews, then restarted them with expanded social media vetting. A travel ban that started with 19 countries grew to 39, plus the Palestinian territory, on Jan. 1. In July, DHS finalized a rule replacing open-ended student status with a fixed four-year limit and called it the end of “foreign student visa abuse.” A federal judge in Massachusetts blocked it in September. Among schools that reported declines this fall, 88% blamed the visa application process and 70% blamed travel restrictions, according to IIE’s snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that the losses were concentrated in one corner of the campus. Graduate students fell 13% to 423,078, and master’s students fell 22%. Doctoral students rose 3%, and undergraduates slipped 0.3%. Indian graduate students, the biggest group, fell 34%.

IIE President and CEO Jason Czyz noted the data “reaffirms the enduring importance of international education to the United States.”.

Industry observers note that colleges don’t report how much tuition they lost to the drop, so here’s a rough estimate. University of North Texas President Harrison Keller has noted each admitted master’s student who didn’t enroll would have brought his school between $20,000 and $25,000. Multiply the roughly 73,000 missing students by that range and you get about $1.5 billion to $1.8 billion in lost tuition. That’s a floor. UNT is a public university, and private schools charge international students much more.

Counting everything students spend, including rent, food and health care, NAFSA estimates international students’ economic contribution fell 7% in 2025–26, to $39.9 billion. That’s about $3 billion less than the year before. NAFSA, the trade group for international educators, puts the cost of this fall’s decline at another $2.4 billion and 31,000 jobs. Its members depend on these students, and its projections rest on surveys.

The money hurts more than the headcount suggests, because these students pay more than their share. Princeton research cited by the Hechinger Report found international students made up 6% of enrollment but 12% of college revenue. They usually pay close to full price and get little aid. In IIE’s survey, 60% of institutions mentioned they recruit them partly for their “financial contributions.”.

In a recent development, for most schools, the loss is manageable. Moody’s found in 2025 that a 15% drop in international tuition would barely affect operating margins at 77% of the universities it rates. But 15% of rated universities have more than 15% international students, and some have more than 30%. Under a 20% drop, Moody’s mentioned, 15 universities could lose 2 to 8 points of operating margin. Moody’s and S&P have negative outlooks on higher education for 2026, and Fitch calls the outlook “deteriorating.” “We see revenue growing for the sector next year, but not as much as expenses,” Moody’s analyst Patrick Ronk told The Bond Buyer.

Trump’s “bottom” turned out to include Denton, Texas. UNT projected a $45 million shortfall as international enrollment fell, on top of a $32 million cut in state funding over two years, and it has eliminated 71 academic programs, the Hechinger Report found. “About 60% of UNT’s growth over the last few years has been in international graduate students,” Keller told the board in August 2025. “We’re overexposed compared to other institutions.” UNT had more than 1,300 fewer international students this fall.

The list is mostly private universities in major cities:.

Industry observers note that the public flagships aren’t immune. International enrollment fell 15.6% at Indiana this fall and 12.7% at Ohio State, Higher Ed Dive reported, and 12% at Pitt, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Sources indicate that domestic students are covering part of the gap. Syracuse, Northwestern, USC and the Fresh School all raised tuition 3% to 4% while losing international students, Hechinger found. “It leaves a really big hole in the budget, which has to get filled one way or another,” UC Santa Barbara economist Dick Startz told the outlet.

Sources indicate that college closures are speeding up too, but for a different reason. Hampshire College in Amherst, Mass., will close at the end of this semester, after enrollment fell by almost half since 2015 and it couldn’t refinance a $21 million bond. It’s one of nine colleges set to close in 2026, by The College Investor’s count. Huron Consulting Group states more than 440 of the country’s 1,700 private nonprofit four-year colleges are at risk, as the number of 18-year-olds starts to shrink.

Industry observers note that the schools that close are mostly small undergraduate colleges with few international students. The schools losing international master’s students are bigger, and they cut jobs and programs instead. Public institutions “hardly ever close,” Higher Ed Dive noted in covering a Philadelphia Fed model. Fortune reported in August that the country’s high school graduating class is projected to shrink 13% by 2041, so both squeezes are arriving at the same time.

Industry observers note that this year, the OPT boom kept the total from looking like a crisis. That’s the program the administration went after next. On Oct. 8, DHS proposed making schools pay $70,000 the first time they recommend a student for OPT and $30,000 for each recommendation after that; schools could pass those costs on to students or employers. In IIE’s survey, 95% of institutions said prospective students would look elsewhere if OPT were restricted. In the fall snapshot, OPT fell 6%, its first decline in five years. The full count for this fall comes in next November’s Open Doors report.

How to Make Clipping Work in Your Marketing Strategy

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • It has been revealed that nobody wants to sit through a two-hour keynote anymore.
  • Clipping started in streaming about three years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

It has been revealed that nobody wants to sit through a two-hour keynote anymore. I don’t, and I’m guessing you don’t either. What people will watch is the 40-second clip of the one moment that mattered. That shift in how we consume content is why clipping has become one of the most cost-efficient ways to market a brand right now. It’s also one of the most misunderstood.

Clipping started in streaming about three years ago. Music picked it up next, the way music picks up every latest marketing method first. Then TV and film distributors got into it, then direct-to-consumer brands, and now B2B companies, including some of the biggest names in fintech and enterprise software. Even so, most marketing teams I talk to still aren’t sure what it is or where it fits.

According to recent reports, most people already understand influencers and UGC creators. They use their own face and record their own content. A clipper is different. A clipper runs their own social media page on Instagram, YouTube, TikTok or X, but instead of making something from scratch, they take content that already exists, pick the moment they think will hit and cut it down into a short clip for their page. The content is already there. The clipper’s job is getting it seen.

Sources indicate that so as a brand, you hand over your long-form content. Maybe that’s an hour-long podcast episode or a conference keynote. Clippers cut it into short pieces, post them on their own accounts and get paid based on views. Right now that’s usually somewhere between $1 and $5 for every thousand views.

When you scroll social media, around 10% of what you see is an ad, and it’s labeled as an ad. The other 90% is organic content. You can run ads, but that only gets you a small slice of the time people spend on these apps. If you want the rest, you need organic content and a lot of it.

That’s where clipping comes in. Instead of deciding in a conference room which moment from that podcast will hit, you put the content in the hands of clippers, each of whom picks their own moments. You end up with hundreds of different cuts in the span of four to eight hours, and the algorithm decides what works best. That’s A/B testing at a speed no internal team can match.

It has been revealed that clipping can’t save bad content. If people don’t want to watch it, putting it in front of more of them doesn’t help.

The easiest way to figure out what good content looks like is to go see what your competitors and the brands you look up to are posting. Then mimic it and improve it.

Recent findings suggest that when you do that research, don’t trust third-party data. Don’t go on ChatGPT and ask what the top people in your industry are making content about, because then you end up making the exact same content everybody else is posting. You need first-party data. Go on YouTube, search it up and look with your own eyes. If you do it, you’re already doing what everybody else isn’t, and that’s an edge.

Recent findings suggest that people don’t purchase from brands. They purchase from people. So either you become the ambassador for your brand, or you put the right ambassadors in front of it and have them help you make the content.

Sources indicate that that’s why I tell brands not to stop doing UGC just because they started clipping. Keep doing UGC. And instead of only paying for short-form clips, pay someone in your space who has real authority to make a long-form video, maybe 10 or 15 minutes. Then feed that into your clipping campaigns too.

Recent findings suggest that keep it raw. People don’t want the perfect, super official, branded clip. They want something that looks organic and doesn’t feel like it’s trying to sell them something every second. People hate being sold to.

In a recent development, before you launch a campaign, decide what it’s for. Awareness and conversion are different campaigns. For most brands, clipping is about awareness. It gets more people hearing about you, and it’s one more touchpoint in the mix alongside your ads, your creators and your influencers.

Once you see clips working, milk them. I’ve had clients tell me they’re seeing the same clip posted too many times and they want more variation. Think about it like ads. If you’ve tested 10 different creatives and one is doing really well, do you stop it and go make more variations? No. You keep putting money behind it. With clipping, you double down by having more accounts post that same clip. That’s how you get that feeling of being everywhere, so don’t be afraid of it.

Sources indicate that not every clipping partner is the same, and the wrong one can hurt your brand. Here’s what I’d look for.

In a recent development, attention spans keep going down; everyone is competing for the same eyeballs, and CPMs on ads are only going up. Clipping won’t replace the rest of your marketing, but it’s one of the most cost-efficient ways to get your best moments in front of a lot more people. Right now, that’s an arbitrage opportunity most brands are still sleeping on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:11 am.

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it looks to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey mentioned he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”.

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Industry observers note that carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey mentioned. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”.

Industry observers note that greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

It has been revealed that radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small organization.

Humphrey stated the firm currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

In a recent development, so, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey remarked. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”.

He acknowledged that following through on the blueprint for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey noted the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the firm’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

Industry observers note that “It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”.

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace tech giant? Humphrey stated that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he mentioned. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”.

According to recent reports, nvidia’s solid third-quarter results will no doubt reassure Gulf investors that the U.S. chipmaking giant is on course to maintain a healthy growth trajectory despite the resignation of Jensen Huang.

Nvidia reported revenue of $116 billion for the three months to October, up 103% from a year ago, and above Wall Street estimates of $109 billion. It has beaten estimates in each of the last five quarters.

For the Gulf states, which are betting big on AI to help move their economies away from oil and rely on Nvidia’s advanced chips to achieve that, the organization’s future success is critical.

Sources indicate that huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has heightened political pressure to tighten export controls amid long-running concerns in the U.S. that China’s access to advanced American AI chips could undermine national security.

It is also likely to sharpen scrutiny of Nvidia’s future dealings with the Gulf as part of a broader effort to prevent China from accessing banned American technology via intermediaries.

Such concerns have previously made securing Nvidia’s advanced chips an uphill battle for regional AI champions such as PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42.

Sources indicate that in July, the U.S. Department of Commerce loosened export restrictions on the UAE so that approved government agencies and entities—including its tech champion G42—can receive advanced computing hardware, including from Nvidia, under broader license exceptions. The rule change set no caps on how many chips or other sophisticated goods can be sold to those entities.

Democratic China hawks have frequently raised the alarm over the large-scale sales of AI chips to the Gulf region, arguing they could give China backdoor access to U.S. technology. Last May, Democratic senators demanded that AI chip deals with Saudi Arabia and the UAE contain adequate guardrails to prevent the leakage of sensitive technology to China.

Both Gulf countries maintain strong commercial ties to Chinese tech entities.

It has been revealed that in September, Chinese tech giant Alibaba Cloud announced plans to ramp up its data center capacity and expand localized AI services across the UAE. Meanwhile, in Riyadh, Lenovo unveiled its first laptop made in Saudi Arabia at its sprawling 200,000-square-meter manufacturing facility, developed as part of a $2 billion partnership with Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

In its first policy response to the Nvidia scandal, on Monday the U.S. Commerce Department introduced an interim rule requiring overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in 22 embargoed countries, including China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.

With Democrats holding majorities in both chambers of Congress from January next year, increased congressional scrutiny of Gulf AI deals is likely.

More broadly, the Gulf’s exposure to the volatility in AI stock prices has been further rattled by Jensen’s resignation amid a broader sell-off in AI tech stocks over the past few months, on the back of valuation and investment bubble concerns.

While not all Gulf funds disclose their individual investments, publicly available filings suggest that Gulf sovereign wealth funds, such as Mubadala, have relatively limited direct exposure to Nvidia shares compared to the scale of their investments in other tech firms.

According to the consultancy, Global SWF, Mubadala ranks among the top institutional backers of AI worldwide.

MGX, a global AI investment fund backed by Mubadala, holds stakes and has participated in funding rounds for OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Databricks, Isomorphic Labs, and SpaceX.

Saudi’s PIF-backed AI venture HUMAIN invested $3 billion in xAI’s $20 billion Series E round in February, shortly before it merged with SpaceX.

Global SWF estimates that Mubadala’s portfolio may have declined by $17.5 billion since the onset of the AI selloff at the end of June, largely driven by a more than 50% drop in chipmaker GlobalFoundries’ share price. PIF, meanwhile, is estimated to have suffered a $5.6 billion decline in the value of its AI-related holdings, largely attributable to its stake in SpaceX.

“Indirectly and strategically, Gulf wealth funds are exposed to the current market turbulence,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me.

“MGX and other Gulf vehicles hold large stakes in AI labs, data center platforms, and other companies whose valuations depend on the AI boom—and Nvidia, of course, is central to that boom. The Gulf’s national AI strategies are built on Nvidia hardware. I think a prolonged loss of confidence in Nvidia would hit the Gulf relatively hard.”.

Sources indicate that in a research note published on Monday, London-headquartered Capital Economics warned that the ongoing shakeout in the AI sector is setting the stage for a larger downturn in the U.S. equity market over the next year.

With Nvidia considered a bellwether for the AI industry, its results should help to calm the markets and buoy investor sentiment ahead of Anthropic’s planned listing on Thursday.

You can read my piece here, which takes a closer look at what the potential fallout from the Nvidia crisis could mean for the Gulf’s AI ambitions, particularly in terms of its planned data center buildout.

Commercially, the project is backed by a hybrid of long-term power purchase agreements with California utilities and corporates.

Globally, Masdar is also pressing ahead with its ambition to reach 100-GW of portfolio capacity by the end of the decade.

According to a report released in July this year, the scaling back of incentives has led to the cancellation ​or delay of $83 billion in investment across hundreds of projects.

A strong recovery in global oil supplies helped the market return to a surplus in October, the first time since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war.

Inventories climbed by 2.3 million barrels per day (bpd) to 105.4 million bpd last month, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), as "Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand.".

The higher export rates prompted the Paris-based agency to "significantly" raise its expectations for global oil supply for the remainder of 2026, with fourth-quarter estimates now 3.3 million bpd higher.

The IEA forecasts fourth-quarter supply will average 105 million bpd, exceeding projected demand by 1.7 million bpd.

The oil market is "straightening out" and "showing tentative signs of rebalancing,” it said.

It follows seven months of disruption to global oil flows, as the ongoing war choked off shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical shipping route that normally carries around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies.

However, Capital Economics sounded a note of caution about the future path to recovery given that the EIA data also shows that the stock of commercial oil inventories in the OECD plunged by 101 million barrels between February and October.

“Rebuilding depleted oil stock inventories–which is key to allowing oil prices to trend lower–will require oil flows sustaining sizeable surpluses into 2027,” it said in a research note published on Monday.

The research firm’s working assumption is that conditions in oil and natural gas markets largely normalize by the end of 2027 and that prices and spreads fall back further.

“But there is an obvious risk that things either fail to improve, or even get worse,” it added.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.
  • Sources indicate that in reality, however, there are tradeoffs.
  • Sources indicate that fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a perfect world, we would all eat meals and snacks that are convenient, taste great and provide optimal nutrition.

Sources indicate that in reality, however, there are tradeoffs. We crave ice cream, chips and candy bars, which make carbs and fat easy to over-consume. Meeting protein goals, meanwhile, can require conscientious effort, particularly for those, like your author, who aren’t keen on eating lots of meat.

Sources indicate that fortunately, as we chronicled earlier this week, both startups and established food brands are making it simpler than ever to up protein intake. From sodas to snack bars to ice cream, it’s now possible to get a fix of this coveted macronutrient with foods and drinks more commonly associated with sugar, starch and fat.

It has been revealed that the looming question is: Do they taste good? To find out, we hit up a local Target for a selection of protein foods sold by venture-backed startups. I and a 10-year-old then subjected them to a taste test.

The verdict? Most of this stuff is indeed edible and drinkable, albeit almost never nearly as tasty as the more protein-deficient alternatives, with just one exception.

No. 1: David Vanilla Bean Frozen Dessert: Anyone who buys or consumes this particular ice cream alternative will be doing so for the nutritional content, not the taste. A single pint packs in a whopping 30 grams of protein and has just 210 calories. The texture is also on point, creamy and easy to spoon, with a distinct vanilla flavor.

That said, you can’t hide the fact that this is not a product made with your typical ice cream ingredients. Those who don’t like artificial sweeteners or the flavor and texture of whey protein will want to pass. For myself and my co-taster, however, it was a reasonably appealing eating experience. Not as good as traditional ice cream, but not bad for a high-protein food.

Made by: Medici Brands (David parent firm).

In a recent development, no. 2 SkyPop Protein Soda: The nutritional stats for SkyPop Protein Soda are also remarkable. A 12-ounce can has just 45 calories, with 10 grams of protein and a single gram of carbohydrates. It’s also properly fizzy, and makes a satisfying pop when you open the can.

It has been revealed that but what about flavor? Our local store only had the Ice Pop flavor in stock and it was, in both tasters’ view, not horrible but not something we’d plan to buy regularly. I could see consuming it when on a clear fluids diet, as is the case before some medical procedures, as it’d be one of the few available sources of protein.

Made by: SkyPop (formerly Don’t Quit).

No. 3: Khloud Protein Popcorn: Unlike many of our other featured foods, Khloud Protein Popcorn isn’t a super protein-rich offering. A serving contains 7 grams of protein and 160 calories, most of which come from carbs and fat. Still, its protein count is higher than other packaged popcorn, which typically has maybe 2 protein grams in a comparable serving.

Overall, the tasters’ conclusion, from our trial of White Cheddar Khloud, was that this is a decent snack food. The flavor of milk protein and whey protein concentrate was palpable, but not overwhelming. It’s not exactly a snack food to savor, but for something to casually munch at one’s desk or while watching a show, it served its purpose.

It has been revealed that no. 4 Mosh: In the third season of “The White Lotus”, Mosh co-founder Patrick Schwarzenegger plays a fitness and finance bro who makes a daily high-protein shake that other family members find revolting. Perhaps this was inspired by Mosh, the brain-supporting protein bar startup he introduced with his mother, Maria Shriver.

It has been revealed that the Mosh bar, which we purchased in the peanut butter cup flavor, crams 20 grams of protein, 6 grams of fiber, plus brain-supporting ingredients like creatine and lion’s mane, into a compact, shelf-stable bar. It’s an impressive feat. Yet while our brains’ may have appreciated the nutrition and supplement boost the Mosh bar provided, our taste buds decidedly did not.

I’d put Mosh in the functional food category. It’s something that you might eat if you wanted that particular nutrient mix. But it’s not something to consume for pleasure.

Sources indicate that no. 5 Cadootz Crackers: We tried two varieties of Cadootz Crackers — cheddar and sea salt — and walked away neither enthused nor repulsed.

For people interested in a gluten- and seed oil-free small snack cracker with about 5 grams of protein per serving, Cadootz rises to the occasion. It’s got a nice crunch and decent flavor.

Sources indicate that as someone who’s not particularly seeking to avoid gluten and seed oils or to get a modest protein bump from my crackers, I’ll probably pass on follow-on purchases. But for its target audience, Cadootz should serve well.

Recent findings suggest that no. 6 Frozen One: For those who thought the David frozen dessert was a marvel of protein engineering, the folks at Frozen One would like a word. Their protein ice cream has a whopping 40 grams of protein in each pint.

Industry observers note that yes, but how does it taste? Not that bad, according to our two-person tasting team. We tried both the chocolate and apple pie varieties, preferring the former. Like the David offering, Frozen One tastes like a product made with milk protein concentrate and sugar substitutes. You won’t mistake it for Ben and Jerry’s. But if the goal is to consume a steak-like quantity of protein in the form factor of a pint of ice cream, it does its job.

Recent findings suggest that no. 7 Brami Protein Pasta: We saved the best for last. That, unexpectedly, was Brami Protein Pasta, a noodle made from semolina and lupini beans that boasts about 70% more protein than standard pasta and more than double the fiber.

With about 12 grams of protein for a 200 calorie serving, Brami isn’t a dense protein source. But, with the right topping, it’s enough to transform a typically starchy noodle meal into something reasonably protein rich.

Most notably, however, Brami tastes quite good, with no discernable weird aftertaste or texture concerns. I made both standard and Brami noodles to taste the difference. For seconds, I went with the Brami.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The senior Brazilian official claimed that converting money into stablecoins could link it to money laundering, even when it was initially obtained legally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The head of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil has claimed that legitimately obtained money could be considered laundered if it’s used to purchase stablecoins.

The senior Brazilian official claimed that converting money into stablecoins could link it to money laundering, even when it was initially obtained legally.

According to a recent report, Gerson Romantini, who is the director of the foreign exchange department at the Central Bank of Brazil, allegedly made the controversial statements at a private event attended by representatives of financial companies.

Romantini claimed that funds acquired legally could be transformed once they enter the stablecoin ecosystem.

In his view, even legally obtained money could effectively be "dirtied" if used in certain stablecoin schemes, and thus be considered part of a money laundering operation.

It’s important to note that the comments attributed to Romantini do not represent an official statement that all conversions into stablecoins could be considered money laundering.

This statement comes as Brazil has already moved to tighten restrictions on how cryptocurrencies are used for international payments.

On April 30, the Central Bank of Brazil published Resolution No. 561, which took effect on Oct. 1.

The resolution limits the use of virtual assets for the settlement of international payment and transfer services, also known as eFX.

In practice, this means that payments between an eFX provider and its foreign partner must be settled through traditional foreign exchange operations or a Brazilian real account opened by nonresidents.

Crypto payments for these particular settlements are off-limits.

A practice called the "stablecoin sandwich" is particularly concerning.

The way it works is that a Brazilian fintech accepts a certain amount of reais from a customer, then uses this money to purchase stablecoins like USDT or USDC and sends the funds in crypto to an offshore company.

This tech giant, in turn, can convert these stablecoins into fiat currency to make payments or send money to families.

This allows users to make international money transfers for a lower fee and circumvent some of the infrastructure banks use.

The controversial statements have already received a response from Brazil’s crypto industry.

Sources indicate that in a statement on Nov. 14, the Brazilian Association of Tokenization and Digital Assets (ABToken) questioned the alleged classification of stablecoin transactions as money laundering.

ABToken maintains that the use of stablecoins is not necessarily illegal.

Furthermore, the association also cautioned that sweeping bans may create legal confusion and hinder legitimate business activities that use stablecoins for international payments.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Solana has officially retired its six-year-old “mainnet beta” designation, with the network’s foundation saying the rebranding highlights the significant strides made since the blockchain first launched in March 2020.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that solana has officially turned a major page in its history, dropping the long-standing ‘beta’ tag after more than six years and adopting protocol version 1.0. The milestone marks a significant step in the network’s evolution as it moves beyond its experimental phase, with ongoing efforts to improve transaction speed, finality, and overall performance. The development could also strengthen Solana’s appeal to developers and institutional players, raising fresh questions about whether SOL is poised for a new bullish chapter.

Solana has officially retired its six-year-old “mainnet beta” designation, with the network’s foundation saying the rebranding highlights the significant strides made since the blockchain first launched in March 2020.

Industry observers note that “Solana 1.0 recognizes the progress on network performance, resilience, and developer experience,” the Solana foundation wrote in a Monday statement. “That progress continues with this simplification of nomenclature.”.

According to recent reports, the foundation emphasized that Solana has operated as a fully live network since its launch, arguing that retaining the beta designation had become outdated. It noted that the label, traditionally associated with technology still in its early testing stages, no longer accurately represented a blockchain already processing transactions and hosting active applications.

According to the Solana Foundation, the reclassification requires no action from users. Existing SOL holdings, account balances, and transaction histories will remain unchanged despite the protocol’s transition to version 1.0.

The foundation also advised developers and validator operators to stick to the specific instructions accompanying software releases, stressing that the new protocol designation does not mean all network upgrades or improvements become active automatically.

Solana’s move to protocol version 1.0 comes as the network continues pursuing major infrastructure improvements, with Alpenglow and Firedancer among its most closely watched developments. Both initiatives aim to strengthen Solana’s performance, reliability, and ability to support growing on-chain activity.

The first major milestone is Alpenglow, Solana’s new consensus protocol, which went live on mainnet on October 21. The upgrade targets transaction finality of approximately 150 milliseconds, a significant improvement from the previous 12.8-second timeframe. Transaction finality refers to the moment a blockchain permanently confirms a transaction, meaning it is considered settled and cannot be reversed under normal network conditions. Faster finality could make Solana more attractive for payments, decentralized finance, and institutional applications that require near-instant transaction settlement.

Meanwhile, Firedancer brings another important improvement through an independently developed validator client built by Jump Crypto. It provides an alternative to Solana’s existing Agave client, reducing the network’s dependence on a single software implementation. This client diversity could strengthen network resilience by limiting the risk that a bug affecting one implementation disrupts the entire blockchain.

The foundation added that the rebranding establishes a unified system for tracking Solana’s updates, allowing developers, validators, and infrastructure providers to identify protocol changes consistently, regardless of the software client they use.

You Can’t Build a Culture of Innovation If You’re the Only One Making Decisions. Here’s How to Empower Your Team.

  • Industry observers note that an employee spots a problem customers keep running into.
  • Industry observers note that two weeks later, it’s still waiting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Industry observers note that an employee spots a problem customers keep running into. She proposes a small change, explains how she would test it and sends it to her manager. The manager likes the idea but wants the founder’s approval.

Industry observers note that two weeks later, it’s still waiting. At the next organization meeting, the founder asks everyone to be more innovative.

Industry observers note that this is an easy contradiction to miss when you’re running a growing business. You want people to take initiative, but you also want visibility into decisions. You hire capable employees, but keep approval processes built back when you knew every customer and reviewed every expense.

According to recent reports, eventually, people adjust. They stop bringing you ideas that take too much effort to get approved. They focus on the work they know they can finish.

In a recent development, as founder of ButterflyMX, I’ve learned that a culture of innovation depends on what happens between someone noticing an opportunity and being able to act on it. Leaders shape that experience through the decisions they delegate, the time they protect and the way they respond when an experiment disappoints.

Before launching another initiative to encourage creativity, look at the last few improvements employees suggested.

Sources indicate that what happened to them? Did anyone have the authority to move them forward? Was there time to do the work? Did the person who raised the idea ever hear why it was accepted, postponed or rejected?

Sources indicate that imagine a support team repeatedly answering the same question during customer onboarding. An employee suggests changing the instructions customers receive. The proposal moves through several departments, each with reasonable concerns. Nobody owns the final decision, so the instructions stay the same.

As companies grow, founders need to revisit processes that once worked well. An approval that took five minutes when everyone sat around the same table may now involve three meetings and a week of waiting.

In a recent development, start by tracing a few stalled ideas through the business. Look for repeated handoffs, unclear ownership and decisions that still come to you out of habit. Fixing one of those obstacles gives employees a concrete reason to bring forward the next idea.

“Use your judgment” sounds empowering. It becomes difficult to follow when employees cannot tell which decisions will trigger a second-guessing session. Useful autonomy requires specificity.

Choose a recurring decision that your team presently brings to you. Explain what they can decide independently, what boundaries apply and what circumstances require escalation. Include the reasoning behind those boundaries so people can apply them to situations you have not anticipated.

A support manager, for example, could have authority to test revised onboarding instructions with a small group of customers. The test might need to stay within existing brand guidelines, preserve required disclosures and include a way to return to the original version. Within those limits, the manager can proceed.

The level of oversight should reflect the consequences of the decision. A limited, reversible test can move quickly. A change involving customer commitments, sensitive information or significant spending deserves more review.

In a recent development, founders also have to honor the authority they delegate. If you ask employees to own a decision and then reopen it whenever you would have chosen differently, they’ll learn to check with you first.

Explain your concerns, help people improve their judgment, and allow reasonable differences in approach. Delegation only creates room for innovation when employees can rely on it.

Innovation takes time that must come from somewhere.

According to recent reports, employees need space to investigate recurring problems, talk to customers and test alternatives. If every hour is already committed, improvement work gets pushed into the margins. It becomes something people attempt after finishing everything else.

Ask a team which repetitive task consumes time without requiring much judgment. It might be manually assigning service requests, assembling a recurring report or entering the same information into multiple systems. Determine whether that work can be simplified, automated or stopped.

Recent findings suggest that consider a team that spends hours routing customer requests. Automating part of that process could give an employee time to examine why a particular request keeps appearing. That investigation might lead to clearer instructions, a product improvement or a change in how customers are onboarded.

When the team identifies an improvement to test, keep the experiment manageable. Define the problem, the proposed change, the person responsible and the evidence that will determine whether it helped. Set a review date. A test should be small enough to finish alongside the team’s other priorities.

This also requires leaders to say what can wait. When every existing commitment remains urgent, employees have little reason to believe experimentation is a real priority.

Employees pay close attention to what happens when a reasonable idea produces a disappointing result.

It has been revealed that suppose a team tests a shorter onboarding process, expecting customers to get started faster. Instead, support requests rise because customers miss information they need.

The team now has evidence about where simplification went too far. What happens next will influence whether they volunteer another idea.

A useful review examines the original hypothesis, how the test was run and what the results support. Did the team stay within the agreed boundaries? Did it notice the problem promptly? Can it explain what to retain, revise or stop?

Leaders should distinguish a disappointing result from careless execution. Ignoring agreed limits or continuing after clear warning signs requires a different response from running a thoughtful test that disproves a hypothesis.

Be equally careful about rewarding activity. A team that launches five experiments has not necessarily contributed more than a team that runs one and makes a valuable decision. Recognize clear reasoning, responsible execution and findings that other people can use.

When a test ends, share what changed, what the team learned and what happens next. That follow-through gives employees a reason to bring forward another idea, with confidence that they can act on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:20 amNovember 17, 2026 at 6:21 am.

Vayo, the Seattle-based AI travel startup introduced by Booking Holdings last month, is expanding beyond its initial focus on tracking travel aims — starting to use AI agents to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities on behalf of people in its invite-only beta.

Sources indicate that that includes bookings on Expedia, the flagship site of Booking Holdings’ biggest rival, Expedia Group. Vayo confirmed that its AI agents book there by navigating Expedia’s website, without a direct integration or partnership for those bookings.

The firm claims Vayo recommends the best option for the traveler, wherever that option is booked, not just through its parent company’s brands.

It has been revealed that vayo is led by Mike Fridgen, a longtime Seattle entrepreneur with deep roots in travel. Booking Holdings, the parent of Booking.com, Priceline, Kayak and OpenTable, said last month that it looks to invest $100 million in Vayo, depending on its progress and market conditions.

According to recent reports, companies are still working out how to handle AI agents that use their sites on behalf of customers. In September, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agent from shopping on Amazon.com, saying the agent didn’t identify itself.

When Vayo launched last month, Fridgen said it was relying on APIs and direct partnerships with travel companies, in part to avoid the risk of being blocked. Vayo notes no site has blocked its bookings so far.

How the bookings work: Vayo’s newly introduced booking features work in two ways. It can book hotels, rental cars and activities through a direct connection with sister firm Booking.com, and it has similar links to OpenTable for restaurants and SeatGeek for event tickets.

Sources indicate that for flights and other bookings, its AI agents navigate the booking websites, signing in to the traveler’s existing accounts where needed and completing the purchase. Every booking requires the traveler’s approval, the company claims.

If a site doesn’t allow AI agents, Vayo leaves that booking to the traveler.

It has been revealed that vayo uses 1Password to sign in to travelers’ accounts and, on sites other than Booking.com, Stripe’s Link agent wallet to pay, without seeing their passwords or card details, the tech giant indicates. It reports a reservation as confirmed only after the supplier confirms it.

Sources indicate that payments and pricing: Travelers pay whichever company they book with, and Vayo is not the merchant of record. The company declined to share details on commissions, saying its partner arrangements are still taking shape and won’t factor into its recommendations.

When Booking.com has the best option, Vayo users get Genius Level 3 pricing, Booking.com’s top loyalty tier, with discounts of up to 20% on select stays.

Industry observers note that the service is free to use during the invite-only beta. Responding to GeekWire’s questions, Vayo didn’t say how many people are using it or how many have completed a booking.

Who’s behind Vayo: Fridgen, the Vayo co-founder and CEO, was on the founding team of Expedia’s vacation-package business, led Alaska Airlines’ digital business and was founding head of product at airfare-prediction startup Farecast, before leading Decide.com and Madrona Venture Labs.

It has been revealed that his co-founder and CTO is Allen Chen, the former CTO of Fanatics Collectibles, who previously co-founded Seattle software startups CloudPress and DataBlade. Ian Fliflet, OfferUp’s former chief growth officer, is head of growth. Vayo had about 20 employees, all working in downtown Seattle, when it launched last month.

Next on its product roadmap, the company says it prepares to work inside the messaging apps people already use, and to let groups of travelers plan trips together.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin has published a lengthy post on EIP-8037, a change planned for the Glamsterdam upgrade. In his latest post, Buterin wrote that something like EIP-8037 is, unfortunately, the only way for Ethereum to scale safely.

According to recent reports, with the update, Ethereum will collect an additional gas fee for the creation of latest accounts. Creating a new account would cost more than five times as much gas as it does now, with new storage slots and contracts getting more expensive too.

According to Buterin, execution is easy to scale, but Ethereum's state already grows by around 110 GiB per year, and every node has to keep it.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, it will bring more pressure on existing contracts, for example, the OP Stack bridge. The bridge has a hardcoded gas limit of 40,000, and even a small increase in state gas costs would push its operation above it. Mainnet has at least 13 contracts like that, according to the security firm ChainSecurity.

It's a double-edged sword: from one standpoint, it limits the ability of spammers and scammers to fill the network with junk accounts used by illicit actors; from the other, it creates additional financial pressure.

It has been revealed that glamsterdam being postponed is another pain factor here: considering the poor state of the market and Ethereum's struggle, it's clear that any delays in major updates negatively affect the network outlook. The upcoming date is yet to be confirmed.

Vitalik Buterin has been hinting at the change in gas consumption for ages now. Back in 2024, he called multidimensional gas the hardest problem in his own post on the topic.

Setting strict limits was never a farsighted option, and developers have been told that for years. However, it's yet another question: who's actually to blame? Buterin himself admitted that this rule hasn't been written down or repeated since 2021, so newer developers simply didn't know about it.

He now suggests writing down a list of features that are likely to change, from gas mechanics to slot time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Major U.S. wealth management firm EP Wealth Advisors has revealed that it holds an investment in an XRP exchange-traded fund (ETF). This was disclosed in the company's latest 13F filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

EP Wealth Advisors, a California-based investment advisory firm with about $24.4 billion in securities holdings, has revealed that it held 18,400 shares in the Volatility Shares XRP ETF (XRPI) as of Sept. 30, 2026.

This was disclosed in the official SEC filing that the company submitted to the commission on Nov. 13. The filing indicated that the investment was valued at $147,936 at the end of the third quarter.

Sources indicate that furthermore, the filing indicated that the total portfolio value reported by EP Wealth Advisors stood at $24,380,879,896. This value comprises 1,603 items in the tech giant's 13F information table.

It's worth noting, however, that this isn't the manufacturer's total assets under management. It's the value of its reportable securities holdings. There are also assets that are not included in Form 13F.

Industry observers note that interestingly, this isn't the first time EP Wealth Advisors has held an investment in XRPI. Data from its historical 13F filings shows that in the second quarter of 2026, the wealth management company held 13,425 shares in XRPI.

Recent findings suggest that the recent filing highlights that the company has now increased the number of shares it holds in the XRP ETF by 4,975 shares. This represents about a 37% increase in the company's XRPI holdings during the third quarter.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, this amount is very small relative to the company's multibillion-dollar securities portfolio. It represents less than 0.01% of the total value of its reported securities holdings.

It has been revealed that it's also worth reiterating that Form 13F is simply a filing that shows institutional holdings at the end of a quarter. It doesn't necessarily represent the investment manager's current holdings.

In a recent development, the Volatility Shares XRP ETF was debuted in May 2025. Its ticker symbol is XRPI, and it is currently trading on Nasdaq.

XRPI isn't a spot XRP ETF. This means it doesn't directly hold the cryptocurrency XRP. Rather, it primarily derives its exposure to XRP's price movements through XRP futures contracts.

This ETF essentially provides investors with a way to invest in XRP without actually having to hold or custody the cryptocurrency. The ETF aims to deliver investment returns that correlate with the performance of XRP.

As of Nov. 13, the most recent available data from the fund issuer indicates that XRPI's net assets stood at about $77.9 million.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been a licensed therapist in private practice for almost 15 years. In 2020, I started doing executive psychology coaching, and I changed my content on LinkedIn to reflect that.

In a recent development, my first major paying coaching gig didn’t come from someone I reached out to. Someone saw my content on LinkedIn and asked if I would like to interview and potentially coach their CEO. I ended up coaching that CEO for a few years.

That client found me because I was visible. But almost everything that’s come since then came from something most leaders skip on LinkedIn: reaching out.

Industry observers note that I kind of fell into executive coaching. The more I worked with leaders and high achievers on their own inner world, the more their businesses grew. So I didn’t keep posting about my therapy practice. I started posting about the psychology of leadership — things like mental health in leadership, communication, interpersonal relationships, emotional intelligence and the neuroscience behind all of it.

I wanted to help leaders understand their brain and what’s working and not working around their success. There are a lot of executive coaches out there — there aren’t a lot of executive psychology coaches. So I wrote from that angle.

I was posting about three times a week, and it took maybe nine to 12 months before anything came of it. That’s a long time to keep posting when nothing is coming back. If you’re just starting, expect that. Keep doing the work anyway, and post about what you want to be known for. But posting is only half of it.

In my work, I talk a lot about how we don’t have problems; we have patterns. One I see over and over in high achievers is “it’s just easier if I do it myself.” On LinkedIn, that pattern looks like posting and logging off. You share your thoughts, you check the likes and you move on. You don’t send the message. You don’t ask for the introduction. You don’t let anyone help you.

Posting feels safe because you’re in control of it. Reaching out means someone might not answer. For a lot of high achievers, that’s harder than it sounds.

Sources indicate that I’ve had people I became friends with on LinkedIn for about 10 years. Some of them I’ve met in person now. Some of them I’ve done speaking events with. We make introductions for each other, and those introductions have led to bigger opportunities.

Sources indicate that one of my significant LinkedIn connections helped me with my TEDx talk. Another one had me on their podcast. We became friends, and going on that show grew my following significantly.

Then a producer saw me on LinkedIn and reached out about being part of a reality docuseries. I said yes, and during production, I met some amazing entrepreneurs who are still good friends of mine. Some of those connections later introduced me to writing for Entrepreneur.

I have close to 30,000 followers on Instagram. But I’ve gotten more business from LinkedIn than from any other social media platform I’ve ever been on, because of the professional relationships built there. One relationship led to another, and then another.

Recent findings suggest that start by seeing who’s already looking at you. For me, that’s the most useful part of LinkedIn Premium Business: the analytics. I can see everyone who’s viewed my profile for up to a year — not just the last few people — which turns quiet interest into leads I would have missed otherwise.

If you run a service business, Premium Business also showcases your services and what clients say about you, right on your profile, so people see why to trust you before you ever reach out.

Put the two together, and your outreach is never cold. Whether someone checked out your profile or commented on your post, go see who they are. Send a message, even if you’re not connected yet. Then get on a call. You can also add a custom button that links to your calendar, so it’s easy for people to book that first conversation.

And when a conversation goes well, don’t let it end there. There’s one person I’ve stayed in touch with for the last 10 years. We have a 30-minute call once a month. If we have to skip one, we move the calendar invite instead of canceling, so we never lose that point of contact.

If you’ve connected with someone on LinkedIn and enjoyed the conversation, put something on the calendar. Then keep it there.

Industry observers note that that CEO found me because I kept showing up. But the business I have today was built by the people I reached out to after that.

If you’re ready to do more than post and log off, LinkedIn’s latest Small Business Playbook shares practical ways to grow your network and turn connections into customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make your next conversation easier to start.

Industry observers note that relationships are what build businesses, and LinkedIn does a very good job of that if you put in the effort and think about it that way. It’s a group of professionals who are all trying to build their businesses. You’d be surprised how many people actually want to help you. And you want to help them.

PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
  • “I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch.
  • The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.

“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”.

The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.

In a recent development, the solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.

More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.

“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”.

That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.

Recent findings suggest that “An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”.

For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.

“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines stated. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”.

According to recent reports, still, while AI has claimed key solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.

Sources indicate that “At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines noted. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.

“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”.

As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this fresh world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.

“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, stated. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the fresh pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”.

It has been revealed that “We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who noted the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 17, 2026 at 7:30 am.

Zonar, the Seattle-based fleet tracking organization, has a latest CEO: Rob Consoli, a longtime tech sales executive who joined the company as chief revenue officer in January.

Consoli is based in Atlanta, but he told GeekWire that Seattle remains Zonar’s headquarters and he has “no looks to change that.” He mentioned he visits the organization’s office in downtown Seattle’s Exchange Building about twice a month.

In a recent development, consoli succeeds Charles Kriete, who led GPS Trackit when the Florida-based firm acquired Zonar from German auto supplier Continental in late 2024. Kriete ran the combined company, which is backed by private equity firm Inverness Graham, until September and is now a board advisor.

Sources indicate that consoli previously held revenue chief roles at legal software manufacturer Assembly Software, Skuid and Liaison Technologies, which OpenText acquired for $310 million in 2018. He also led North American sales at asset-tracking company I.D. Systems, and started his career as an aerospace engineer at General Dynamics.

Zonar sells GPS tracking hardware, cameras and software that fleet operators use to monitor vehicle location, fuel use and driver behavior, and says it has more than 400,000 active units installed.

Its biggest market is student transportation. Consoli stated Zonar serves about half of the school bus market, and its customers also include trucking and delivery fleets such as US Foods, utilities and small businesses.

According to recent reports, zonar’s Seattle-area customers include the Kirkland Police Department, which in 2024 became the first agency to roll out Zonar’s mobile inspection app and GPS asset trackers in its patrol fleet after a pilot program. Officers use the app to complete a digital inspection of their patrol car before each shift, checking tire pressure, emergency equipment such as defibrillators and the rear enclosure used to transport suspects. Each inspection takes two to four minutes, according to the company.

Zonar has 409 employees after combining with GPS Trackit, including 70 in Seattle, more than in any other state. Consoli declined to share revenue figures but remarked Zonar has “more than doubled our profitability in the last 10 months,” helped by newly introduced pricing, a reorganized sales team, renegotiated hardware contracts and cost cuts.

Recent findings suggest that zonar has added 1,000 new customers so far this year, a spokesperson said. Sales to existing customers are running at 118% of the company’s 2026 initiative, while new customer wins are at 97%.

“We’re a very attractive asset in this market right now,” Consoli noted.

Zonar competes with larger players including Samsara, Motive and Geotab. Consoli said Zonar sets itself apart through customer service and flexibility. It offers Zonar One, a turnkey system that customers can install the day after ordering, and Zonar Flex, which is customized for large enterprise fleets.

He said those customers are “not going to get that level of tailoring and customization from any of the big players.”.

Consoli also wants to lean further into AI. The goal is to send customers proactive alerts instead of making fleet managers dig through dashboards after the fact: a driver running stop signs, a truck off its route, or a school bus running late. Zonar already lets school districts notify parents through an app when a bus is delayed.

“Fleet operators today are really focused on outcomes,” Consoli mentioned. “They want to know that compliance is handled, safety is improved.”.

In a recent development, founded in Seattle in 2001, Zonar was majority-owned by Continental from 2016 until the 2024 sale. The company cut 57 jobs in August 2024, when it had more than 300 employees, and made more layoffs after the acquisition.

Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K.
  • Two models just posted the same score.
  • Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

Two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

Nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

Behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis states Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

Industry observers note that the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a newly introduced Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

Industry observers note that the model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab notes it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card highlights 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

Sources indicate that the two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

According to recent reports, output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each latest token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Recent findings suggest that nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

Artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

According to recent reports, the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

It has been revealed that this release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

Anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

It has been revealed that three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

Ripple CTO emeritus David Schwartz has replied to XRP holders who criticized him for selling most of his XRP with a Saturday Night Live GIF of Natalie Portman saying, "I never noted I was a role model.".

According to Schwartz, his XRP holdings are down 88%, from a peak of roughly 26 million tokens to 3 million. His Bitcoin went from about 1,500 coins to one, and his Ether went from about 40,000 to six.

Schwartz wrote that he "really doesn't like risk." According to Schwartz, he and his wife agreed years ago to sell some of their coins every time crypto reached a upcoming all-time high. In 2025, Schwartz sold around 2.5 million XRP and paid about $1.7 million in capital gains tax on the sale. He had received these tokens in 2020 and 2023.
