Schwartz mentioned that all of his sales were made under written trading plans, and a lawyer approved each strategy at least 30 days before each sale. According to Schwartz, his largest risk asset is still his stake in Ripple.

Sources indicate that schwartz also said that he was a skeptic from the start and did not believe in the early price records of crypto. "When XRP hit 10 cents, that seemed ridiculous. When ETH hit $1, that seemed ridiculous," he wrote.

In his view, the price of XRP today depends on overall sentiment in the crypto market, and fees on the network barely move it. Schwartz allows that the token could capture some of the value of a successful ecosystem in the future, but there are no guarantees. On Monday, the price of XRP stands at $0.956.

On Nov. 16, Schwartz also posted a review of the XRPL codebase by the Qwen AI model. "I asked Qwen to rate my work on the XRPL software. It was mostly good. But this was harsh and it's not wrong," he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that according to the review, the overall architecture of XRPL is good. Still, Qwen stated that some components of the code are too tightly coupled, and the migration to a new testing framework stopped halfway. The AI model also called the code generation in XRPL opaque.

It has been revealed that several XRPL developers replied to the post and noted that they are already rewriting some of these parts of the code. Other users asked for formal verification of the XRPL core before the new features planned for 2027 go live.

Want VC Funding? Here Are 6 Ways to Stand Out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • I’ve seen founders with brilliant ideas struggle to get a single investor meeting.
  • From an investor’s perspective, originality and market potential matter, but they’re rarely enough to justify an investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’ve seen founders with brilliant ideas struggle to get a single investor meeting. I’ve also seen entrepreneurs with unimpressive pitch decks attract serious investment interest.

From an investor’s perspective, originality and market potential matter, but they’re rarely enough to justify an investment. What matters more is the founder, the team they’ve assembled and whether they can turn their vision into a successful business.

Recent findings suggest that as an entrepreneur and angel investor, I’ve reviewed countless opportunities. Some came with compelling presentations and enormous market projections. Others came from less polished founders with limited resources but a better understanding of how to build a sustainable business.

The second group frequently interests me more.

Founders need to ask themselves a simple question: Why should an investor believe I’m capable of building the business I’m describing?

Here are six ways to improve your chances of getting funded.

Venture capitalists aren’t buying your product. They’re investing in the potential return relative to the risk they’re taking.

Your experience, financial performance, customer traction and business model all influence that decision. The more uncertainty surrounding those factors, the harder it becomes to justify an investment.

Consider Airbnb. Its founders struggled to convince investors that people would pay to stay in strangers’ homes. With limited resources, they began selling politically themed cereal boxes to generate enough money to keep the business alive.

Their resourcefulness eventually helped persuade Y Combinator to accept them, despite skepticism about the business concept.

Industry observers note that the lesson isn’t that investors should overlook risk. It’s that a founder’s ability to solve problems under difficult circumstances can be as notable as the original idea.

Understand the risks investors see in your business and address them before asking for capital. You can’t eliminate every uncertainty, but you can give investors fewer reasons to say no.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest mistakes founders make is confusing market opportunity with market demand. A billion-dollar market doesn’t automatically mean you’ve built something customers want. Investors need evidence that customers will pay for your solution.

Mailchimp offers an interesting example. Its founders initially operated a web design business before recognizing that smaller customers needed a simpler way to manage email marketing.

Rather than immediately pursuing venture capital, they developed the product around actual customer needs and grew the business through revenue. In 2021, Intuit acquired Mailchimp in a transaction valued at approximately $12 billion.

Industry observers note that the lesson isn’t that every founder should avoid venture capital. It’s that customer demand provides stronger evidence of a business opportunity than projections alone.

When reviewing investments, I pay close attention to customer retention, repeat purchases, revenue growth and customer acquisition costs.

A founder who demonstrates that customers repeatedly pay for a solution has a stronger argument than one relying entirely on estimates of future market share.

Founders frequently believe securing the highest possible valuation is a victory. Sometimes it’s the beginning of their problems.

Industry observers note that consider a startup that raises $5 million at a $50 million valuation despite limited revenue. Eighteen months later, sales have doubled, but financial performance still doesn’t justify a higher valuation.

Sources indicate that now the founder needs more capital, and latest investors aren’t willing to pay what previous investors paid. The company is growing, yet fundraising has become harder.

Industry observers note that weWork provides a cautionary example. The firm reached a reported valuation of $47 billion before its attempted public offering collapsed in 2019. Concerns about financial performance, governance and its business model undermined investor confidence. WeWork eventually filed for bankruptcy protection in 2023.

Its problems extended beyond valuation, but the experience illustrates how quickly investor enthusiasm can reverse.

I’d rather see a founder raise sufficient capital at a defensible valuation than celebrate an inflated number that makes the next round unnecessarily difficult.

Sources indicate that A high valuation tells you what investors will pay today. It doesn’t guarantee your business will be worth more tomorrow.

According to recent reports, investors don’t expect founders to know everything. They expect them to recognize what they don’t know.

Sources indicate that canva co-founder Melanie Perkins offers a useful example. Before building the design platform into a global business, Perkins faced more than 100 investor rejections. Her early presentations focused heavily on technical capabilities. She eventually recognized that investors needed to understand the problem before appreciating the solution.

By explaining the frustrations people experienced with complicated design software, she made the opportunity easier to understand. That willingness to recognize what wasn’t working and change her approach helped her communicate the tech giant’s potential.

Building a strong team requires similar judgment. Founders must understand which skills they lack, what to delegate and what still requires their direct involvement.

I’d rather back a founder who recognizes a weakness and has a credible proposal to address it than one who claims to have everything figured out.

It has been revealed that fundraising isn’t simply a numbers game. Venture funds have specific investment mandates, preferred industries, funding stages, check sizes and return expectations. A company can be attractive and still be completely wrong for a particular investor.

It has been revealed that canva’s fundraising experience demonstrates this challenge. Despite repeated rejections, the founders eventually attracted investors who recognized the potential of simplifying design for a much broader audience.

Before approaching an investor, research their portfolio. Have they funded companies in your industry? Does your business fit their investment strategy? Are they comfortable investing at your current stage?

A targeted introduction explaining why your company fits their interests is more effective than sending hundreds of generic emails.

Industry observers note that keep your pitch concise. Explain the problem, who pays for your solution, what you’ve accomplished and how additional capital will accelerate growth.

Give investors a reason to ask the next question.

It has been revealed that the most compelling companies often aren’t the ones desperately seeking capital. They’re the ones making progress regardless of whether their next funding round happens.

Sources indicate that mailchimp’s history demonstrates that building a valuable business doesn’t necessarily require venture capital. Its founders focused on customers, revenue and product development rather than making fundraising the central measure of success.

Not every business can follow that path. Some companies require substantial upfront capital to develop technology, build infrastructure or enter competitive markets. But investors still want evidence that founders can allocate resources effectively and execute against measurable objectives.

When I meet a founder who understands their customers, knows their financials, has assembled a capable team and can explain exactly how additional capital will accelerate growth, the conversation changes.

Sources indicate that I’m no longer being asked to finance an untested ambition. I’m being invited to participate in a business that’s already demonstrating its potential.

Sources indicate that the best way to get a venture capitalist’s attention isn’t to convince them that you need their money. It’s to demonstrate what you’re capable of building with or without it.

Sources indicate that I’ve seen founders with brilliant ideas struggle to get a single investor meeting. I’ve also seen entrepreneurs with unimpressive pitch decks attract serious investment interest.

In a recent development, from an investor’s perspective, originality and market potential matter, but they’re rarely enough to justify an investment. What matters more is the founder, the team they’ve assembled and whether they can turn their vision into a successful business.

As an entrepreneur and angel investor, I’ve reviewed countless opportunities. Some came with compelling presentations and enormous market projections. Others came from less polished founders with limited resources but a better understanding of how to build a sustainable business.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, openAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson.
  • According to recent reports, terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire.
  • It has been revealed that an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson indicates in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel.

According to recent reports, terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters proposal millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down.

It has been revealed that an OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.”.

However the AI lab has not announced latest travel-specific products or intends. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses.

According to recent reports, openAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot consumers frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson remarked.

Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later stated in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025.

When a key partnership with Marriott fell through, the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with over $600 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values.

So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store with travel now that he’s joined the organization.

Note: This story was updated with OpenAI’s comments and updated revenue for Sonder.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:34 amNovember 17, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Glenn Kelman famously told “60 Minutes” in 2007, “Real estate, by far, is the most screwed up industry in America.” It looks like health care is next on his list.

The former Redfin CEO has co-founded Sojourn, a Seattle startup that aims to give working people “better healthcare at a lower cost,” according to its website.

“Since technology by itself can’t fix a broken system, we’re rebuilding the whole system to make it work for you — combining a software firm, a group of doctors and nurses, and an insurance company,” reads the introductory message on the site.

Industry observers note that his co-founder is Dr. Connie Chen, an internist who co-founded digital health company Vida Health and spent more than seven years at mental health benefits company Lyra Health, first as chief medical officer and then as chief operating officer, as Lyra grew to a $5.6 billion valuation.

This is not a modest app for booking doctor’s appointments. Under the corporate name Silica Health Inc., the company filed a trademark application last month covering health maintenance organization services — HMOs are health aims that pair insurance coverage with their own networks of doctors — along with insurance administration, medical billing and claims management.

In a recent development, kelman, who is rarely at a loss for words, confirmed in response to our inquiry that he wasn’t ready to talk yet. He wrote in a GeekWire guest column this month that he and his business partner would announce their looks “after we’ve built our product.”.

Industry observers note that but after he posted about his team on LinkedIn last week, we got curious and couldn’t help but look around. Their resumes were a tip-off: In addition to Chen, the team includes an engineer who spent nearly seven years at tech-driven health insurer Oscar Health.

Industry observers note that searching Kelman’s name in state business licenses turned up Silica Health, with Kelman and Chen listed as officers. Plugging that name into the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office’s database produced exactly one result: the application for “Sojourn Health.”.

From there, it was a short trip to sojournhealth.com, which sketches out the proposal.

Why health care: Kelman spent 20 years running Redfin, which stood out in the real estate industry for employing its agents rather than treating them as independent contractors. That turns out to be part of the origin story.

In a recent development, “Almost every year after its IPO, Redfin had to re-consider whether to keep employing its own agents, because of their rising healthcare costs,” Sojourn’s founders page explains. The options were to make agents contractors, ask employees to pay more, or cover less care.

“The choices were all terrible,” it states.

Chen’s bio on the site describes a career spent on one problem: how employers can give their employees better care at lower cost.

As a primary-care doctor, she saw her patients’ health and finances rise and fall together, the site states, and concluded that “a system taped together from broken parts couldn’t serve either.”.

Kelman, by his own account, is upcoming to the field. In his guest column, he wrote that when he thought about the companies he would have been proud to start, they were all in one particular industry. He didn’t say which one, but it’s not hard to guess now.

“I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing,” he wrote.

The team: In a LinkedIn post last week, Kelman stated the founding team also includes Jennifer Chao and Ben Baker, with Sasha Aickin “adding some part-time magic.” He promised that “the mission is good and the ambition is vast.”.

The lineup draws on Kelman’s past and the health insurance world:.

Chao and Aickin both worked with Kelman at Plumtree Software, the enterprise software manufacturer he co-founded in 1996, before following him to Redfin. Sojourn’s recruiting page nods to the pattern: “We’re honored by the old friends who have worked with us from company to company, but we’re also eager to bring in latest blood.”.

The Sojourn site indicates the company is likely to have engineering hubs in Seattle for the member experience, San Francisco for the clinical platform, and Austin for the claims system.

AI all the way down: Sojourn is hiring software engineers and product managers “at every level of the organization.” The first thing on its list of qualifications: experience using frontier AI tools “to generate reliable, high-scale production code.”.

It has been revealed that that fits with his guest column. A recruiter told him Seattle’s startup scene was “dead,” he wrote, and a friend described CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at companies with old code. Kelman wrote that “the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.”.

What we don’t know: The website doesn’t say when Sojourn intends to launch or where it will offer coverage first, although Chen’s bio suggests employers will be key customers, describing a care model “designed around the member and the employer who pays for it.”.

A new health initiative typically requires state insurance licenses and significant capital reserves, and the company hasn’t disclosed any funding. Kelman wrote in his column that he “met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea,” but he didn’t name them, and a search of SEC filings for Sojourn Health and Silica Health found no record of a fundraise.

In June, he joined venture firm Greylock as an executive in residence, saying at the time that he was still looking to start a fresh mission-driven enterprise, a process that involved “exploring ideas that are never going to work and howling at the moon.” It’s not clear whether Greylock is among his backers.

Recent findings suggest that kelman stepped down as Redfin CEO in January, six months after Rocket Companies completed its $1.75 billion acquisition of the Seattle brokerage. He noted at the time that he wanted to find “another mission-driven enterprise outside of real estate.”.

He appears to have found one. Whether health care is more or less screwed up than real estate is a question that will have to wait until he’s ready to chat.

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.

According to recent reports, with co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the manufacturer and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

In a recent development, the largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.).

The firm also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

According to recent reports, of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the tech giant’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity highlights how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

Sources indicate that the venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI tech giant Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The manufacturer or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under newly introduced leadership.

Eligible participants can apply through Binance Wallet using USDC, with a minimum subscription of 100 USDC. Sources indicate that the ANT IPO campaign uses an allocation system based on Binance Alpha Points. Users with more than zero Alpha Points receive a subscription quota of $20,000. Higher balances unlock substantially larger limits. Users holding more than 40 points qualify for $100,000, while those exceeding 100 points receive $200,000.

Recent findings suggest that the highest tier requires more than 200 Alpha Points and unlocks a $500,000 subscription quota. Binance also offers an additional $50,000 quota to eligible people holding its Trenchers Badge.

In a recent development, these figures are the maximum subscription limits, not guaranteed allocations. The campaign uses an oversubscription model, meaning successful applicants could receive full or partial allocations.

Participants must commit USDC through a non-custodial smart contract. Unused funds will return to their Binance Wallet after allocation calculations finish. The subscription also carries a 5% partner service fee charged by xStocks. Binance Wallet does not charge an additional participation fee.

Binance has set an indicative subscription price between $70 and $78 per token. This matches Anthropic’s proposed IPO pricing range in its registration filing. Anthropic aims to offer 825 million Class A shares under the proposed listing. The organization has applied to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

At the upper end of its proposed price range, the offering implies a valuation of approximately $1.41 trillion. At $70 per share, the implied valuation falls to $1.26 trillion.

The final offering price will depend on demand, valuation conditions, and arrangements between the issuer and underwriters.

Industry observers note that staking adds another incentive, with rewards offered at 35% APY. That gives early holders an opportunity to accumulate additional HYPER while the project prepares its token launch.

Industry observers note that bitcoin Hyper is building a Bitcoin Layer 2 using Solana Virtual Machine technology. The goal is to combine Bitcoin’s liquidity with Solana-style transaction speed, opening the door to faster BTC transfers, decentralized applications, and on-chain finance.

Early data points to Vulcan’s first stage in launch failure that cost Amazon 40 Leo satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:52 am.
  • Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA stated Tuesday.
  • In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 17, 2026 at 8:52 am.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA stated Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

In a recent development, that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

Industry observers note that the Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA stated. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

ULA said Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based organization hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and Latest Glenn for our return to flight.”.

It has been revealed that impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Recent findings suggest that amazon also has 24 introduces reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

According to recent reports, before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has noted it intends to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K.
  • Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips.
  • However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated.

Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.

However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.

Sources indicate that as a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source.

Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity.

This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.

In a LinkedIn post, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the newly introduced funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe.

In a recent development, with the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital, Atomico and Index Ventures, which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years.

Industry observers note that “Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi, a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.”.

Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy. In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica, whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co., which develops space transportation.

Sources indicate that in robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental, which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics, which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub, which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics, which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum, which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute.

Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, stated Tamkivi.

Sources indicate that “Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the major labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he remarked.

The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022.

Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder of Wise, and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport, both early employees at Skype, as well as Ian Hogarth, co-founder of Songkick, and Khaled Helioui, former CEO of Bigpoint.

The team has two other partners: Carina Namih, co-founder of HelixNano, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty, a former Uber executive.

Each partner aims to make one to three upcoming investments per year, leaving  bandwidth to work hands-on with founders.

The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and  double down and triple down,” Tamkivi mentioned, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

XRP Ledger Foundation Director of Community Hussein Zangana (Vet) shared a tidbit of XRPL's early history in a recent X post.

Vet noted that the XRP Ledger (XRPL) still carries traces of Satoshi Nakamoto’s original Bitcoin design, highlighting two features.

In 2011, three engineers—David Schwartz, Jed McCaleb, and Arthur Britto—began developing the XRP Ledger (XRPL). Fascinated by Bitcoin, they set out to create a better version that improved upon its limitations—with the goal of creating a digital asset that was more sustainable and built specifically for payments.

As reported, the first line of code for the core of what would become the XRP Ledger (XRPL) was written by David Schwartz, who is Ripple CTO emeritus, about 15 years ago, on November 11, 2011.

Vet delves into the earliest part of XRP Ledger history, noting that 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Bitcoin's pseudonymous creator, Satoshi Nakamoto, wrote. Vet added that Jed McCaleb also copied Satoshi’s timekeeping code into the XRPL, even including one of the Bitcoin creator’s comments shared as a screenshot.

Industry observers note that did you know all of us on the XRP Ledger use design choices by Satoshi daily? 15 years ago, the XRP Ledger started out using some Bitcoin code, including helper functions from the Bitcoin client that Satoshi wrote. Jed copied Satoshi's timekeeping code into the XRPL, including one of Satoshi's comments. By the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone. In December 2014, Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment. Two design choices of Satoshi still remain on the XRPL and all of us use at least one of it. Signature curve secp256k1 (we also support Ed25519 thus not everyone uses this) and how XRPL addresses are generated from the public key with SHA-256 followed by RIPEMD-160, that's what all of us use.

The quote "Never go to sea with two chronometers; take one or three" is a classic maritime adage famously included by Satoshi Nakamoto (the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin) within the Bitcoin source code.

Vet explained that by the end of 2014, the original Satoshi code was gone from the XRP Ledger. In December 2014, former Ripple engineering lead Nik Bougalis removed the last of the timekeeping code, along with Satoshi's comment.

Recent findings suggest that however, two of Satoshi's design choices still remain on the XRP Ledger: the first is the secp256k1 signature curve, which Bitcoin uses and which the XRP Ledger continues to support. However, the ledger also supports Ed25519, meaning not every XRPL user relies on secp256k1.

"I remember David saying they used secp256k1 so no one would doubt the security because it's the same as Bitcoin's, etc.," Vet stated, citing the insight of the Ripple CTO emeritus on secp256k1, adding, "Lots of interesting things to dig into from the early days.".

According to recent reports, the second is the method used to generate XRP Ledger addresses from public keys. The process applies SHA-256 hashing followed by RIPEMD-160, a design inherited from Bitcoin that remains common to all XRPL addresses.

Asked why the timekeeping code and Satoshi's comment were removed, Vet explained that this became leftover code as new code was introduced, so it was cleaned up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, softBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed intends for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the manufacturer and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in New York, SoftBank mentioned it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

Recent findings suggest that forty-six attorneys general have joined a New York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials announced this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the organization’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

Compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into fresh venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” notes one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

Industry observers note that the result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too promptly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any fresh relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

According to recent reports, softBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one massive reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it launched a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TechCrunch’s yearly Startup Battlefield 200 competition sees hundreds of companies from across the world trying every year to get a chance to pitch in front of VCs and the international tech community at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference.

This week, nine early-stage South Korean startups pitched at DETO 2026, a technology conference in Seoul, to earn a spot in next year’s Startup Battlefield 200.

Sources indicate that the startups work across the deep tech sector, including healthcare, fintech, energy, semiconductors, and AI. All nine startups are looking to enter the U.S. market as part of the broader international expansion plans.

Voinosis, which develops AI to detect changes in brain health through voice analysis, won the competition. The other eight startups are listed below in alphabetical order.

Recent findings suggest that voinosis is developing an AI tool that analyzes speech patterns such as pitch, pauses, rhythm, and response times to detect changes linked to brain health. Each voice check takes less than five minutes.

Industry observers note that the organization states its technology has been tested in Greek, Japanese, and English, and its product doesn’t require separate training for each language. In a clinical study involving 146 participants, the startup claims its tech achieved 88% accuracy in screening for potential cognitive complications.

Voinosis targets hospitals, senior living facilities, insurers, and individual consumers. It also plans to link voice checks with cognitive training, assessments, and treatment provided by healthcare professionals.

It has been revealed that the startup was founded by Grace Shin, who spent more than 25 years as an otologic surgeon. The startup is at the moment raising a Series A round and has already secured a South Korean pharmaceutical organization as a strategic investor.

Awesome Lab, based in Seoul, makes ThermoFlux, a heating system that uses water electrolysis and ionization to generate heat. The system can manage heat production for buildings, water supply, and industrial processes. The company says its technology can reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, for its international expansion, Awesome Lab is taking a different approach in each market. In the U.S., it prepares to supply core OEM modules and work with boiler, water heater, and HVAC companies on product development.

Crosshub helps travelers and international visitors verify their identities and set up payment methods abroad. Its platform, IDBlock, combines identity verification and payment services using self-sovereign identity (SSI) and zero-knowledge proof.

The organization notes its platform helps users prove their identity across borders without sharing unnecessary personal information. Crosshub is also integrating this technology with payment systems to improve access to financial services for travelers.

It has been revealed that deepFusion AI has developed a 4D radar-based imaging system with additional sensors for autonomous mobility, robotaxi, maritime surveillance, and defense applications. The system combines RF sensors with radar and lidar to detect objects, movement, or distance without a direct line of sight. All sensors are supposedly packed into a single, customizable unit.

According to recent reports, EFLOW develops special motors that can produce more torque, or rotational force, while taking up less space for use in robots, drones, satellites, and other mobility applications. The startup also develops actuators that control how robotic joints move.

In a recent development, otiton Medical makes two medical devices: One specializes in measuring body temperature, while another can capture ear canal images and analyze the eardrum. The organization says its AI was trained on about 55,000 images of eardrums, and the device has received medical certification in South Korea.

In a recent development, riibotics states it can deploy robots into warehouses within a day. Riibotics wants to reduce deployment costs for warehouses by streamlining setup, which includes infrastructure setup, warehouse mapping, system integration through custom middleware, task programming, and safety checks.

Ternell, a semiconductor startup based in Ulsan, is developing a newly introduced type of memory to help AI chips use less power.

It has been revealed that unlike conventional two-state memory, Ternell’s T-SRAM system adds a third state for more efficient data storage. Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips indicated a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM.

Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions.

Industry observers note that the startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella remarked the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

Sources indicate that “We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he mentioned. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

Recent findings suggest that it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

From there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

AI Is Giving Us Time Back. What Are We Doing With It?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • A few years ago, they might have messaged a colleague, walked over to someone’s desk or waited until the next team meeting.
  • Sources indicate that that question has stayed with me as I have reviewed forthcoming BambooHR research on how AI is changing the workday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

An employee has a question. A few years ago, they might have messaged a colleague, walked over to someone’s desk or waited until the next team meeting. Today, they can ask AI and have an answer in seconds.That is progress. Good technology should remove friction, reduce waiting and help people move forward. I understand the instinct. If I can get the same answer in 30 seconds without interrupting someone else, of course I am going to do that.But I wonder if the old conversation was producing more than an answer. It may have shown the employee how someone more experienced approached the problem or surfaced context that was never written down. Sometimes a small interaction becomes a relationship that matters much later. From the perspective of the task, the interaction may have looked inefficient. From the perspective of the organization, it may have been building something.

Sources indicate that that question has stayed with me as I have reviewed forthcoming BambooHR research on how AI is changing the workday. Employees estimate that they now spend nearly an hour and a half each day interacting with AI. Among the part of the day they spend in conversation rather than working alone, about 2 in 5 interactions are with AI rather than another person.

It has been revealed that there are good reasons for that. AI is fast. It is always available. It does not look busy or make you feel as though you should already know the answer. You can ask the same question three different ways without testing anyone’s patience.

Many employees say they would rather quietly ask AI than admit they need help. I get why. Asking another person carries a little social risk, and AI takes most of that away. That can make people more independent, and there is real value in that. But I wonder if we are also removing one of the simplest ways workplace relationships begin.

It has been revealed that when I ask someone for help, I am doing more than getting information. I am showing that I value their judgment. They get a little window into how I am thinking. Sometimes the relationship that follows matters more than the answer itself.

Technology leaders have spent years trying to remove unnecessary friction from work. That is usually the right goal. Poor systems, repetitive processes, pointless approvals and meetings without a purpose drain people’s time and energy. AI gives us a upcoming opportunity to remove much more of that.

Before we automate an interaction away, though, I think we have to understand what it was actually doing inside the organization.

The newly introduced research points to a meaningful difference between time spent with AI and time spent with coworkers. AI time is concentrated on completing tasks, experimenting, refining prompts and correcting output. Coworker time includes execution too, but much more of it goes toward sharing knowledge, brainstorming, mentoring and building relationships.

Those things are harder to measure because they do not always produce an immediate deliverable. Their value often shows up later, when a junior employee knows whom to call during a difficult moment or when someone has watched an experienced colleague make a judgment call where the answer was not obvious.

In a recent development, this matters especially for people early in their careers. Most employees say they have learned something valuable from a colleague at a different career stage. Many also believe cross-generational mentorship is becoming harder as younger employees rely more heavily on AI.

There is something important in that tension. We value what we learn from one another while adopting tools that let us skip some of the awkwardness, delay and vulnerability that often start the learning process.

AI can give you a good answer. It may even explain the answer better than a rushed colleague. But professional judgment is rarely just the answer. It is knowing when the technically correct answer will not work in this organization, understanding which trade-off matters most or recognizing a pattern because you have seen some version of the problem before.

A lot of that is learned by watching other people think. If employees become more self-sufficient task by task, leaders still have to ask whether the organization is becoming more capable over time.

Industry observers note that we have spent a great deal of time deciding what AI should do. We have spent less time deciding what people should be freer to do because of it.

The default answer in many organizations is more work. A task that once took an hour now takes 20 minutes, so the remaining time fills up with another task, another message or another expectation. The efficiency disappears into a fuller calendar.

My instinct is that the answer cannot simply be more output. If AI gives a manager back an hour, maybe some of that hour should go toward coaching. If it gives an experienced employee more capacity, maybe there is more room to explain how they reached a decision rather than simply sending the answer.

Sources indicate that that is work too. And I suspect it becomes more valuable as transactional work gets easier.

Some friction should disappear. Poor systems and unnecessary interruptions aren’t worth preserving simply because they create human interaction.

Sources indicate that the opportunity is to be more deliberate about what fills the capacity AI creates. Judgment, coaching, creativity and connection become more important as transactional work gets easier. So the question is where speed matters most and where another person actually changes the quality of the outcome.

Sources indicate that the employee from the beginning of this article may still be right to ask AI. The answer arrives quickly, the task moves forward and no one is interrupted.

Recent findings suggest that AI is going to make it easier for us to need one another less for a lot of everyday work. The more interesting question is what we do with that freedom. Ideally, we use some of it for the things that become better when another person is actually there.

According to recent reports, tesla delivered a strong third-quarter earnings report after the bell today, posting a surprise profit and telling shareholders it’s ahead of schedule with a new factory in Shanghai. Shares rose more than 20 percent after hours. CNBC has more here.

A couple of years ago, the cofounder and CEO of a blood-testing company was publicly taken to task for implying in articles and professional profiles that he has a PhD when in reality, he’d left a prestigious graduate group three years after enrolling, without a degree.

Industry observers note that the CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

In a recent development, it happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the manufacturer’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to upgrade it).”.

Cardano DReps have rejected a proposal by Toto Finance to spend 22 million ADA from the Cardano treasury on a "Strategic Copper Reserve.".

The vote closed on Nov. 15, and DReps holding 2.86 billion ADA voted against the proposal, according to Cardano governance data. DReps with 20.02 million ADA voted in favor of it.

DRep John MacPherson was among those who voted "No," and he explained his decision in a post on X.

MacPherson wrote that he is not against real-world assets on Cardano. Still, he stated the proposal asks the treasury "to take on both the copper price and the ada price," and Toto Finance would collect "up to about 3.4M ada in fees.".

At the same time, MacPherson mentioned that the proposal is “more honest about its risks than most.”.

Toto Finance, a company led by Monty Metzger, submitted the proposal on Oct. 15. ADA is trading at $0.152 on Monday, and the requested 22 million ADA is now worth around $3.3 million.

The blueprint was to buy copper with 14.72 million ADA and store it in a warehouse near Fresh Orleans. Toto Finance wanted to issue one CuTT token for each pound of copper. The metal would be sold in 18 to 24 months.

The Cardano Foundation, which votes as a DRep, unveiled its "No" vote in October.

"We recognize the opportunity in real-world asset tokenization; however, this proposal places 22,000,000 ada under the recipient's sole control to fund a fee-heavy concentrated commodity position whose safeguards are not yet in place," the foundation wrote.

Three members of the Constitutional Committee voted "No," and the other four members did not vote.

Crypto commentator Ingeniero Cripto agreed with MacPherson in the replies under his post. He called the "double exposure" to the prices of copper and ADA the key problem of the proposal, as the Cardano treasury already holds ADA.

According to him, RWAs on Cardano make sense, but “funding the asset itself is a different question than funding the rails.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.
  • It has been revealed that chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon.
  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club unveiled Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

It has been revealed that chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a new job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club unveiled Tuesday.

Sources indicate that “His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer noted in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation company toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the firm’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

Chew stated his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

Recent findings suggest that “In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Industry observers note that chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he said. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew said.

The job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew noted.

In a recent development, chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

It has been revealed that on the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and said, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he remarked. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

He recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew stated, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew noted he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a big win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

It has been revealed that “It has to be approachable for folks,” he noted. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

The Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he stated.

Five Forged Receipts Drained $304.5K From Ankr's Ethereum Bridge Using a 0.0044 ankrETH Deposit

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit.
  • It has been revealed that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge.
  • All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

SlowMist says five forged receipts with valid signatures let an attacker drain about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum bridge using one old Optimism deposit. Here is how the check failed.Every one of the five receipts was signed by the bridge's own trusted signer. Every one pointed to a deposit that had already been paid out.

It has been revealed that on November 9, an attacker drained about $304,500 from Ankr's Ethereum cross-chain bridge. According to SlowMist's alert, the attacker built five forged receipts that all referenced a single legitimate Optimism transaction, changing the recipient, the token and the withdrawal amount in each one.

All five carried valid signatures from the bridge's trusted consensus signer.

According to recent reports, the reused transaction was tiny: a deposit of about 0.0044 ankrETH made on Optimism on November 3, which SlowMist's analysis says had already been redeemed on Ethereum the same day. Six days later, that one settled deposit was cited five times. The incident is recorded in the SlowMist Hacked database.Blockaid flagged the exploit as it unfolded, at about 08:42 UTC, with roughly $292,000 already gone. SlowMist followed at 09:14 UTC with the higher $304,500 estimate and an explanation of the forged receipts. Ankr paused withdrawals, and no recovery proposal has been confirmed.

The design is common across lock-and-release bridges. A user deposits on the source chain, and an off-chain set of signers watches for that deposit and signs a receipt describing it. The destination contract, in this case Ankr's Ethereum bridge contract, checks that the receipt carries a valid signature and then releases the funds.That setup makes the signers the source of truth. The contract can't see Optimism, so it leans on the signature to prove the deposit happened. The weak point sits in the gap between "the signer signed this" and "this really happened." A contract that treats the first as proof of the second inherits every mistake the signing process makes.

In a recent development, the Ethereum transactions show the attacker extracted about 82.91 ankrETH, 515,206 ankrPOL and 7.98 million ANKR tokens. Blockaid described the five withdraw calls as using the tiny Optimism deposit to unlock the bridge's locked inventory and send it to a new wallet.The mix of assets tells its own story. Each forged receipt named a different token and amount, which suggests the attacker picked targets based on what the bridge held. That fits receipts built entirely by the attacker, apart from the one real transaction reference. Anyone wanting to trace them can open the bridge contract's transaction list on Etherscan and filter for the five `withdraw` calls on November 9.

The most crucial fact is still missing. SlowMist claims the origin of the unauthorized signatures is under investigation, and it hasn't confirmed whether the signers were compromised.A valid signature on a forged receipt has a short list of explanations. A signing key, or the service holding it, could have been accessed. A signing service could have been tricked into signing attacker-supplied data. Or the signing logic itself could have a flaw that produces signatures for receipts it shouldn't. Each one points to a different fix: a stolen key means rotating signers, a manipulated service means tightening input validation off-chain, and a logic flaw means rewriting the signing rules.Whichever it turns out to be, the on-chain contract and the off-chain signer both failed to ask the same question. Either one verifying the source event would likely have stopped the attack, and neither did.

Sources indicate that the lessons are narrow and practical. Replay protection should key on the immutable identity of the source event, not on the receipt's contents, and a source event should be consumable exactly once. The destination contract should confirm that the receipt's recipient, token and amount match what the source-chain event actually recorded, using a proof or an independent verifier instead of trusting the signer alone.Signer infrastructure needs its own scrutiny. Threshold schemes, hardware-backed keys and strict limits on what a signing service will sign all shrink the damage from a single failure. Rate limits and per-withdrawal caps help as well. A bridge that can release its entire locked inventory in five calls has no brake once a signature check is defeated.Trust in a bridge comes in layers, and one layer rarely holds up alone. People with funds in Ankr's bridge should watch for the project's post-mortem and its plan for restoring withdrawals. For developers, the question to put to their own code is a blunt one: if a signer signs something false, what stops the contract from believing it?

Breaking: Phota Labs uses AI to turn everyday photos into professional-looking shots

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming iOS app called Phota Labs gives people access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.
  • Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.
  • The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming iOS app called Phota Labs gives people access to a personal AI photo assistant that turns everyday snapshots into images that look like they were taken by a professional photographer, all while preserving the authenticity of the image.

Rather than giving consumers yet another photo-editing tool, Phota Labs aims to use advances in AI to automate the editing process so it’s easier for anyone to get access to better photos.

The a16z-backed startup was founded by Cecilia Zhang and Zach Xia, who met at Adobe while working on computational photography products, including Project Indigo, Lightroom, and Photoshop.

The duo saw a gap in the editing tools on the market and believed that although editing tools can be powerful for enhancing photos, they aren’t very effective at fixing a photo that wasn’t captured well in the first place. Phota Labs changes that by focusing on fixing the shot itself while preserving the natural appearances of those in the image.

In a recent development, “Phota is your personal photo assistant that can make great photos for any moment you want to keep before you even ask, which means that it’s a very proactive experience,” Zhang told TechCrunch in an interview. “Think of it almost like a photographer or virtual photographer who looks over your camera roll and tries to understand what’s happening and how they could have taken that photo for you on the spot for that scene.”.

The idea is to use AI to transform photos, whether that’s turning a wide-angle group photo into a tighter portrait or transforming a selfie into a regular shot.

Owners can choose from different photography styles that determine how AI transforms their images, ranging from subtle edits that preserve the original lens and composition to more dramatic transformations that introduce effects like fish-eye lenses, alternative angles, and entirely different perspectives.

While some people turn to ChatGPT and other generative AI tools to enhance or edit images, these tools can often alter a person’s appearance, especially when working with blurry photos because they don’t know what that person actually looks like.

According to recent reports, “For Phota, we built our own tech,” Zhang noted. ”We built this personalization technology that actually learns about people’s identity and is able to preserve them in any transformation we do to a photo.”.

Images edited with Phota Labs feature invisible watermarks that identify them as altered by AI when shared on social platforms.

The startup is initially targeting people who take tons of photos and like to share them on social media, but don’t want to deal with the tedious process of editing photos. Over time, the founders envision a broader audience, from retirees looking to create beautiful photos for their grandchildren to parents who want to share polished family albums with friends and relatives.

“We have this obsession with authenticity,” Xia remarked. “I think there’s so much value in connecting AI with real moments and making sure those photos are not perfect, in a sense. That’s why we spend a lot of research into understanding personal context, into building this identity model because we want to make sure the photos are authentic. They’re just better photos of the same moment, rather than saying, ‘Oh, this is an AI image’.”.

Recent findings suggest that xia said beta people were excited to see better versions of moments they had actually lived and saw the results as photos of real memories rather than AI-generated images. The founders discovered that users were taking more photos because they knew Phota Labs could enhance them later.

“We’re turning something that’s unusable into something that people want to print,” Zhang stated. “People who just love photos but never really got into editing can now experience professional quality that could never have been possible. So, I think that meant so much to us. There’s so many cherished moments for photos, and we really want them to be actually meaningful and something that you can remember.”.

In terms of funding, the company raised a $5.6 million seed round led by a16z last year.

Sources indicate that phota Labs is launching as a free app to build an initial user base before exploring a freemium model. The startup also looks to launch an Android app in the future.
